PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper Airway:
Overview — stridor & upper airway
Causes of upper-airway obstruction in children, presenting with stridor. The skill is separating the emergency (epiglottitis) from common, benign causes.
The organising principle: acute barking cough = croup (viral); toxic child, drooling, tripod, no cough = epiglottitis (emergency — don't examine the throat); chronic stridor from birth, worse supine/feeding = laryngomalacia (usually benign).
ConditionAge / causeFeatures & management
Croup6mo–3yr, parainfluenzabarking cough, stridor, worse at night; oral dexamethasone (nebulised adrenaline if severe)
EpiglottitisHibtoxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, NO cough; secure airway + IV antibiotics
Laryngomalaciacongenitalinspiratory stridor from birth, worse supine/feeding; self-limiting by ~18–24 mo
Epiglottitis is a life-threatening emergency — keep the child calm, do not examine the throat or lie them flat; call senior anaesthetics/ENT to secure the airway. Now rare thanks to the Hib vaccine.
What & Why

Croup is an acute viral upper-airway infection causing subglottic inflammation → the classic barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor in a young child. It matters because it’s extremely common (~2–3% of children/year), and because — although usually mild and self-limiting — it sits at the top of the paediatric stridor differential, where the job is to recognise it, treat it with a single dose of steroid, and confidently exclude the dangerous mimics.

The framing that matters: croup is the common, viral, gradual-onset, barking-cough, well-ish child. The mimics are rarer but lethal: epiglottitis (toxic, drooling, no cough), inhaled foreign body (sudden, choking), bacterial tracheitis (toxic, high fever). Get the pattern right and management is easy; miss a mimic and a child dies.
The Decisive Fork — Croup or a Dangerous Mimic?
FeatureCroupEpiglottitisInhaled foreign bodyBacterial tracheitis
OnsetGradual (days, after coryza)Rapid (hours)SuddenViral illness then deteriorates
CoughBarking (“seal-like”)Absent/minimalSudden choking ± coughBarking then toxic
Voice/cryHoarseMuffled (“hot potato”)VariableHoarse
DroolingNoYes (can’t swallow)NoNo
Fever/toxicityLow-grade, looks well-ishHigh, toxic, stillAfebrileHigh, toxic

Key ruleSteroid, don’t distressDo NOT examine throatRigid bronchoscopyIV antibiotics + airway
The golden rule across all of these: keep the child calm and do NOT distress them (no throat exam, no cannulas, keep on parent’s lap) — agitation worsens airway obstruction and can precipitate complete obstruction.
Epidemiology & Cause
  • Age 6 months – 3 years (peak ~2 years); rare <6 months; autumn/early winter seasonality
  • Parainfluenza virus (types 1 & 3) is the commonest cause; also RSV, adenovirus, influenza, and increasingly SARS-CoV-2
  • Higher risk of severe croup: children with pre-existing airway narrowing (subglottic stenosis, laryngomalacia) and Down syndrome — admit even if symptoms look mild
Clinical Features
  • Barking (“seal-like”) cough — the hallmark
  • Inspiratory stridor (harsh, on breathing in) — worse when upset
  • Hoarse voice/cry; preceding coryza and low-grade fever; symptoms worse at night
  • Signs of respiratory distress in more severe cases: suprasternal/intercostal recession, tracheal tug, tachypnoea; late/danger signs = fatigue, drowsiness, cyanosis, silent chest → impending obstruction
Severity Assessment

The Westley croup score grades stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and conscious level (clinical gestalt is used in practice). Practically:

SeverityPicture
MildBarking cough, stridor only when upset, no/mild recession, happy, eating/drinking
ModerateStridor at rest, recession at rest, but not distressed/agitated
SevereStridor at rest + marked recession, agitation or lethargy, tachycardia
Impending failureFatigue, ↓ consciousness, cyanosis, silent chest, bradycardia — peri-arrest
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Steeple sign — symmetrical subglottic narrowing on AP neck X-ray (croup); imaging not routinely needed as the diagnosis is clinical
  • Diagnosis is CLINICAL
  • Do NOT perform investigations that distress the child — no bloods, no cannula, no throat exam in a child with stridor
  • Imaging is not routine; the classically-taught “steeple sign” (subglottic narrowing on AP neck X-ray) is not needed and is rarely done
Management
Guideline-verified — NICE CKS / BNFc.
All children with croup — a single dose of oral corticosteroid, regardless of severity
  • Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg — the standard
  • Alternatives: oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg, nebulised budesonide 2 mg, or IM dexamethasone
  • Steroids reduce symptoms within ~2 hours, shorten illness, and cut re-attendance
  • Mild croup: single steroid dose → manage at home; safety-net advice (return if stridor at rest, distress, drooling, colour change). No antibiotics (viral)
  • Moderate croup: steroid + observe; admit if not settling
  • Severe / impending obstruction: nebulised adrenaline (1:1000, 0.4–0.5 mL/kg, max 5 mL) — rapid but temporary relief (wears off ~2 hours → observe ≥3–4 hours for rebound) + oxygen (minimal handling) + steroid + senior/anaesthetic + ENT airway support; keep the child calm on the parent’s lap
  • Admit if: moderate–severe croup, stridor at rest not settling, respiratory distress, hypoxia, needing repeated adrenaline, poor intake, age <6 months, high-risk group (Down syndrome, pre-existing airway narrowing), or diagnostic uncertainty. Discharge once stridor-free at rest
Complications

Usually none (self-limiting over ~48 hours). Rarely: secondary bacterial tracheitis, dehydration from poor intake, and — very rarely — airway obstruction requiring intubation.

Exam Pearls
What it is
Viral (parainfluenza) subglottic inflammation; age 6 months–3 yrs; barking cough + inspiratory stridor + hoarse voice, worse at night.
Diagnosis
Clinical — no investigations; don’t distress the child.
Mimics
Epiglottitis (toxic, drooling, muffled, NO cough, Hib — don’t examine the throat), inhaled foreign body (sudden choking), bacterial tracheitis (toxic, Staph).
Treatment
Single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for ALL severities (even mild).
Severe
Nebulised adrenaline (temporary — observe ≥3–4 h for rebound) + oxygen + senior airway support.
Imaging
Steeple sign = subglottic narrowing on X-ray (not needed — clinical diagnosis).
High-risk
Down syndrome & pre-existing airway narrowing → more severe croup; low threshold to admit. Also admit if <6 months, hypoxia, repeated adrenaline.
What & Why

Epiglottitis is rapidly progressive inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures that can cause complete upper-airway obstruction within hours. It is the “can’t-miss” paediatric airway emergency — the dangerous mimic of croup — and the single most important management principle is counterintuitive: you do NOTHING that might upset the child until the airway is secured (no throat exam, no cannula, no lying flat).

The framing that matters: unlike croup (common, viral, gradual, well-ish child with a barking cough), epiglottitis is the acutely toxic, drooling, still, silent child with a rapid onset and no cough. The wrong move (a tongue depressor to “have a look”) can precipitate fatal obstruction. This is the one where you sit on your hands and call the airway team.

Epidemiology — the vaccine story: classically children aged 2–6, caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Since the Hib vaccine, it has become rare in children, and the epidemiology has shifted toward unvaccinated children and adults — now often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Strep pyogenes, and Staph aureus. Consider it in an incompletely immunised child.

The Decisive Fork — Epiglottitis or Croup?
FeatureEpiglottitisCroup
OnsetRapid (hours)Gradual (days, after coryza)
CoughAbsent / minimalBarking (“seal-like”)
VoiceMuffled (“hot potato”)Hoarse
DroolingYes (can’t swallow)No
SwallowingPainful, refuses to eat/drinkUsually able
PostureTripod / sitting forward, stillVariable
Fever/toxicityHigh, toxic, unwellLow-grade, looks well-ish
CauseHib (now Strep/Staph)Parainfluenza
StridorSoft, late (ominous)Harsh, prominent
The single golden rule: do NOT examine the throat, do NOT lie the child down, do NOT distress them (no cannula, no bloods, keep with parent). Any of these can trigger complete obstruction.
Clinical Features — the “4 D’s”
The 4 D’s
  • Dysphagia — can’t swallow
  • Drooling — saliva pools because swallowing is too painful
  • Dysphonia — muffled, “hot potato” voice (not hoarse)
  • Dyspnoea — respiratory distress

Plus: rapid onset high fever, toxic/septic appearance, severe sore throat, the tripod position (leaning forward on hands, mouth open, tongue out), minimal or absent cough, and soft inspiratory stridor (a late, ominous sign — quiet stridor here means near-obstruction). The child is anxious, still, and quiet — an eerily calm, unwell child.

Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Thumbprint sign — a swollen epiglottis on lateral neck X-ray (epiglottitis); only if airway support is present — never delay securing the airway
Diagnosis is clinical, and securing the airway comes BEFORE any investigation.
  • No throat examination, no venepuncture, no X-ray in a distressed child with suspected epiglottitis until the airway is safe
  • Definitive diagnosis: direct visualisation of a cherry-red, swollen epiglottis — but only in a controlled setting (theatre) by the airway team during intubation
  • Lateral neck X-ray (only if stable, low suspicion, airway support present): “thumbprint sign” — the swollen epiglottis resembling a thumb. Must not delay airway management
  • After the airway is secured: blood cultures, throat swabs, FBC/CRP guide antibiotics
Management
Guideline-verified — airway-first.
The steps
  • Do NOT distress the child — keep them calm on the parent’s lap, sitting upright, in their position of comfort. Give oxygen only if tolerated (parent holds it near the face)
  • Summon the airway team immediately — a “call everyone” emergency: senior anaesthetist/ENT/paediatrician + ICU (the exam answer to “first step” = call for senior airway help, don’t touch the throat)
  • Secure the airway — controlled intubation in theatre (gas induction, ENT ready for emergency tracheostomy if intubation fails)
  • THEN IV antibiotics — a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) covering Hib/Strep, once the airway is safe; step down to oral (e.g. co-amoxiclav) after improvement
  • Supportive: IV fluids, ICU monitoring. Steroids (dexamethasone) often given to reduce oedema (limited evidence)
  • Prevention: Hib vaccination is why it’s now rare; rifampicin prophylaxis for close/household contacts of a confirmed Hib case
Complications

Complete airway obstruction and death (the feared outcome), epiglottic abscess, sepsis/bacteraemia, and rarely aspiration or secondary pneumonia.

Exam Pearls
What it is
Rapid supraglottic swelling → airway obstruction; classically Hib, age 2–6.
Vaccine
The vaccine changed the epidemiology — now rare in children (think unvaccinated), rising in adults (Strep/Staph).
4 D's
Dysphagia, Drooling, Dysphonia (muffled/hot-potato), Dyspnoea + high fever, toxic, tripod position, NO cough.
Golden rule
DO NOT examine the throat, lie the child flat, cannulate, or distress them — can precipitate complete obstruction.
First step
Call the airway team (anaesthetics/ENT/ICU); secure the airway BEFORE anything else.
Imaging
X-ray (only if safe): “thumbprint sign.” Croup = “steeple sign.”
Antibiotics
AFTER airway: IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime. Prevention: Hib vaccine; rifampicin prophylaxis for Hib contacts.
vs Croup
Barking cough + hoarse + gradual + well-ish = croup; no cough + drooling + muffled + toxic + rapid = epiglottitis.
What & Why

Laryngomalacia (literally “soft larynx”) is congenital softening/immaturity of the supraglottic cartilage so that the tissues above the vocal cords collapse inward during inspiration, producing chronic inspiratory stridor in an infant. It matters because it’s the single commonest cause of stridor in infants (~60–75% of congenital stridor), because it’s the benign, chronic, “well baby” end of the stridor differential, and because the key skill is recognising the reassuring pattern and knowing the small minority of red flags.

The framing that matters: the whole topic is “noisy but thriving.” A laryngomalacia baby is otherwise well, feeding and growing, just noisy on breathing in — and it self-resolves. The job is to (1) recognise that reassuring picture, (2) not mistake it for something dangerous, and (3) spot the ~10–20% with severe features (feeding failure, distress, apnoea) who need intervention.
The Decisive Fork — Thriving or Failing?
Mild laryngomalacia (majority)Severe laryngomalacia (~10–20%)
BabyOtherwise well, feeding and growingFailure to thrive, feeding difficulty
BreathingInspiratory stridor, no distressRespiratory distress, recession, cyanosis, apnoea
ActionReassure + watchful waitingENT referral → supraglottoplasty
CourseResolves by ~18–24 monthsMay need surgery; still usually good outcome
Clinical Features
  • Inspiratory stridor — high-pitched, from congenital softening of laryngeal cartilage collapsing on inspiration
  • Positional and situational: worse when supine, feeding, crying/agitated, or with intercurrent URTI; better prone (a classic diagnostic clue)
  • Onset typically in the first 2 weeks of life, often peaks around 6 months, then improves
  • Otherwise well infant (the key reassurance)
  • Feeding-related symptoms in more significant cases: regurgitation, choking/coughing with feeds, slow feeds, difficulty coordinating suck–swallow–breathe → in severe cases poor weight gain / failure to thrive
  • Strong association with gastro-oesophageal reflux (GORD) — reflux and laryngomalacia coexist and aggravate each other
The Mechanism (why it’s “omega-shaped”)
📷 Image placeholder — Omega-shaped epiglottis with short aryepiglottic folds on flexible nasolaryngoscopy — the dynamic supraglottic collapse of laryngomalacia

The supraglottic structures are floppy/immature, with a combination of an omega-shaped (curled) epiglottis, short (tight) aryepiglottic folds, and redundant arytenoid mucosa that prolapse into the airway on inspiration. This is what the ENT surgeon sees and targets.

Investigations
  • Diagnosis is often clinical in a well, thriving infant with classic positional stridor
  • Gold standard = flexible (awake) nasolaryngoscopy — visualises the dynamic supraglottic collapse and the omega epiglottis. Indicated if diagnosis unclear, severe, or atypical
  • Consider looking for a second (synchronous) airway lesion if features are severe or don’t fit — bronchoscopy if needed
  • Airway fluoroscopy is not recommended (low yield, radiation)
Management
  • Mild/most cases → conservative: reassure parents, watchful waiting. Self-resolves before ~2 years. Feeding support and upright/positional feeding help
  • Treat coexisting GORD (positioning, feed thickening, anti-reflux medication) — can meaningfully reduce symptoms
  • Surgery (supraglottoplasty) — division of tight aryepiglottic folds ± trimming redundant mucosa — for the ~10–20% with severe stridor + respiratory distress, failure to thrive from poor feeding, significant apnoea/hypoxia, or pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale from chronic obstruction. High success rate (~90%+)
  • Tracheostomy — rarely, for severe cases not suitable for/failing supraglottoplasty
Red Flags — When Noisy Breathing Is NOT Simple Laryngomalacia
Any of these warrants ENT referral and nasolaryngoscopy.
  • Failure to thrive / poor feeding, cyanosis or apnoeic episodes, severe recession/distress
  • Biphasic stridor (inspiratory + expiratory) → suggests a glottic/subglottic lesion (vocal cord palsy, subglottic stenosis) rather than pure laryngomalacia
  • Stridor from birth that is severe/worsening, or not improving after age 2
  • Weak/abnormal cry → think vocal cord pathology
Complications

Usually none. In severe untreated cases: failure to thrive, feeding aspiration, obstructive sleep apnoea, and — from chronic hypoxia — pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale.

Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest cause of stridor in infants; congenital soft/floppy supraglottic cartilage collapsing on inspiration.
Reassuring picture
Inspiratory stridor in an otherwise WELL, thriving infant.
Positional
Worse supine / feeding / crying / URTI; better prone. Onset first 2 weeks, peaks ~6 months.
Anatomy
Omega-shaped epiglottis + short aryepiglottic folds. Strongly associated with GORD — treat the reflux.
Diagnosis
Flexible awake nasolaryngoscopy (gold standard).
Management
Reassurance + watchful waiting → self-resolves by ~18–24 months.
Surgery
Supraglottoplasty for the ~10–20% with failure to thrive, respiratory distress, apnoea, or pulmonary hypertension.
Red flags
Biphasic stridor, failure to thrive, cyanosis/apnoea, weak cry, worsening/persisting past 2 yrs → ENT + scope.
PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respiratory Infection:
Overview — lower respiratory infection & wheeze
Lower respiratory tract infections and wheeze in young children — bronchiolitis, whooping cough, and viral-induced (pre-school) wheeze.
The organising principle: age + pattern. Bronchiolitis <1yr (RSV: coryza → cough/wheeze/feeding difficulty); pertussis = paroxysmal cough + whoop/apnoea + post-tussive vomiting; viral-induced wheeze = episodic wheeze with viral URTIs and no interval symptoms (not asthma).
ConditionClueManagement
Bronchiolitis<1yr, RSV; coryza then wheeze/crackles, poor feedingsupportive (oxygen, feeding support); admit if severe/apnoea
Pertussisparoxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, apnoea in infants, post-tussive vomitingmacrolide; notifiable; vaccine-preventable
Pre-school / viral-induced wheezeepisodic wheeze with viral URTI, well between episodesSABA; distinguish from asthma (atopy, interval symptoms)
In bronchiolitis watch for apnoea and feeding failure in young/ex-premature infants (admit). Pertussis is notifiable and dangerous (apnoea) in unimmunised infants.
What & Why

Bronchiolitis is an acute viral lower respiratory tract infection of the small airways (bronchioles) in infants, causing inflammation, mucus, and airway obstruction → a distinctive picture of coryza → cough, wheeze/crackles, and feeding difficulty. It matters because it’s the commonest LRTI and the commonest cause of hospital admission in infants under 1 year, because RSV is the main cause and severe disease clusters in the very young/vulnerable, and because management is a key “less is more” teaching point — it’s supportive; bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics DON’T work. It’s also topical: the new RSV immunisation programmes (nirsevimab / maternal vaccine) are changing its epidemiology.

The core mechanism: a virus (usually RSV) infects and inflames the bronchiolar epithelium → oedema, mucus, and sloughed cells plug the tiny airways. Because infant airways are so small, even minor narrowing causes big obstruction → air trapping/hyperinflation, wheeze, crackles, and work of breathing → feeding difficulty and, in the youngest, apnoea.
Aetiology & Epidemiology
  • RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) — ~70–85% of cases (the classic cause); others: parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, influenza, adenovirus, rhinovirus
  • Age: under 2 years, peak ~3–6 months; winter epidemics
  • Spread by droplets/contact (very contagious)
The Decisive Fork — Bronchiolitis vs the Mimics
📷 Image placeholder — Chest signs — widespread fine crackles ± wheeze in a coryzal <1yr (bronchiolitis) vs focal consolidation on CXR with high fever >39°C (pneumonia)

NICE stresses distinguishing bronchiolitis from viral-induced wheeze/asthma and pneumonia — the age and signs differ:

BronchiolitisViral-induced wheeze / asthmaPneumonia
Age<1–2 yrsUsually >1 yrAny
SignsWidespread crackles ± wheezeWheeze (no crackles), recurrentFocal crackles, high fever
FeverLow-grade (high fever >39°C uncommon)VariableHigh/persistent
ClueFirst episode, coryzal prodromeRecurrent episodes, atopy/family historyPersistent focal signs, high fever
High fever (>39°C) or focal crackles → think PNEUMONIA. Recurrent wheeze/atopy in an older infant → think viral-induced wheeze/asthma (both unusual under 1 year).
Clinical Features
  • Coryzal prodrome (runny nose, mild fever) for 1–3 days, then:
  • Persistent cough
  • Tachypnoea, increased work of breathing — subcostal/intercostal recession, nasal flaring, head bobbing, grunting
  • Wheeze and/or fine bibasal crackles on auscultation
  • Feeding difficulty — a key marker of severity (from respiratory effort/nasal blockage)
  • Apnoea — especially in infants <6 weeks / preterm; may be the presenting feature (and life-threatening) — a crucial point
  • Signs typically peak at days 3–5, then improve; cough can linger ~3 weeks
Investigations
Bronchiolitis is a CLINICAL diagnosis — a “less is more” point (guideline-verified).
  • Do NOT routinely do blood tests or a chest X-ray (CXR can mimic pneumonia → unnecessary antibiotics)
  • Pulse oximetry — for hypoxia (guides admission)
  • Nasopharyngeal aspirate / viral PCR (RSV) — mainly for cohorting/infection control, not diagnosis
  • Capillary blood gas only if severe/impending respiratory failure; suction if apnoea/secretions
Management
Supportive care is the mainstay — most are managed at home (guideline-verified, NICE NG9).
Supportive care (the mainstay)
  • Oxygen if saturations persistently low — give supplemental O2 if SpO2 <90% in children ≥6 weeks (or <92% if <6 weeks/comorbid)
  • Fluids/feeding support — smaller/more frequent feeds; nasogastric/orogastric or IV fluids if not feeding adequately
  • Nasal suctioning if secretions/apnoea; minimal handling
  • Escalation: high-flow humidified oxygen (Optiflow)/CPAP → ventilation for respiratory failure
What does NOT work (do NOT use routinely)
  • Bronchodilators (salbutamol), nebulised adrenaline, corticosteroids, nebulised hypertonic saline, montelukast, and antibiotics
  • None are effective in bronchiolitis — a favourite exam point
  • (Antibiotics only if genuine evidence of secondary bacterial infection)
Admission — Refer to Hospital

Immediate emergency referral if: apnoea, looks seriously unwell, severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked recession, RR >70), central cyanosis, or SpO2 persistently <92% in air.

Consider referral if: RR >60, difficulty feeding / inadequate oral intake (50–75% of normal), clinical dehydration.

Lower the threshold if risk factors for severe disease: age <3 months, prematurity (especially <32 weeks), chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease.
Prevention (RSV) — a Current Development
📷 Image placeholder — UK infant RSV protection — the maternal vaccine (from 28 weeks) as the routine route vs nirsevimab reserved for high-risk/unprotected infants (replacing palivizumab)
  • Nirsevimab — a long-acting anti-RSV monoclonal antibody; a single injection lasts the RSV season and (unlike palivizumab) can protect term/late-preterm infants. In the UK the routine infant offer is the maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) from 28 weeks (since Sept 2024); nirsevimab is targeted at high-risk infants and those whose mothers were not vaccinated (replacing palivizumab); palivizumab (monthly, high-risk infants only) is being phased out
  • Maternal RSV vaccination (given in pregnancy to protect the newborn) — also part of the new UK programme
  • General: breastfeeding, hand hygiene, avoid smoke exposure
Exam Pearls
What it is
Viral LRTI of infants (<1–2 yrs, peak 3–6 months); RSV in ~70–85%; winter epidemics.
Presentation
Coryzal prodrome → cough, tachypnoea/recession, WHEEZE + fine crackles, feeding difficulty; peaks day 3–5.
Danger sign
APNOEA can be the presenting/life-threatening feature in infants <6 weeks/preterm.
Diagnosis
CLINICAL — NO routine bloods or CXR (CXR mimics pneumonia → unnecessary antibiotics).
Management
SUPPORTIVE (O2 if SpO2 <90–92%, feeding/fluid support). Bronchodilators, steroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, antibiotics DON’T work.
Admit
Apnoea, cyanosis, severe distress/RR >70, SpO2 <92%, poor feeding/dehydration; lower threshold if <3 months/preterm/CHD/CLD/immunodeficiency.
Mimics
High fever + focal crackles = pneumonia; recurrent wheeze + atopy in older infant = viral wheeze/asthma.
Prevention
NIRSEVIMAB (RSV monoclonal, single seasonal dose) + maternal RSV vaccine — new UK programmes; palivizumab being phased out.
What & Why

Pertussis is a highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterised by a prolonged paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory “whoop”. It matters because — despite being vaccine-preventable — it’s resurgent (major UK/global outbreaks from 2024), because it’s most dangerous in young infants (<6 months), in whom it causes apnoea, pneumonia, and death, and because prevention hinges on maternal vaccination in pregnancy. It’s a notifiable disease.

The core mechanism: Bordetella pertussis (a Gram-negative coccobacillus) infects the ciliated respiratory epithelium and releases toxins (pertussis toxin) that paralyse mucociliary clearance → mucus accumulates and can’t be cleared → the violent, repetitive paroxysms of coughing. The “100-day cough” reflects how long symptoms persist.
The Stages (catarrhal → paroxysmal → convalescent)
📷 Image placeholder — Pertussis timeline — catarrhal phase MOST infectious; a macrolide still reduces transmission within 21 days of cough onset; the whoop is typically ABSENT in infants (apnoea instead)

The classic triphasic course — high-yield:

StageDurationFeatures
1. Catarrhal~1–2 weeksCoryzal — indistinguishable from a cold (runny nose, mild cough, low-grade fever); MOST infectious phase
2. Paroxysmal~2–6 weeksParoxysms — bursts of coughing ending in an inspiratory “WHOOP” (forced inspiration against a closed glottis); post-tussive vomiting; worse at night; cyanosis/exhaustion; whoop often ABSENT in infants (→ apnoea instead) and in adults
3. Convalescentweeks–monthsGradual improvement; cough can linger for months, recurring with later URTIs
Clinical Features
  • Coryzal prodrome → then paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting (vomiting after a coughing fit — a useful clue)
  • Typically afebrile / low-grade (high fever suggests another/secondary infection)
  • Between coughing fits, the child often looks WELL — a characteristic feature
  • Coughing paroxysms can cause: cyanosis, subconjunctival haemorrhages, petechiae, syncope
  • Infants (<6 months) — atypical & dangerous: may have NO whoop; present with APNOEA, cyanosis, poor feeding, or a “brief resolved unexplained event” rather than the classic cough — the group to worry about
Investigations
  • B. pertussis PCR (nasopharyngeal swab/aspirate) — first-line in the early weeks (most sensitive)
  • Culture (nasopharyngeal, Bordet-Gengou/charcoal media) — specific but slower/less sensitive
  • Anti-pertussis toxin IgG serology / oral fluid testing — for patients coughing >2 weeks (when PCR/culture sensitivity falls); the mainstay of confirmation later
  • FBC: marked lymphocytosis (a classic clue, especially in infants)
  • Notify UKHSA on clinical suspicion — don’t wait for confirmation
Management
Antibiotics (a MACROLIDE) if within 21 days of cough onset: they reduce infectivity/transmission but do little for symptoms once the paroxysmal stage is established (toxin-mediated) — a high-yield nuance. Guideline-verified (NICE CKS / UKHSA).
Antibiotic choice (macrolide, within 21 days)
  • <1 month old: clarithromycin
  • >1 month + non-pregnant adults: azithromycin or clarithromycin
  • Pregnant women: erythromycin
  • Macrolide-intolerant/contraindicated: co-trimoxazole (NOT in pregnancy or infants <6 weeks)
  • (Note: emerging macrolide-resistant strains — a current concern)
  • Supportive care; ADMIT infants — <6 months, apnoea/cyanosis, severe paroxysms, feeding difficulty, or complications (oxygen, monitoring, feeding/fluid support, sometimes ICU)
  • Exclusion: stay off school/nursery/work until 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics (or 21 days from cough onset if untreated)
  • Chemoprophylaxis (a macrolide) for close contacts — targeted at vulnerable contacts (young infants, late-pregnancy women, and those in contact with them) per UKHSA guidance
Complications (mainly in infants)
  • Apnoea, secondary pneumonia (commonest cause of death), pulmonary hypertension, seizures, encephalopathy (hypoxia), and death
  • From the force of coughing: subconjunctival/nasal haemorrhage, rib fracture, hernia, syncope, pneumothorax
Prevention (Vaccination)
  • Routine childhood immunisation — pertussis is in the 6-in-1 vaccine (2, 3, 4 months) and the pre-school (4-in-1) booster
  • Maternal vaccination in pregnancy (~16–32 weeks) — the key intervention to protect newborns (passive transfer of maternal antibodies covers the vulnerable first weeks before the infant is immunised). Uptake dips have been linked to recent UK outbreaks and infant deaths
  • Immunity (vaccine or natural) wanes → older children/adults get milder disease and act as a reservoir for infants
Exam Pearls
What it is
Bordetella pertussis (Gram-negative coccobacillus); toxin paralyses mucociliary clearance → “100-day cough.” Highly contagious; NOTIFIABLE; resurgent (2024 outbreaks).
Three stages
Catarrhal (cold-like, MOST infectious) → paroxysmal (coughing fits + inspiratory WHOOP + POST-TUSSIVE VOMITING, well between fits) → convalescent (lingers).
Infants
<6 months may have NO whoop — present with APNOEA/cyanosis/poor feeding; highest risk of death.
Investigations
PCR (early), serology/oral fluid if coughing >2 weeks; FBC = LYMPHOCYTOSIS. Notify UKHSA on suspicion.
Treatment
Macrolide if within 21 days (azithro/clarithro; clarithro if <1 month; ERYTHROMYCIN in pregnancy; co-trimoxazole if macrolide unsuitable) — reduces spread, not symptoms. Exclude until 48h of antibiotics.
Admit / contacts
Admit infants (<6 months/apnoea/severe). Chemoprophylaxis for vulnerable close contacts.
Complications
Infants: pneumonia (commonest cause of death), apnoea, seizures, encephalopathy.
Prevention
Childhood 6-in-1 + preschool booster + MATERNAL vaccine in pregnancy (protects newborns).
What & Why

Preschool wheeze is recurrent wheezing in children under ~5 years, most commonly triggered by viral upper respiratory tract infections (“episodic viral wheeze”). It matters because it’s extremely common (up to a third of preschoolers wheeze at some point), because it’s a frequent cause of GP/ED attendance and admission, and because the key clinical challenges are (1) distinguishing it from asthma — you generally can’t confidently diagnose asthma under 5 — and (2) managing acute episodes without over-treating.

The core concept: small preschool airways narrow easily when inflamed by a virus → wheeze during colds. Most children “grow out of it” as their airways enlarge (usually by age ~6) — but ~1 in 3 who wheeze persistently go on to be diagnosed with asthma, especially those with atopy/allergic sensitisation and a family history. So preschool wheeze is a mixed bag — some is early asthma, much is transient viral airway narrowing.
The Decisive Fork — Episodic Viral vs Multiple-Trigger Wheeze
Episodic viral wheeze (EVW)Multiple-trigger wheeze (MTW)
TriggersONLY with viral URTIsViral URTIs PLUS other triggers — exercise, allergens, cold air, smoke
Between episodesSymptom-FREEInterval symptoms (cough/wheeze between colds)
Underlying inflammationLessMore (closer to asthma)
PrognosisOften resolves by ~6More likely to become asthma
Caveat (current thinking): the EVW/MTW distinction is less rigid than once taught — children move between phenotypes over time, and parental reporting is imperfect. It’s a useful framework, but treatment is increasingly guided by frequency/severity and atopy risk rather than the label alone.
Is It Asthma? (the key distinction)
Features favouring asthma / higher risk of progression
  • Interval (between-episode) symptoms — cough/wheeze when well, night cough, exercise-induced wheeze
  • Personal/family history of atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, parental asthma) — the Asthma Predictive Index
  • Clear response to a bronchodilator/ICS trial, frequent/severe exacerbations
You generally do NOT formally diagnose asthma under 5 (can’t do reliable spirometry; many will grow out of it) — use a watch, treat, and review approach and reassess with age (guideline-verified).
Clinical Features
  • Wheeze + cough + increased work of breathing, appearing WITH a viral cold (coryzal prodrome → wheeze)
  • Expiratory polyphonic wheeze, tachypnoea, recession; often recurrent, self-limiting episodes
  • Well between episodes (EVW) or interval symptoms (MTW)
  • Red flags suggesting an alternative diagnosis (NOT simple preschool wheeze): symptoms from birth / very early, failure to thrive, wet/productive chronic cough (CF, bronchiectasis), focal signs/stridor, choking episode (inhaled foreign body), finger clubbing, cardiac signs
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — usually no investigations needed for typical episodic wheeze
  • Consider CXR if atypical/red flags (exclude foreign body, structural/cardiac cause), sweat test if CF suspected (chronic wet cough, faltering growth)
  • Spirometry/lung function is not reliable under ~5 (can’t cooperate)
Management
Acute exacerbation
  • Inhaled SABA (salbutamol) via a spacer (± face mask) — the mainstay; titrate to response (e.g. burst therapy, then spacing out)
  • Oxygen if hypoxic; oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) for moderate–severe exacerbations (especially if needing admission / an asthma-like picture); escalate (nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium, IV therapies) as for acute asthma if severe
  • Admit if poor response, hypoxia, severe distress, or unable to feed
Episodic viral wheeze (EVW)
  • First-line: SABA (or anticholinergic/ipratropium) via spacer — as needed for episodes
  • Second-line (if frequent/severe): intermittent LTRA (montelukast) and/or intermittent ICS — started at the onset of a viral episode
Multiple-trigger wheeze (MTW)
  • Trial of a regular preventer — ICS or LTRA (montelukast) — for 4–8 weeks, then REVIEW
  • Continue only if clear benefit (a treatment trial, not open-ended)
  • ICS tends to work better in MTW than EVW
  • General: avoid tobacco smoke exposure (a major modifiable trigger), inhaler technique/spacer education, written action plan
  • Montelukast caution: counsel about neuropsychiatric side effects (sleep disturbance, mood/behaviour change, nightmares) — a recent safety emphasis
Exam Pearls
What it is
Recurrent wheeze in <5 yrs, usually VIRAL-triggered; very common; most grow out of it by ~6, but ~1/3 become asthma (especially if atopic/FHx).
EVW vs MTW
EVW: wheezes ONLY with viral URTIs, symptom-free between. MTW: viral + other triggers (exercise/allergen/smoke) + interval symptoms.
Is it asthma?
Generally DON’T diagnose asthma under 5 (no reliable spirometry) — watch, treat, review; interval symptoms + atopy/FHx favour asthma.
Acute
SABA via SPACER (mainstay) ± oxygen ± oral prednisolone; escalate as for acute asthma; admit if severe/hypoxic/not feeding.
Preventer — EVW
1st-line SABA/ipratropium via spacer PRN → 2nd-line intermittent montelukast and/or intermittent ICS.
Preventer — MTW
Trial regular ICS or montelukast for 4–8 weeks, then REVIEW (continue only if benefit).
General
Avoid smoke exposure; check inhaler/spacer technique; counsel montelukast neuropsychiatric side effects.
Red flags
Symptoms from birth, faltering growth, wet cough (CF), focal signs/choking (foreign body), clubbing → think alternative diagnosis.
PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Heart Disease:
Overview — congenital heart disease
Structural heart defects present from birth, classified as acyanotic (left→right shunt) or cyanotic (right→left shunt). Innocent murmurs are common and benign.
The organising principle: acyanotic (VSD, ASD, PDA) → L→R shunt, often a murmur ± heart failure; cyanotic (ToF, TGA) → R→L shunt → cyanosis; duct-dependent lesions deteriorate as the PDA closes (prostaglandin keeps it open).
LesionTypeKey feature
Acyanotic CHD (VSD, ASD)L→R shuntVSD pansystolic murmur; ASD fixed split S2; failure / recurrent LRTI
Cyanotic CHD (ToF, TGA)R→L shuntToF: boot-shaped heart, tet spells; TGA presents day 1–2
Patent ductus arteriosuspersistent ductcontinuous “machinery” murmur; indometacin closes it
Innocent murmurnonesoft, systolic, asymptomatic, varies with posture; no investigation
A collapsing/cyanotic neonate as the duct closes = duct-dependent CHD → start prostaglandin (PGE) to keep the duct open and get urgent cardiology. Distinguish innocent murmurs (well child) from pathological ones.
What & Why

Acyanotic congenital heart defects shunt blood left-to-right (oxygenated blood recirculating through the lungs) — so the child is NOT cyanosed. VSD and ASD are the two commonest, both “holes” between the chambers. Many are small and close spontaneously; large untreated ones cause heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and — the feared endpoint — Eisenmenger syndrome.

The core haemodynamic principle: the left heart is at higher pressure → a hole lets blood flow left → right (acyanotic, but extra blood floods the lungs). Over years → pulmonary vascular disease → pulmonary hypertension → right pressure exceeds left → the shunt REVERSES to right→left → deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation → CYANOSIS = Eisenmenger syndrome. This is the through-line for all left-to-right shunts.
The Decisive Fork — Left-to-Right vs Right-to-Left
📷 Image placeholder — Acyanotic left→right shunt (VSD/ASD/PDA) vs cyanotic right→left shunt (ToF/TGA), with the Eisenmenger crossover showing when an acyanotic lesion turns blue
Acyanotic (L→R shunt)Cyanotic (R→L shunt)
ExamplesVSD, ASD, PDA, AVSDToF, TGA, tricuspid atresia
CyanosisNo (initially)Yes
ProblemToo much blood to lungs → HF, pulmonary HTNDeoxygenated blood to body
Late riskEisenmenger (→ becomes cyanotic)—
Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
  • The commonest congenital heart defect — a hole in the interventricular septum. Associations: Down, Edwards, Patau, fetal alcohol syndrome; often isolated
  • Small VSD: often asymptomatic (incidental murmur). Counterintuitively, a small VSD → LOUDER murmur (more turbulence through the tiny hole)
  • Large VSD: heart failure at ~4–6 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls (↑ L→R shunt): poor feeding, sweating with feeds, tachypnoea, faltering growth, recurrent chest infections, hepatomegaly
  • Murmur: pansystolic (holosystolic) at the LEFT LOWER STERNAL EDGE, ± a thrill (smaller defect → louder/harsher)
  • Management: small VSDs often close spontaneously (watchful waiting); large/symptomatic → treat HF (diuretics ± ACEi), high-calorie feeds → surgical or transcatheter closure; endocarditis risk → dental hygiene
Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
  • A hole in the interatrial septum. Types: ostium secundum (commonest) — central (fossa ovalis); ostium primum — part of an atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), strongly associated with Down syndrome (+ AV valve regurgitation); sinus venosus, coronary sinus (rarer)
  • Often presents in ADULTHOOD — dyspnoea, palpitations (atrial fibrillation/flutter), recurrent chest infections, or paradoxical embolism → stroke. Frequently asymptomatic in childhood
  • Murmur: ejection systolic at the upper left sternal edge (pulmonary area) — from increased flow through the pulmonary valve (the L→R shunt), NOT flow across the defect
  • FIXED splitting of the second heart sound (S2) — the hallmark: increased RV loading delays pulmonary valve closure, and the delay is “fixed” (doesn’t vary with respiration) because the ASD equalises the respiratory effect between the atria
  • Management: small secundum ASDs (esp. <8 mm) often close spontaneously; primum and sinus venosus do NOT; significant (RV overload) → transcatheter device closure (secundum) or surgical closure (primum/sinus venosus)
The Shared Complication — Eisenmenger Syndrome
Chronic high pulmonary flow → pulmonary arterial hypertension → pulmonary vascular resistance rises → the shunt REVERSES (right→left) → cyanosis. Once Eisenmenger’s develops, closing the defect is CONTRAINDICATED (the shunt is now the only decompression) → management becomes supportive/pulmonary vasodilators ± heart-lung transplant.
  • Signs: cyanosis, clubbing, polycythaemia, right heart failure, loud P2
  • This is why large shunts are closed early — to prevent Eisenmenger’s
Investigations (both)
  • Echocardiography — the definitive/diagnostic test (defect, shunt direction, RV overload)
  • ECG: VSD (LVH/biventricular); ASD (RV hypertrophy, RBBB, right axis; primum → left axis)
  • CXR: cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings (“plethora”) with large shunts; pulse oximetry (newborn screening)
Exam Pearls
Acyanotic CHD
LEFT-to-RIGHT shunt (no cyanosis initially); VSD (commonest CHD), ASD, PDA, AVSD.
VSD
Pansystolic murmur at LEFT LOWER sternal edge (± thrill); SMALL VSD = LOUDER murmur; large → heart failure at 4–6 weeks.
ASD
Ejection systolic murmur (pulmonary area) + FIXED splitting of S2. Often presents in adulthood (AF, dyspnoea, paradoxical embolism/stroke).
ASD types
Secundum (commonest), primum (= AVSD, DOWN syndrome, AV valve regurg), sinus venosus.
Spontaneous closure
Many small VSDs/secundum ASDs close; primum/sinus venosus do NOT.
Management
Echo diagnoses; large shunts → close (device/surgery); treat HF with diuretics ± ACEi.
Eisenmenger
Untreated large L→R shunt → pulmonary HTN → shunt REVERSES → cyanosis; closure then CONTRAINDICATED.
Endocarditis
VSD → dental hygiene.
What & Why

Cyanotic congenital heart defects send deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation (a right-to-left shunt) → the baby is blue (cyanotic). The two most important: Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) — the commonest cyanotic CHD overall — and Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) — the commonest cyanotic CHD presenting in the newborn. Neonatal cyanosis is an emergency; the life-saving move is prostaglandin E1 to keep the duct open.

The core principle: the systemic and pulmonary circulations don’t mix properly → deoxygenated blood reaches the body. Survival often depends on a “mixing point” — a VSD, ASD, or the ductus arteriosus — so prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) maintains a patent ductus arteriosus as a holding measure until surgery.
The “5 T’s”: Tetralogy of Fallot, Transposition, Truncus arteriosus, Total anomalous pulmonary venous return, Tricuspid atresia.
Presentation & the Cyanotic-CHD Framework
  • Central cyanosis — clinically apparent when reduced haemoglobin >5 g/dL
  • Distinguish from acrocyanosis (peripheral/perioral blueness, benign, normal in the first 24 h)
  • Nitrogen washout (hyperoxia) test — give 100% O₂ for ~10 min then ABG: PaO₂ <15 kPa → cyanotic congenital heart disease (fails to correct because the problem is shunting, not the lungs)
  • Pre-/post-ductal saturations (newborn pulse oximetry), echocardiography (diagnostic)
Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF)
📷 Image placeholder — The four PROVe lesions in one heart — pulmonary stenosis, RV hypertrophy, overriding aorta astride a large VSD — with the boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) on CXR

Caused by anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum → four coexisting lesions (“PROVe”):

  • Pulmonary stenosis / right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO) — the key determinant of severity
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Overriding aorta (sits over the VSD, receiving blood from both ventricles)
  • Ventricular septal defect (VSD) — large
The degree of pulmonary stenosis determines how cyanotic the child is (more obstruction → more right-to-left shunt → more cyanosis).
  • Presentation: cyanotic from birth or later in infancy; poor feeding, dyspnoea, faltering growth
  • Hypercyanotic “tet spells” — sudden severe cyanosis (RV infundibular spasm ↑ the right-to-left shunt), often on crying/feeding/waking; can cause loss of consciousness/death. Older children squat (or a baby is put knee-to-chest) → ↑ systemic vascular resistance → reduces the R→L shunt → improves cyanosis
  • Ejection systolic murmur (pulmonary area) — from the pulmonary stenosis (NOT the VSD); CXR: “boot-shaped heart” (coeur en sabot); ECG: RV hypertrophy, right axis; echocardiography — diagnostic
Management: tet spell (acute): knee-to-chest, high-flow O₂, morphine, IV fluids, beta-blockers (reduce infundibular spasm) ± phenylephrine. Duct-dependent neonate → prostaglandin E1; Blalock-Taussig shunt (temporising); definitive: total surgical repair (close VSD + relieve RVOTO), usually in infancy.
Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)
📷 Image placeholder — TGA — aorta off the RIGHT ventricle, pulmonary artery off the LEFT (two parallel circulations surviving only via a mixing point: PDA/ASD/VSD); the “egg-on-a-string” silhouette
  • The aorta arises from the RIGHT ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the LEFT ventricle → two parallel, separate circulations. Incompatible with life UNLESS there’s mixing (PDA, ASD/PFO, or VSD). Association: infants of diabetic mothers
  • Severe cyanosis within the first day(s) of life — the commonest cyanotic lesion in the neonate; profound, unresponsive to oxygen; worsens as the duct closes → collapse. Often no murmur (unless a VSD)
  • CXR: “egg on a string” — narrow superior mediastinum (great vessels lie AP) + egg-shaped silhouette; echocardiography — diagnostic (may be detected antenatally, but commonly missed on the routine four-chamber view)
  • Management: prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) immediately (maintain the PDA for mixing) → balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) (tears the atrial septum to allow mixing) → definitive: arterial switch operation (first ~2 weeks of life)
ToF vs TGA — the Contrast
Tetralogy of FallotTransposition (TGA)
CommonestCyanotic CHD overallCyanotic CHD in the newborn
Onset of cyanosisOften later infancy (± tet spells)First day of life, severe
MurmurESM (pulmonary stenosis)Usually none
CXRBoot-shaped heartEgg on a string
Key acute moveTet spell → knee-chest, O₂, morphine, β-blockerProstaglandin + balloon septostomy
Definitive surgeryTotal repair (close VSD, relieve RVOTO)Arterial switch
Exam Pearls
Cyanotic CHD
Right-to-left shunt → blue baby; the “5 T’s” (ToF, TGA, Truncus, TAPVR, Tricuspid atresia).
Cyanosis
Reduced Hb >5 g/dL; hyperoxia (nitrogen washout) test: 100% O₂, PaO₂ <15 kPa → cardiac cause.
Prostaglandin
Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) keeps the DUCT open — the emergency holding measure in duct-dependent cyanotic lesions.
ToF
Commonest cyanotic CHD; “PROVe” (Pulmonary stenosis, RVH, Overriding aorta, VSD); tet spells → KNEE-TO-CHEST + O₂ + morphine + β-blocker; ESM (pulmonary area); BOOT-SHAPED heart; total repair.
TGA
Commonest cyanotic lesion in the NEWBORN; severe day-1 cyanosis unresponsive to O₂; EGG-ON-A-STRING; prostaglandin → balloon atrial septostomy → arterial switch.
Associations
TGA associated with maternal diabetes; ToF is usually detected antenatally, but TGA is commonly missed on the routine four-chamber view.
What & Why

Patent ductus arteriosus is persistence of the ductus arteriosus beyond the neonatal period — the fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta fails to close after birth. It’s a common acyanotic left-to-right shunt (esp. in premature infants), produces the classic “machinery murmur”, and ties together two opposite drug strategies: prostaglandin inhibitors (indomethacin/ibuprofen) to CLOSE it vs prostaglandin (alprostadil) to keep it OPEN.

The core physiology: in fetal life the ductus arteriosus shunts pulmonary artery → aorta (bypassing the non-functioning lungs), kept open by prostaglandins + low fetal oxygen. After birth, the rise in PaO₂ and fall in prostaglandins → the duct constricts + closes (~1–3 days). If not, blood shunts the other way — aorta → pulmonary artery (left-to-right, acyanotic). This explains why NSAIDs (↓prostaglandins) close it and why prematurity/hypoxia keep it open.
Risk Factors & the Decisive Fork
  • Prematurity (the biggest — immature ductal tissue, common with RDS); hypoxia / respiratory distress syndrome; congenital rubella (PDA is part of the triad); female sex, high altitude, genetic syndromes
Isolated PDA vs duct-dependent lesion — this determines whether you close or keep open the duct.
Isolated PDA (a problem)Duct-dependent lesion (duct is life-saving)
SituationOtherwise-normal heart; the PDA causes L→R shunt/HFTGA, severe pulmonary atresia/stenosis, coarctation, hypoplastic left heart — flow depends on the duct
GoalCLOSE the ductKEEP the duct OPEN until surgery
DrugIndomethacin / ibuprofen (↓prostaglandins → constrict)Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) (↑prostaglandins → keep open)
Clinical Features
  • Small PDA: often asymptomatic — an incidental murmur
  • Large PDA: L→R shunt → pulmonary overcirculation + heart failure — poor feeding, sweating with feeds, faltering growth, tachypnoea, recurrent chest infections
  • In preterm infants: difficulty weaning off ventilation / increased O₂ requirement, and associations with necrotising enterocolitis, IVH, chronic lung disease
  • Continuous “machinery” murmur — best at the left upper sternal edge / below the left clavicle, running through systole and diastole
  • Bounding/collapsing pulses + wide pulse pressure (diastolic run-off into the pulmonary circuit); active precordium, ± thrill
Investigations & Management
  • Echocardiography — diagnostic (visualises the duct, shunt direction/size); ECG normal or LVH; CXR normal or cardiomegaly + plethora if large
  • Isolated PDA — close it. Preterm (significant PDA): ibuprofen (often first choice) or indomethacin (↓prostaglandins → constriction); paracetamol an increasingly used alternative; add fluid restriction ± diuretics (NSAID cautions: renal impairment, NEC, GI bleeding, IVH)
  • Term infants / older children: NSAIDs don’t work → transcatheter (device) closure (or surgical ligation) if symptomatic/persistent; small asymptomatic often close spontaneously (endocarditis risk)
  • Duct-dependent lesion — keep it open: prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion until surgical correction
The clean exam contrast: indomethacin/ibuprofen CLOSE the duct (isolated PDA); prostaglandin (alprostadil) KEEPS it open (duct-dependent lesions).
Complications (untreated large PDA)
  • Heart failure, faltering growth, recurrent chest infections
  • Pulmonary hypertension → Eisenmenger syndrome (L→R reverses to R→L → cyanosis, differential clubbing of the toes)
  • Infective endocarditis; (preterm) NEC, IVH, chronic lung disease
Exam Pearls
What it is
Ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth → acyanotic LEFT-to-RIGHT shunt (aorta → pulmonary artery).
Physiology
Duct normally closes after birth: ↑PaO₂ + ↓prostaglandins. Risk factors: PREMATURITY, hypoxia/RDS, congenital rubella.
Signs
Continuous “MACHINERY” murmur (left upper sternal edge/below clavicle) + BOUNDING pulses + wide pulse pressure.
Preterm
Large PDA → heart failure; failure to wean off ventilator, NEC, IVH.
Close it
PRETERM → indomethacin/ibuprofen (± paracetamol) + fluid restriction; TERM/older → transcatheter device closure or surgery (NSAIDs don’t work in term).
Keep it open
Duct-dependent lesions (TGA/coarctation/pulmonary atresia) → PROSTAGLANDIN E1 (alprostadil).
The contrast
NSAIDs CLOSE / prostaglandin OPENS.
Other
Untreated → Eisenmenger, endocarditis. PDA is part of the CONGENITAL RUBELLA triad.
What & Why

An innocent murmur (functional/benign/flow murmur) is a heart murmur from normal blood flow through a structurally NORMAL heart. Murmurs are heard at some point in ~50–80% of children, yet only ~1% reflect real pathology — so the essential skill is confidently distinguishing an innocent murmur from a pathological one: to reassure the well child while not missing structural heart disease.

The core principle: turbulent flow makes sound. In a normal heart, brisk/high flow (fever, anaemia, exercise, thin chest wall) creates audible turbulence → an innocent murmur. Because it’s just flow (no obstruction/shunt), it’s soft, systolic, and changes with physiology — the opposite of a fixed, harsh pathological murmur.
The Decisive Fork — Innocent vs Pathological
Innocent murmurPathological murmur
TimingSystolic only (except venous hum)Diastolic or continuous → pathological
IntensitySoft (grade ≤2), no thrillLoud (≥grade 3) ± thrill
QualityMusical/vibratory (“sweet”)Harsh
RadiationNone (localised)Radiates
Added soundsNone (no clicks/gallops)Clicks, gallops, abnormal S2
PostureVaries/disappears with positionFixed/constant
Symptoms/signsAsymptomatic, well child, normal examCyanosis, HF, faltering growth, abnormal pulses
The “S” Features of an Innocent Murmur
  • Soft
  • Systolic (never purely diastolic)
  • Single — no added heart sounds (no clicks, gallops)
  • Sensitive — varies with posture (louder lying down, softer/gone on standing) and respiration
  • Short — doesn’t last all of systole
  • Small — no radiation, localised
  • (+ often Sweet/musical and aSymptomatic with a normal exam)
The gestalt: a soft, systolic, musical murmur in a well, asymptomatic child, with normal pulses/S2, that changes with position = innocent.
The Named Innocent Murmurs
  • Still’s murmur — the commonest; a low-pitched, vibratory/musical systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge/apex; loudest lying down, softer on standing; peak age 3–6 years
  • Pulmonary flow murmur — soft systolic at the left upper sternal edge (pulmonary area); common in infants/adolescents; louder lying down
  • Venous hum — the only innocent murmur with a diastolic (continuous) component; soft continuous murmur below the clavicle/neck; disappears on lying down or turning/compressing the neck (distinguishing it from a PDA, which is fixed)
  • Carotid/supraclavicular bruit — systolic, over the supraclavicular area (school-age)
Red Flags → Refer / Echocardiogram
  • Any diastolic murmur (always pathological)
  • Continuous murmur (except venous hum) — e.g. PDA
  • Loud murmur (≥ grade 3) or a thrill; harsh quality; radiation
  • Abnormal/added sounds — clicks, gallops, abnormal or fixed-split S2
  • Symptoms: cyanosis, breathlessness, poor feeding, faltering growth, syncope, exertional symptoms
  • Abnormal pulses (weak femorals/radio-femoral delay → coarctation), abnormal precordium/apex, hepatomegaly
  • Family history of CHD/sudden death; neonatal murmur (higher pathology rate → refer)
Assessment & Investigations
  • Full history + cardiovascular examination — pulses (all four limbs / BP in arms and legs), precordium, heart sounds, signs of heart failure, growth, cyanosis
  • Pulse oximetry (pre-/post-ductal) — all infants, to screen for critical CHD
  • ECG and CXR are NO LONGER recommended routinely to distinguish innocent from pathological murmurs (poor sensitivity/specificity)
  • Echocardiography is the definitive test if pathology is suspected (red flags) — not needed for a clearly innocent murmur; reassure (a murmur during a febrile illness may disappear on recovery)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Normal flow through a STRUCTURALLY NORMAL heart; heard in ~50–80% of children, only ~1% pathological.
The “S”s
Soft, Systolic, Single (no added sounds), Sensitive (varies with posture), Short, Small (no radiation) (± Sweet/musical, aSymptomatic).
Named ones
Still’s murmur (commonest — vibratory, LLSE/apex, louder lying down), pulmonary flow murmur (LUSE), venous hum (continuous, below clavicle, DISAPPEARS lying down).
Venous hum
The ONLY innocent murmur with a diastolic component — any other diastolic/continuous murmur is pathological.
Red flags → refer/echo
Diastolic, continuous (not venous hum), ≥grade 3/thrill, harsh, radiating, added sounds/abnormal S2, symptoms, abnormal pulses, FHx, neonatal murmur.
Investigations
Don’t routinely do ECG/CXR; echo only if pathology suspected; reassure if clearly innocent.
Accentuators
Fever/anaemia/exercise/thin chest → accentuate flow murmurs.
What & Why

Coarctation is a congenital narrowing of the aorta, usually just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery (at the aortic isthmus, near the ductus insertion). It’s a common obstructive acyanotic lesion with a bimodal presentation — a critically unwell neonate in shock when the duct closes, or an asymptomatic older child/adult with hypertension and weak leg pulses — and the classic cause of radio-femoral delay, closely linked to Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve.

The core mechanism: the narrowing obstructs blood flow to the lower body. Upstream (heart, arms, head) → high pressure (upper-limb hypertension); downstream (abdomen, legs) → low pressure/reduced flow (weak femoral pulses). Over time collateral vessels (intercostal arteries) develop to bypass the obstruction → the classic rib notching. “High above, low below the block” explains every sign.
Acyanotic — but Note the Neonatal Caveat
Coarctation is an ACYANOTIC obstructive lesion (no shunt/mixing). BUT critical neonatal coarctation is duct-dependent — the lower body is perfused via the PDA. When the duct closes → differential cyanosis (pink upper body, blue lower body) + shock.
The Decisive Fork — Neonatal (Critical) vs Older Child/Adult
Neonatal (critical, duct-dependent)Older child / adult
PresentationCollapse/SHOCK as the duct closes (days 1–2 weeks)Asymptomatic; incidental HYPERTENSION
FeaturesGrey, floppy, poor feeding, tachypnoea, acidosis, absent femorals, differential cyanosisHeadache, epistaxis, leg claudication/cold legs on exertion, radio-femoral delay
ManagementProstaglandin E1 + resuscitation → urgent repairElective repair (surgery/stent) + BP control
Associations
  • Turner syndrome (45,X)
  • Bicuspid aortic valve (in up to ~two-thirds of infants with coarctation)
  • Male sex, family history
  • Other left-heart lesions (VSD, PDA, aortic valve stenosis, mitral valve anomalies, Shone complex), and complex cyanotic CHD
Clinical Features & Signs
🚨 Neonate (critical)
  • Weak/absent femoral pulses — often the only sign; brachio-femoral / radio-femoral delay
  • Circulatory collapse, grey/mottled, floppy, poor feeding, tachypnoea, metabolic acidosis as the duct closes
  • Differential cyanosis (pre-ductal arms pink / post-ductal legs blue)
🩺 Older child / adult
  • Upper-limb hypertension with lower BP in the legs (measure BP in all four limbs)
  • Radio-femoral delay (femoral pulse delayed/weaker than radial)
  • Ejection systolic murmur — best at the left infraclavicular area / between the scapulae (back); ± a systolic click (bicuspid valve)
  • Left ventricular heave; underdeveloped legs / cold feet; headaches, epistaxis; palpable collateral vessels
Investigations
  • Four-limb BP + pulse examination (arm-leg gradient, radio-femoral delay) — the key bedside test
  • Pre-/post-ductal oxygen saturations (differential cyanosis)
  • Echocardiography — diagnostic (narrowing, gradient, associated lesions/bicuspid valve, LV function)
  • CXR: “Figure 3 sign” (aortic contour — pre-stenotic dilatation + indentation + post-stenotic dilatation); rib notching (dilated collateral intercostals eroding the ribs — usually only after ~age 5, not in neonates)
  • ECG: LV hypertrophy (older); RV/biventricular in neonates. CT/MR angiography for detailed anatomy
Management
🚨 Neonate (critical/duct-dependent)
  • Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion — reopen/maintain the ductus arteriosus to perfuse the lower body + stabilise
  • Resuscitation: manage shock, acidosis, respiratory support; inotropes (dopamine/dobutamine)
  • Urgent surgical repair (resection + end-to-end anastomosis, or subclavian flap)
🩺 Older child / stable
  • Elective repair — surgery or balloon angioplasty ± stenting (favoured in older children/adults)
  • Antihypertensive control (beta-blockers); treat associated lesions
Complications / lifelong follow-up: re-coarctation (esp. after neonatal repair), persistent/late hypertension (even after successful repair), aneurysm at the repair site, aortic dissection, and (if bicuspid valve) aortic valve disease + endocarditis.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Narrowing of the aorta (distal to left subclavian) → ACYANOTIC obstructive lesion.
Neonate
Duct-dependent → collapse/shock + differential cyanosis + absent femoral pulses when the duct closes → PROSTAGLANDIN E1 + urgent repair.
Older child/adult
Upper-limb HYPERTENSION + weak legs + RADIO-FEMORAL DELAY (measure BP in all 4 limbs).
Murmur
ESM at left infraclavicular area / between the scapulae (back); ± systolic click (bicuspid valve).
Associations
TURNER syndrome + BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE.
CXR
“Figure 3 sign” + RIB NOTCHING (rib notching only after ~age 5, from collateral intercostals).
Diagnosis
Echocardiography.
Management
Prostaglandin (neonate) → surgical repair; balloon/stent for older children/adults; BP control. Lifelong follow-up: re-coarctation, persistent hypertension, aneurysm, dissection.
PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surgical GI:
Overview — paediatric surgical GI
The paediatric surgical abdomen — causes of obstruction, bilious vomiting and acute abdominal pain needing prompt surgical assessment.
The organising principle: age + vomiting character + stool. Bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate = malrotation/volvulus until proven otherwise; non-bilious projectile at 4–6 wks = pyloric stenosis; colicky pain + redcurrant-jelly stool 6mo–2yr = intussusception.
ConditionAgeClue
Intussusception6mo–2yrcolicky pain, redcurrant-jelly stool, sausage mass; air/contrast enema ± surgery
Pyloric stenosis4–6 wksnon-bilious projectile vomiting, olive mass, hypochloraemic alkalosis; pyloromyotomy
Malrotation / volvulusneonate/infantbilious vomiting; upper-GI contrast; emergency Ladd's procedure
Hirschsprung's diseaseneonatedelayed meconium (>48h), distension; rectal biopsy (absent ganglia)

Bilious vomiting in a neonate = malrotation with volvulus until excluded → urgent upper-GI contrast + surgical review (bowel-ischaemia risk). Correct fluids/electrolytes before pyloromyotomy.
What & Why

Intussusception is the telescoping (“invagination”) of one segment of bowel into the adjacent distal segment — the proximal bowel (intussusceptum) slides into the lumen ahead of it (intussuscipiens), like a collapsing telescope. It matters because it’s the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in infants/young children (6 months–2 years) and is a surgical emergency — untreated, the trapped bowel’s blood supply is cut off → ischaemia, necrosis, perforation, and peritonitis.

The core mechanism: the bowel telescopes → the mesentery is dragged in with it → venous compression → oedema and congestion → the bowel “weeps” blood and mucus (the redcurrant jelly stool) → if unrelieved, arterial supply is compromised → ischaemia/gangrene/perforation. Most are ileocolic (~90%) — the ileum invaginates through the ileocaecal valve into the colon.
Cause & the “Lead Point”
  • Most (in infants) are idiopathic — often follows a viral illness → hypertrophied Peyer’s patches / lymphoid hyperplasia in the terminal ileum act as the lead point (rotavirus/adenovirus links)
  • A pathological “lead point” becomes more likely with older age (>2–3 yr) or recurrence — always look for one:
  • — Meckel’s diverticulum (the classic), intestinal polyp, duplication cyst
  • — Henoch-Schonlein purpura (intramural haematoma), lymphoma (e.g. Burkitt’s) in older children, cystic fibrosis (inspissated stool), post-op, tumours
  • Slight male predominance
Clinical Features
  • Sudden, severe, PAROXYSMAL colicky abdominal pain — episodes every ~15–20 min; the child draws the knees/legs up, screams, goes pale, then appears well/settled between episodes (the classic pattern)
  • Vomiting — initially non-bilious/reflex; becomes bilious as obstruction develops (bilious vomiting in a child = surgical until proven otherwise)
  • “Redcurrant jelly” stool — blood + mucus; a LATE sign — don’t wait for it
  • A palpable “sausage-shaped” mass — typically right upper quadrant / along the colon, with emptiness in the right iliac fossa (Dance’s sign)
  • Lethargy — may be the sole or dominant feature (an “atypical/apathetic” presentation — a lethargic, pale infant “as if drugged”; ~15% present without the colic phase)
  • Late: abdominal distension, dehydration/shock, fever, peritonism (→ perforation/gangrene)
The classic triad (colicky pain + redcurrant jelly stool + sausage mass) is present in <25% of cases — so a high index of suspicion is needed; don’t wait for all three.
Investigations
  • Ultrasound — the investigation of choice (sensitive, quick, no radiation): shows the “target”/“doughnut” sign (concentric rings on transverse view) or “pseudokidney” sign (longitudinal)
  • Abdominal X-ray — not diagnostic but may show signs of obstruction (distended loops, paucity of gas in right iliac fossa), a soft-tissue mass, or free air (perforation → contraindicates enema)
  • Bloods — FBC, U&Es, group & save; assess hydration/shock
Management
  • Resuscitate first — “drip and suck”: IV fluids (often dehydrated/shocked), NG tube for decompression, analgesia, and involve paediatric surgery
  • Non-operative reduction — first-line in a stable child: AIR (pneumatic) enema (or contrast enema) under radiological guidance — both diagnostic AND therapeutic (~80–90% success)
  • Contraindicated if: peritonitis, perforation, or haemodynamic instability/shock → straight to surgery
  • Surgery — if: enema fails, there’s perforation/peritonitis/shock, or a pathological lead point is found → operative reduction ± bowel resection (if gangrenous)
  • Recurrence ~5–10% after enema reduction (usually within 24–48h); recurrent episodes raise suspicion of a lead point. Antibiotics if perforation/peritonitis suspected
Exam Pearls
What it is
Bowel telescopes into adjacent segment (usually ILEOCOLIC ~90%); commonest cause of obstruction in infants 6 months–2 years.
Cause
Mostly idiopathic (post-viral lymphoid hyperplasia); look for a LEAD POINT if older/recurrent (Meckel’s, HSP, polyp, lymphoma).
Presentation
Paroxysmal colic (draws legs up, pale) + WELL between episodes + vomiting (→ bilious) + REDCURRANT JELLY stool (late) + sausage-shaped mass (right upper quadrant) ± lethargy.
Triad
Classic triad present in <25% — don’t wait for redcurrant jelly stool.
Investigation
Ultrasound = investigation of choice: TARGET/doughnut sign (± pseudokidney).
Management
Resuscitate (IV fluids + NG) → AIR ENEMA (diagnostic + therapeutic, ~80–90%) → surgery if enema fails / perforation / peritonitis / shock / lead point.
Cautions
Enema contraindicated in peritonitis/perforation/shock. Recurrence ~5–10%. Lethargy may be the only sign (“apathetic” presentation).
What & Why

Pyloric stenosis is hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter muscle → gastric outlet obstruction in an infant. It matters because it’s a classic, high-yield exam scenario — a firstborn baby boy, projectile NON-bilious vomiting at a few weeks old, and a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — and because the electrolyte/acid-base picture is the single most-examined paediatric biochemistry question. It’s also a management point: it is NOT a surgical emergency — you correct fluids and electrolytes FIRST, then operate.

The core mechanism: the pyloric muscle progressively hypertrophies → narrows/obstructs the gastric outlet → the stomach can’t empty → forceful (projectile) vomiting of gastric contents only (so non-bilious — the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct). Persistent vomiting of hydrochloric acid (HCl) drives the entire biochemical picture.
Epidemiology
  • Presents at ~2–8 weeks of age (peak 3–6 weeks) — well at birth, then progressive vomiting
  • Boys ~4:1, especially firstborn males
  • Positive family history (especially maternal); associated with maternal smoking
Clinical Features
  • Projectile, NON-bilious vomiting — forceful, shortly after feeds (the hallmark)
  • The baby remains HUNGRY and eager to feed again (“hungry vomiter”) — helps distinguish from an unwell/septic infant
  • Weight loss / failure to thrive, dehydration, reduced urine/wet nappies, constipation
  • On examination during a “TEST FEED”: a palpable, firm, non-tender “OLIVE”-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant/epigastrium (the hypertrophied pylorus) + visible peristalsis (left-to-right waves after a feed)
  • Late: lethargic, sunken fontanelle/eyes, poor perfusion (dehydration/shock)
Non-bilious = pyloric stenosis; BILIOUS vomiting is NOT pyloric stenosis → think malrotation/volvulus (surgical emergency).
The Single Most-Examined Point — the Biochemistry
📷 Image placeholder — Pyloric stenosis biochemistry cascade — vomiting of HCl → hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis → RAAS-driven K⁺ loss → paradoxical aciduria
Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic METABOLIC ALKALOSIS — with paradoxical aciduria. Understand why (a classic reasoning question).
The reasoning (three steps)
  • Vomiting loses HCl → loss of H+ and Cl− → ↓Cl− (hypochloraemia) + ↑bicarbonate → metabolic alkalosis
  • Volume depletion → kidney activates RAAS/aldosterone → retains sodium and water, but excretes potassium → ↓potassium (hypokalaemia)
  • “Paradoxical aciduria”: despite the systemic alkalosis, once potassium is depleted, the kidney is forced to excrete H+ (instead of potassium) to reabsorb sodium → the urine becomes acidic despite the blood being alkaline (the “paradox”)
Exam summary: ↓Cl−, ↓potassium, ↑bicarbonate, alkalotic pH, acidic urine.
Investigations
  • Ultrasound — the investigation of choice (diagnostic): shows pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm and pyloric channel length >15–17 mm
  • Venous/capillary blood gas + U&Es — to identify and quantify the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (and guide fluid correction)
  • (Test feed is the classic clinical diagnostic step; ultrasound has largely superseded the need to feel the olive)
Management
It is NOT an immediate surgical emergency — resuscitate and correct fluids/electrolytes FIRST. Operating on an alkalotic, hypokalaemic baby risks post-op apnoea/arrhythmia and anaesthetic danger.
  • Stop oral feeds, pass an NG tube (decompress/aspirate)
  • IV fluid resuscitation + correct electrolytes — typically 0.9% saline with added potassium (± dextrose); monitor gas/U&Es until alkalosis and potassium/chloride normalise
  • Definitive treatment: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy — surgical division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle (down to but not through the mucosa), open or laparoscopic
  • Excellent prognosis — feeds restart within hours–a day post-op; recurrence rare
Exam Pearls
What it is
Hypertrophied pylorus → gastric outlet obstruction; presents 2–8 weeks (peak 3–6); FIRSTBORN BOYS (~4:1).
Presentation
Projectile NON-BILIOUS vomiting + HUNGRY afterwards (“hungry vomiter”) + weight loss/dehydration.
Discriminator
Non-bilious → pyloric stenosis; BILIOUS → malrotation/volvulus (emergency).
Exam sign
Palpable “OLIVE” mass (right upper quadrant) + visible peristalsis on a TEST FEED.
Biochemistry
HYPOCHLORAEMIC, HYPOKALAEMIC METABOLIC ALKALOSIS + PARADOXICAL ACIDURIA (loss of HCl → alkalosis; potassium depletion → kidney excretes H+ → acidic urine).
Diagnosis
ULTRASOUND (muscle >3 mm thick, channel >15 mm long).
Management
FLUIDS + ELECTROLYTE CORRECTION FIRST (NOT an emergency op) → Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
What & Why

Intestinal malrotation is a congenital abnormality of the position and fixation of the gut, from failure of the normal rotation of the midgut during fetal development. It matters because it leaves the bowel anchored on a dangerously narrow mesenteric base, predisposing to midgut volvulus — the whole midgut twisting around the superior mesenteric artery → a true paediatric surgical emergency: the twist strangles the artery → rapid ischaemia and necrosis of the entire small bowel within hours (short-bowel syndrome or death).

The core mechanism (embryology): normally the midgut undergoes a 270° anticlockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery and fixes the duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure to the left of the midline and the caecum in the right iliac fossa — a broad, stable mesenteric base. In malrotation this rotation is incomplete → the caecum ends up high/midline, the DJ flexure is malpositioned, and the mesentery has a narrow pedicle → the bowel can twist (volvulus), and abnormal peritoneal “Ladd’s bands” stretch across and obstruct the duodenum.
Associations
  • Exomphalos (omphalocele)
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
  • Intrinsic duodenal atresia
  • Also: gastroschisis, heterotaxy/situs abnormalities & congenital heart disease
  • (These are all “the gut/abdominal wall didn’t develop/position normally” conditions)
Clinical Features
  • BILIOUS (green) vomiting — the cardinal red flag; from duodenal obstruction (Ladd’s bands or the volvulus twist), which is distal to the ampulla → bile-stained
  • Neonate/young infant (often first month, but can present at any age); signs of obstruction (abdominal pain/distension, poor feeding)
  • Late/ischaemic signs (volvulus with strangulation): abdominal tenderness/peritonism, PR bleeding (haematochezia), a distended tense abdomen, and shock — indicate bowel ischaemia → emergency
  • Older children: chronic intermittent bilious vomiting, recurrent abdominal pain, or failure to thrive (intermittent volvulus/Ladd’s band obstruction)
THE rule: bilious vomiting in a neonate = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. Contrast with pyloric stenosis = NON-bilious projectile vomiting.
Investigations
  • Upper GI contrast study — the gold standard/diagnostic test: shows the DJ flexure malpositioned (not in its normal left-of-midline position) and, in volvulus, the pathognomonic “corkscrew” appearance of the twisted duodenum/proximal jejunum
  • Ultrasound (with Doppler): the “whirlpool sign” — the superior mesenteric vein and mesentery wrapping clockwise around the superior mesenteric artery (indicates volvulus); may show the artery/vein relationship inverted
  • Abdominal X-ray — often non-specific; may show a “double bubble” ± distal gas (duodenal obstruction) or a gasless abdomen (concerning). Not diagnostic
  • Do NOT delay surgery for imaging in an unstable/ill child with suspected volvulus — go straight to theatre
Management
Midgut volvulus is a surgical EMERGENCY — resuscitate (IV fluids, NG decompression, correct electrolytes, broad-spectrum antibiotics), and urgent paediatric surgery.
Ladd’s procedure — the definitive operation
  • Detorse the volvulus (untwist — usually anticlockwise)
  • Divide Ladd’s bands (relieve duodenal obstruction)
  • Broaden the mesenteric base (widen the pedicle to prevent re-twisting)
  • Place the small bowel on the right, caecum/colon on the left (non-rotated position)
  • Appendicectomy (the repositioned caecum would make future appendicitis present atypically)
  • Resect any frankly necrotic/gangrenous bowel; a “second-look” laparotomy may be needed if viability is borderline
  • Asymptomatic malrotation (found incidentally) → usually elective Ladd’s procedure (~15–20% lifetime volvulus risk), individualised
Complications
  • Bowel ischaemia/necrosis → short-bowel syndrome (if extensive resection needed) — the feared outcome
  • Perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, death (untreated volvulus)
  • Recurrence (rare after Ladd’s)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Failed normal 270° midgut rotation → narrow mesenteric base + high/midline caecum + Ladd’s bands; predisposes to MIDGUT VOLVULUS (twist around the superior mesenteric artery).
THE rule
BILIOUS (green) VOMITING in a neonate = malrotation/volvulus until proven otherwise (vs pyloric stenosis = NON-bilious).
Emergency
Volvulus strangulates the artery → whole small bowel ischaemia within hours; late signs = tenderness, PR bleed, shock.
Associations
Exomphalos, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, duodenal atresia, gastroschisis, heterotaxy/congenital heart disease.
Investigation
UPPER GI CONTRAST (gold standard) — malpositioned DJ flexure + “CORKSCREW” sign; ultrasound Doppler — “WHIRLPOOL” sign. Don’t delay surgery in an unstable child.
Management
Resuscitate → LADD’S PROCEDURE (detorse + divide Ladd’s bands + broaden mesentery + reposition bowel + appendicectomy); resect necrotic bowel.
Feared complication
Short-bowel syndrome from extensive necrosis.
What & Why

Hirschsprung’s disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the distal bowel — the nerves that drive peristalsis fail to develop, so the affected segment can’t relax or propel stool → functional bowel obstruction. It matters as a key cause of failure to pass meconium / neonatal bowel obstruction, it’s the classic delayed meconium (>48 h) + abdominal distension + bilious vomiting scenario, it’s strongly associated with Down syndrome, and its complication — Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) — can be life-threatening.

The core mechanism: during embryogenesis, neural crest cells migrate craniocaudally down the gut to form the enteric nervous system (Meissner submucosal and Auerbach myenteric plexuses). In Hirschsprung’s, this migration stops short → the distal bowel has NO ganglion cells. The aganglionic segment is tonically contracted/unable to relax → functional obstruction → the proximal (normally innervated) bowel dilates hugely (megacolon), with a transition zone between them.
Key Facts & Associations
  • The aganglionosis is always DISTAL and continuous from the anus proximally — ~75% is short-segment (rectosigmoid); rarely total colonic
  • Boys ~4:1
  • Strongly associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — also Waardenburg syndrome, MEN2, congenital central hypoventilation
  • RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10) is the strongest genetic association; can be familial
Clinical Features
  • Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life — the classic red flag (normally passed within 24–48 h)
  • Neonatal distal bowel obstruction: abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and delayed meconium (the classic triad)
  • Older infants/children (short-segment, milder): chronic severe constipation, abdominal distension, failure to thrive
  • On PR examination — the “squirt/blast sign”: a tight/empty rectum, then explosive passage of stool and gas when the finger is withdrawn (decompression of the obstructed proximal bowel)
Contrast with functional constipation: Hirschsprung’s = from birth / delayed meconium, empty rectum on PR; functional constipation = later onset, stool in the rectum, responds to laxatives.
Hirschsprung-Associated Enterocolitis (HAEC)
A life-threatening complication — inflammation/infection of the obstructed bowel: fever, explosive/foul diarrhoea, abdominal distension, sepsis; can → toxic megacolon and perforation. Can be the presenting feature; needs urgent resuscitation, IV antibiotics, rectal washouts/decompression.
Investigations
  • Rectal (suction) biopsy — the GOLD-STANDARD diagnostic test: shows ABSENCE of ganglion cells in the submucosal/myenteric plexuses, with hypertrophied/thickened nerve fibres and increased acetylcholinesterase staining
  • Abdominal X-ray — signs of distal bowel obstruction (dilated loops)
  • Contrast (barium) enema — may show the transition zone (narrow aganglionic distal segment → dilated proximal colon); helps plan surgery but is not diagnostic on its own
  • Anorectal manometry — absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex (the internal sphincter fails to relax); a screening adjunct
Management
  • Initial: if obstructed/HAEC → resuscitate, NG decompression, bowel/rectal washouts (to decompress and bridge to surgery), IV antibiotics if enterocolitis
