  • Definitive: surgical “pull-through” procedure — resect the aganglionic segment and anastomose normally innervated bowel to the anus (e.g. Soave, Swenson, Duhamel), often a single-stage operation (± an initial defunctioning colostomy in sick/late cases)
  • Long-term: many children do well, but some have ongoing constipation, faecal incontinence, or recurrent enterocolitis → follow-up. There are no effective medical (drug) cures — surgery is essential
Exam Pearls
What it is
Congenital ABSENCE of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in DISTAL bowel → functional obstruction + proximal megacolon; usually rectosigmoid (~75%); boys 4:1.
Mechanism
Neural crest cells fail to migrate → no Meissner/Auerbach plexus → segment can’t relax.
Presentation
DELAYED MECONIUM (>48h) + abdominal distension + bilious vomiting in a neonate; chronic constipation/failure to thrive in older children.
PR sign
Empty rectum → explosive stool on withdrawal (“squirt/blast sign”).
Association
Strongly associated with DOWN SYNDROME (+ RET gene, Waardenburg).
Diagnosis
RECTAL SUCTION BIOPSY (gold standard) — absent ganglion cells + hypertrophied nerves. Contrast enema shows transition zone.
HAEC
Life-threatening: fever, explosive foul diarrhoea, distension, sepsis → resuscitate + antibiotics + washouts.
Management
Bowel washouts → surgical PULL-THROUGH (resect aganglionic segment).
What & Why

Meckel’s diverticulum is the commonest congenital anomaly of the GI tract — a true diverticulum of the distal ileum that is a remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct. It matters because although most are asymptomatic, it is the number-one cause of painless, massive lower-GI bleeding in young children, and it can mimic appendicitis or cause bowel obstruction.

The core mechanism: the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct connects the developing gut to the yolk sac; it normally obliterates by ~week 7. Incomplete obliteration leaves a blind-ending pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum — a true diverticulum (all bowel-wall layers). It often contains ectopic (heterotopic) tissue — most commonly GASTRIC mucosa (also pancreatic): this ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid → ulcerates adjacent normal ileal mucosa → painless bleeding.
The Rule of 2s
📷 Image placeholder — Meckel's diverticulum — antimesenteric ileum ~60 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve, with ectopic gastric mucosa causing acid-induced bleeding
A classic memory aid — Meckel’s:
  • Occurs in ~2% of the population
  • Is 2 feet (~60 cm) proximal to the ileocaecal valve
  • Is ~2 inches (~5 cm) long
  • 2:1 male predominance, usually symptomatic before age 2
  • Has 2 common ectopic tissue types (gastric + pancreatic), and ~2% become symptomatic
Clinical Features

Most are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, three classic presentations:

  • Painless rectal bleeding: Meckel’s is the No. 1 cause of painless, massive lower-GI bleeding in children aged 1–2 years requiring transfusion — bright red/maroon PR bleed from acid-induced ileal ulceration. (The other classic paediatric painless-PR-bleed cause is a juvenile polyp)
  • Abdominal pain mimicking appendicitis (“Meckel’s diverticulitis”) — inflammation → right iliac fossa/periumbilical pain, indistinguishable from appendicitis (think of Meckel’s if the appendix looks normal at appendicectomy)
  • Intestinal obstruction — via an omphalomesenteric (fibrous) band, volvulus, or acting as a lead point for intussusception
  • Rarely: perforation/peritonitis
Investigations
  • Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan (“Meckel’s scan”) — the investigation of choice (especially for the bleeding presentation): the radiotracer is taken up by GASTRIC mucosa — including the ectopic gastric mucosa in the diverticulum → highlights it. High sensitivity/specificity when ectopic gastric mucosa is present (won’t detect a non-gastric-lined Meckel’s)
  • Bloods (FBC — anaemia from bleeding; group & save/crossmatch), resuscitation for significant bleeds
  • CT/angiography or laparoscopy if the scan is negative but suspicion remains (obstruction/diverticulitis often diagnosed at surgery); plain films/ultrasound have limited value
Management
  • Symptomatic Meckel’s → surgical resection (diverticulectomy or small-bowel segmental resection), open or laparoscopic; resuscitate/transfuse first if bleeding
  • Incidentally found Meckel’s: management is debated — resect if features suggest higher complication risk (young patient, long/narrow-necked diverticulum, palpable ectopic tissue, band); often left alone if truly incidental in an older adult
  • Excellent prognosis after resection
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest congenital GI anomaly; remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct; TRUE diverticulum on the antimesenteric ileum; often contains ectopic GASTRIC (± pancreatic) mucosa.
Rule of 2s
2% of population, 2 feet from ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2:1 male, symptomatic <2 years, 2 tissue types.
Bleeding
Ectopic gastric mucosa → acid → ileal ulceration → PAINLESS massive PR bleed — the No. 1 cause of painless significant lower-GI bleed in 1–2-year-olds. (Other cause: juvenile polyp)
Other presentations
Appendicitis-mimic (Meckel’s diverticulitis — think of it if the appendix is normal) and obstruction (band, volvulus, intussusception lead point).
Diagnosis
TECHNETIUM-99m PERTECHNETATE scan (“Meckel’s scan”) — detects ectopic gastric mucosa.
Management
Resuscitate → surgical resection (diverticulectomy) if symptomatic.
What & Why

Mesenteric adenitis is inflammation/enlargement of the mesenteric lymph nodes (usually those in the right iliac fossa), typically following a viral illness. It matters almost entirely because it is the commonest mimic of acute appendicitis in children — a child with right-sided abdominal pain who does NOT need an operation — so the examinable point is recognising the benign, self-limiting picture and distinguishing it from appendicitis (which must not be missed).

The core concept: enteric/respiratory pathogens are ingested or reach the gut → drain to the mesenteric lymph nodes → the nodes react and enlarge (reactive lymphadenopathy). Because the ileocaecal mesenteric nodes sit in the right iliac fossa, the resulting pain and tenderness overlap with appendicitis — hence the diagnostic difficulty. It is benign and self-limiting.
Cause
  • Usually post-viral — often follows an upper respiratory tract infection or gastroenteritis
  • Viruses: adenovirus, coxsackievirus, EBV, measles
  • Bacteria — classically Yersinia enterocolitica (the best-known bacterial cause; also Streptococcus, E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella)
  • Commonest in children/adolescents <16
Clinical Features
  • Abdominal pain — often central or right iliac fossa — but without the guarding/rigidity of appendicitis
  • Preceded by (or concurrent with) a viral illness / recent cold or sore throat (the classic clue)
  • Higher/spiking fever may be present (often more than in appendicitis)
  • Associated URTI features: cough, coryza, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy (nodes enlarged elsewhere too)
  • Nausea/vomiting or diarrhoea may occur, but the child is often less “toxic” than with appendicitis
  • Self-limiting — the pain often fluctuates/moves and settles over days
The classic vignette: “a child had a cold a week ago, now has abdominal pain, normal stools, and is tender on palpation.”
The Decisive Fork — Mesenteric Adenitis vs Appendicitis
📷 Image placeholder — Mesenteric adenitis (preceding URTI, fluctuating pain, absent peritonism) vs appendicitis (migrating RIF pain with guarding/rebound)
FeatureMesenteric adenitisAppendicitis
Preceding illnessRecent viral URTI/sore throatUsually none
PainCentral/right iliac fossa, often fluctuating/less localisedMigrates periumbilical → right iliac fossa, then localises/worsens
Guarding/peritonismAbsent/mildPresent (McBurney’s, rebound, guarding)
FeverOften higher/spikingLow-grade
AssociatedCough, coryza, cervical nodesAnorexia, focal signs
CourseSelf-limiting, improvesProgressive, worsens
Because it’s hard to be certain, appendicitis must always be excluded — a period of active observation (“watch and wait” with serial examination) is often used; if doubt remains, imaging or diagnostic laparoscopy may be needed. Never anchor on mesenteric adenitis at the expense of missing appendicitis.
Investigations
  • Largely a clinical/exclusion diagnosis — the aim is to rule out appendicitis and other surgical causes
  • Bloods (FBC, CRP) — of limited discriminatory value (can be raised in both; a normal WCC/CRP doesn’t exclude appendicitis)
  • Ultrasound — the mainstay: shows enlarged mesenteric nodes (≥3 nodes, short-axis ≥8 mm) with a NORMAL appendix and no other pathology
  • Urinalysis, throat swab as appropriate; diagnostic laparoscopy if appendicitis genuinely can’t be excluded (may find enlarged nodes + normal appendix)
Management
  • Supportive and self-limiting: reassurance, analgesia/antipyretics, hydration — resolves in ~2–4 weeks (usually much sooner)
  • Safety-net: advise return if pain worsens, localises, becomes constant, or fever persists (i.e. could be evolving appendicitis)
  • No antibiotics for typical (viral) cases; treat a specific bacterial cause (e.g. Yersinia) if identified/severe
Exam Pearls
What it is
Reactive enlargement of mesenteric lymph nodes (usually right iliac fossa), typically POST-VIRAL; the commonest MIMIC OF APPENDICITIS in children.
Classic stem
Child with a recent cold/URTI, now abdominal pain, NO guarding, self-limiting.
Causes
Viruses (adenovirus, coxsackie, EBV) and bacteria — classically YERSINIA enterocolitica.
Distinguish
From appendicitis: preceding URTI, higher/spiking fever, cervical nodes, NO peritonism, fluctuating pain that settles (vs appendicitis = migrating right iliac fossa pain, guarding/rebound, progressive).
Safety
Always EXCLUDE appendicitis — use active observation/serial exams ± ultrasound; don’t anchor.
Ultrasound
≥3 enlarged mesenteric nodes (≥8 mm) + NORMAL appendix. Bloods (WCC/CRP) don’t reliably discriminate.
Management
Supportive (reassurance, analgesia, fluids) — self-limiting in ~2–4 weeks; safety-net for evolving appendicitis.
PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & Abdominal Wal:
Overview — neonatal GI & abdominal wall
Congenital gut and abdominal-wall anomalies plus the acquired bowel emergency of prematurity (NEC).
The organising principle: many present with neonatal bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension, failure to pass meconium) or are seen at birth (abdominal-wall defects). NEC is an acquired emergency in preterm/formula-fed neonates.
ConditionClue
Duodenal atresiabilious vomiting, “double bubble” on X-ray; assoc. Down syndrome
Biliary atresiaprolonged conjugated jaundice, pale stools/dark urine; Kasai portoenterostomy early
Gastroschisis & omphalocelegastroschisis (no sac, right of cord, isolated) vs omphalocele (sac, assoc. anomalies)
Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC)preterm; feeding intolerance, distension, bloody stool, pneumatosis; stop feeds, antibiotics, surgery if perforation
Prolonged conjugated (direct) jaundice with pale stools = biliary atresia until proven otherwise → urgent referral (Kasai success depends on early surgery). In NEC: stop feeds, decompress, antibiotics; watch for perforation.
What & Why

Duodenal atresia is a congenital complete obstruction of the duodenal lumen — the commonest cause of congenital (proximal) small-bowel obstruction in the neonate. It matters because it presents in the first day of life with vomiting, because it has the classic “double bubble” sign (a favourite radiology teaching image), and because of its strong association with Down syndrome and other anomalies — so a diagnosis of duodenal atresia mandates a hunt for those.

The core mechanism: failure of recanalisation of the duodenal lumen during the ~8th week of fetal development (the duodenum normally becomes a solid cord then re-hollows; if it doesn’t → an atretic, blind-ending segment). This is different from the ischaemic/vascular cause of more distal (jejunal/ileal) atresias.
The Decisive Fork — Level Relative to the Ampulla of Vater (bilious or not?)

This determines whether the vomit is green — a key exam discriminator:

Distal to the ampulla (~85%)Proximal to the ampulla (~15%)
VomitingBILIOUS (green) — bile enters above the obstructionNON-bilious (clear/milk)
FrequencyMost casesMinority
Because most obstructions are distal to the ampulla, duodenal atresia usually causes BILIOUS vomiting — but a proximal one is non-bilious. Remember: ANY bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until obstruction is excluded (the key differential being malrotation with volvulus).
Clinical Features
  • Vomiting within the FIRST DAY of life (a complete obstruction presents early); usually bilious (distal to ampulla), non-bilious if proximal
  • “Double bubble” on imaging (see below)
  • Epigastric distension only (or no distension) — the abdomen is often scaphoid/flat distally (obstruction is high → distal bowel is empty/gasless), unlike distal obstructions which distend the whole abdomen
  • Failure to pass meconium may occur; excessive salivation
  • May be picked up ANTENATALLY — polyhydramnios (fetus can’t swallow/absorb amniotic fluid past the obstruction) + a double bubble on the fetal ultrasound
Associations
A diagnosis of duodenal atresia triggers a search for these — high-yield.
  • Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — ~1/3 of duodenal atresia cases (the classic link); karyotyping is indicated
  • Congenital heart disease (~half)
  • Annular pancreas, malrotation, oesophageal atresia/tracheo-oesophageal fistula, imperforate anus, renal anomalies, biliary anomalies (VACTERL-type)
  • Prematurity, maternal polyhydramnios
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — “Double bubble” on AXR — dilated gas-filled stomach + proximal duodenum with no distal gas (duodenal atresia); distal gas instead points to stenosis or malrotation/volvulus
  • Abdominal X-ray — “DOUBLE BUBBLE” sign: two gas-filled bubbles (dilated stomach + dilated proximal duodenum) with NO/little gas distally (the atresia blocks air passing on). Usually diagnostic — often no further imaging needed
  • Gas distal to the double bubble → suggests duodenal STENOSIS (partial) or, importantly, MALROTATION/VOLVULUS rather than complete atresia — a crucial distinction
  • Upper GI contrast study + ultrasound — for equivocal cases / to exclude malrotation
  • Echocardiography + karyotype (screen the associations); electrolytes (dehydration/losses)
Management
  • Immediate/supportive: nasogastric tube (decompress the stomach), IV fluid resuscitation, and correct electrolyte disturbance (vomiting → hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis) — stabilise first
  • Definitive: surgical repair — duodenoduodenostomy (bypass the atretic segment, joining the two duodenal ends); good outcomes
  • Screen/manage the associated anomalies (cardiac, Down syndrome, etc.)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest congenital proximal small-bowel obstruction; failure of duodenal recanalisation (~week 8).
Presentation
Day 1 vomiting — BILIOUS if distal to the ampulla (~85%), NON-bilious if proximal.
Red flag
Any bilious vomiting in a neonate = surgical emergency (exclude malrotation/volvulus).
Imaging
“DOUBLE BUBBLE” on AXR (dilated stomach + proximal duodenum, no distal gas) = diagnostic; gas distally → think stenosis or malrotation/volvulus.
Antenatal
Polyhydramnios + double bubble on ultrasound.
Associations
DOWN SYNDROME (~1/3 — karyotype!), congenital heart disease, annular pancreas, malrotation, oesophageal atresia, VACTERL.
Management
NG decompression + IV fluids + correct hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis → duodenoduodenostomy.
Abdomen
Often scaphoid/flat distally (high obstruction) — contrast with distal obstructions that distend the whole abdomen.
What & Why

Biliary atresia is a progressive, obliterative cholangiopathy of the newborn — an inflammatory destruction and fibrosis of the bile ducts that blocks bile flow (obstructive cholestasis) and, if untreated, leads to cirrhosis, liver failure, and death by ~2 years. It matters because it’s the commonest surgical cause of neonatal cholestasis and the leading indication for paediatric liver transplantation, and — crucially — because outcome depends entirely on EARLY diagnosis and surgery: the Kasai portoenterostomy works far better if done before ~60 days of life. This is why any baby jaundiced beyond 14 days must have a SPLIT (conjugated/unconjugated) bilirubin.

The core mechanism: progressive inflammation and fibrosis obliterate the extrahepatic (± intrahepatic) bile ducts → bile can’t drain → conjugated (direct) bilirubin backs up (obstructive/cholestatic picture) → progressive hepatic fibrosis → cirrhosis. The cause is unknown (likely immune/inflammatory ± viral/genetic).
The Decisive Fork — Conjugated vs Unconjugated Jaundice

This is THE reason biliary atresia matters in the jaundice work-up — it flips a benign picture into a surgical emergency:

Conjugated (direct) — pathologicalUnconjugated (indirect) — usually benign
SuggestsBiliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, infection, metabolic (galactosaemia, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency)Physiological jaundice, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis
Stools/urinePALE stools + DARK urine (obstructive)Normal-coloured stools/urine
ActionUrgent liver/surgical work-upReassure/monitor (mostly)
The rule: any TERM infant still jaundiced at >14 days (or preterm >21 days) → do a “jaundice screen” including a SPLIT bilirubin. A raised CONJUGATED fraction → think biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Clinical Features
  • Persistent (prolonged) neonatal JAUNDICE beyond 2 weeks — the presenting feature
  • PALE / acholic (clay-coloured) stools — a specific clue (no bile pigment reaching the gut); can be missed → false reassurance
  • DARK urine (conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble → excreted renally)
  • The baby often initially looks WELL and thrives early on — a trap; hepatomegaly develops
  • Later (if untreated, >3 months): hepatosplenomegaly, faltering growth, ascites, coagulopathy (vitamin K malabsorption → bleeding), signs of cirrhosis
  • Associations: Biliary Atresia Splenic Malformation (BASM) syndrome — polysplenia/asplenia (~10–15%), situs inversus, cardiac defects, intestinal malrotation
Investigations
  • SPLIT (conjugated/unconjugated) bilirubin — the key first test: raised CONJUGATED (direct) fraction
  • LFTs: raised transaminases and especially raised GGT
  • Coagulation screen (vitamin-K-dependent factors; bleeding risk)
  • Jaundice screen: TFTs (hypothyroid), FBC/blood film, urine MC&S (UTI), U&E, galactosaemia screen (reducing substances/enzyme), infection/TORCH, alpha-1-antitrypsin, metabolic
  • Abdominal ultrasound — absent/abnormal gallbladder, “triangular cord” sign; excludes a choledochal cyst
  • HIDA (hepatobiliary) scan — no excretion of tracer into the bowel
  • Liver biopsy (bile duct proliferation, fibrosis) + intra-operative cholangiogram — the definitive/confirmatory test (demonstrates the obstruction)
Management
Time-critical — guideline-verified.
  • Kasai portoenterostomy — the first-line surgical treatment: a Roux loop of jejunum is anastomosed to the porta hepatis to allow bile drainage (bypassing the obliterated extrahepatic ducts)
  • Time-critical — best outcomes if done BEFORE ~60 days of life (some say <45 days); the older the infant, the worse the result (progressive fibrosis) — age at surgery is the single most important prognostic factor
  • Supportive: fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K) (cholestasis → malabsorption), nutritional support (MCT-based feeds), ursodeoxycholic acid, treat/prevent cholangitis (a common post-Kasai complication)
  • Liver transplantation — the definitive treatment if the Kasai fails or cirrhosis/liver failure develops; biliary atresia is the commonest indication for paediatric liver transplant (many children ultimately need one, even after a successful Kasai)
  • Centralised care — in the UK, managed in a few specialist supraregional centres
Exam Pearls
What it is
Progressive fibro-obliteration of bile ducts → obstructive (CONJUGATED) cholestasis → cirrhosis/death by ~2 yrs if untreated.
Presentation
PROLONGED neonatal jaundice (>2 wks) + PALE stools + DARK urine; baby initially thrives (a trap).
THE rule
Any term infant jaundiced >14 days (preterm >21) → SPLIT bilirubin. Raised CONJUGATED fraction = biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Investigations
↑conjugated bilirubin, ↑GGT/transaminases; ultrasound (absent gallbladder, “triangular cord”); HIDA (no bowel excretion); liver biopsy + intra-op cholangiogram (definitive).
Treatment
KASAI portoenterostomy — best if BEFORE ~60 days (age = key prognostic factor); fat-soluble vitamins (A,D,E,K); LIVER TRANSPLANT if Kasai fails/cirrhosis (commonest paediatric transplant indication).
Association
BASM (polysplenia), situs inversus, cardiac/malrotation.
Contrast
Breast-milk/physiological jaundice = UNconjugated, normal stools/urine, benign.
What & Why

Gastroschisis and omphalocele (exomphalos) are the two congenital anterior abdominal wall defects in which abdominal contents herniate out through the wall at birth. They matter because they’re the classic neonatal surgical emergencies of the abdominal wall — usually diagnosed antenatally (allowing planned delivery in a tertiary centre) — and because a single feature (a covering sac or not) separates them and drives everything: the associations, the delivery plan, the immediate management, and the prognosis.

The Decisive Fork — Is There a Covering Sac?
📷 Image placeholder — Gastroschisis (no sac, defect right of the cord, bowel exposed/matted, isolated) vs omphalocele/exomphalos (midline defect covered by an amnion+peritoneum sac, strong chromosomal/syndromic associations)

This ONE feature separates them:

GastroschisisOmphalocele (exomphalos)
Covering sacNO sac — bowel exposed to amniotic fluidYES — covered by a sac (amnion + peritoneum)
LocationDefect LATERAL to the cord (usually to the right)Defect AT/THROUGH the umbilicus itself
AssociationsFew/none (usually isolated)STRONG — chromosomal & syndromic
BowelExposed → inflamed, matted, at risk of ischaemia/atresiaProtected by the sac (unless it ruptures)
DeliveryVaginal delivery can be attemptedC-section (protect the sac from rupture)
RepairUrgent — theatre ASAP (± silo)Staged/gradual closure
PrognosisGenerally good (isolated)Depends on associated anomalies
Memory: “gastroSCHISIS = Split/exposed (no sac, lateral); omphalocele/exomphalos = Encased (sac, midline/umbilical).”
Gastroschisis
  • A full-thickness defect LATERAL to the cord (usually right); NO covering sac → bowel is exposed to amniotic fluid → inflamed, thickened, matted (“peel”), and at risk of ischaemia, atresia, and heat/fluid loss
  • Risk factors: young maternal age (<20), maternal smoking, alcohol, and recreational drug use. Incidence rising
  • Usually ISOLATED — few associated anomalies (a key contrast with omphalocele)
  • Delivery: vaginal delivery can be attempted; deliver in a tertiary centre with neonatal surgery
  • Management: newborn to theatre ASAP — primary closure if possible, or a “silo” (the bowel is suspended and gradually reduced over days before closure)
Omphalocele (Exomphalos)
  • Protrusion of abdominal contents through the abdominal wall AT the umbilicus, COVERED by a sac of amniotic membrane and peritoneum → the defect is in the umbilicus itself; may contain bowel, liver, and other viscera
  • STRONG associations (the high-yield part):
  • — Chromosomal abnormalities — trisomy 13 (Patau), 18 (Edwards), 21 (Down) → karyotyping is essential
  • — Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — exomphalos + macroglossia + gigantism/overgrowth + neonatal hypoglycaemia (+ Wilms’/hepatoblastoma risk)
  • — Cardiac defects (common — echo needed), Pentalogy of Cantrell, cloacal exstrophy, renal anomalies
  • Delivery: C-section — to reduce the risk of sac rupture
  • Management: staged repair — gradual closure over 6–12 months allows the abdominal cavity/pulmonary system to accommodate the returning contents (forcing a large volume back suddenly → respiratory compromise/abdominal compartment syndrome)
Antenatal Diagnosis & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Pneumatosis intestinalis — curvilinear intramural bowel-wall gas (pathognomonic of NEC); progression to portal venous gas and free air (Rigler’s) signals perforation
  • Both are usually detected on the routine antenatal (20-week) ultrasound → plan delivery in a tertiary centre
  • Maternal serum AFP is raised in both (higher in gastroschisis)
  • Omphalocele → karyotyping (amniocentesis) + echocardiography + renal ultrasound (screen for the associations); gastroschisis → fewer investigations (usually isolated), serial growth scans (IUGR risk)
Immediate Neonatal (Postnatal) Management
  • Cover the exposed bowel/defect — wrap in clingfilm / a clear occlusive covering (or a “bowel bag”) to prevent heat and fluid loss and protect the bowel (gastroschisis especially)
  • Fluid resuscitation (large insensible losses) + thermoregulation (high heat-loss risk) + nasogastric tube (decompress the bowel) + IV antibiotics
  • Monitor perfusion of the exposed bowel; then surgical closure (primary or staged/silo)
Exam Pearls
What they are
Congenital anterior abdominal wall defects with bowel herniation; usually diagnosed on antenatal ultrasound.
Key difference
The SAC: gastroschisis has NO sac (bowel exposed); omphalocele has a covering sac (amnion + peritoneum).
Gastroschisis
Defect LATERAL to cord (right); no sac; ISOLATED (few associations); RFs = young mother, smoking/alcohol/drugs; vaginal delivery OK; theatre ASAP (± silo).
Omphalocele
Defect AT the umbilicus; covered by sac; STRONG associations — trisomy 13/18/21 (karyotype!), Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia + gigantism + hypoglycaemia), cardiac defects; C-section (avoid sac rupture); STAGED repair over months.
Both
Raised maternal serum AFP.
Immediate management
Cover the defect (clingfilm/bowel bag), fluids, keep warm, NG decompression, antibiotics → surgery.
Prognosis
Gastroschisis generally good (isolated); omphalocele depends on associated anomalies.
What & Why

Necrotising enterocolitis is a devastating inflammatory bowel disease of the neonate — inflammation, ischaemia, and bacterial invasion of the bowel wall → necrosis, which can progress to perforation, peritonitis, and death. It matters because it’s the commonest gastrointestinal emergency in the neonatal unit and one of the leading causes of death in premature infants, because it’s strongly linked to prematurity and enteral (especially formula) feeding, and because breast milk is protective — a key prevention point. Survivors risk short bowel syndrome, strictures, and neurodevelopmental impairment.

The core mechanism: a “perfect storm” in the immature gut — an immature intestinal barrier + abnormal bacterial colonisation (dysbiosis) + mucosal ischaemia/hypoperfusion + enteral feed as a substrate → bacteria breach the fragile bowel wall → inflammation and ischaemic necrosis → gas tracks into the bowel wall (pneumatosis) and portal system → perforation. This explains why it clusters in preterm, formula-fed babies after feeds are established (typically weeks 2–4).
Risk Factors
  • Prematurity + very low birth weight (the biggest — the more preterm, the higher the risk)
  • Formula feeding (breast milk is PROTECTIVE)
  • Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) / placental insufficiency, hypoxia/perinatal asphyxia
  • Anything reducing gut perfusion: congenital heart disease (especially duct-dependent/PDA), polycythaemia, exchange/RBC transfusion, sepsis, hypotension
  • Rapid advancement of enteral feeds
Clinical Features
  • Feeding intolerance — increased/bilious gastric aspirates, vomiting (often bile-stained)
  • Abdominal distension — often the first sign; ± tenderness, visible loops
  • Bloody stools (blood/mucus per rectum)
  • Systemic/non-specific: lethargy, temperature instability, apnoea/bradycardia, poor perfusion → can progress to sepsis/shock, DIC
  • Severe/late features: abdominal wall discolouration (erythema), perforation, peritonitis — signs of advanced disease needing surgery
Investigations
Abdominal X-ray — the key investigation
  • Dilated bowel loops
  • Bowel wall oedema (thickened wall)
  • Pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas — gas within the bowel WALL) — the pathognomonic/classic sign
  • Portal venous gas — a marker of more severe disease
  • Pneumoperitoneum (free air) → PERFORATION — look for “Rigler’s sign” (gas on both sides of the bowel wall) and the “football sign”
  • Bloods: FBC — thrombocytopenia (a useful early clue), anaemia, leukocytosis/leukopenia; metabolic acidosis; raised CRP; blood culture (sepsis); coagulation/DIC screen; blood gas
  • Bell staging — stages NEC I (suspected) → II (definite) → III (advanced/perforation) on clinical + radiological features (guides management)
Management
Medical (Bell I–II) — the mainstay
  • STOP enteral feeds (bowel rest / nil by mouth) and NG tube on free drainage (decompress the bowel) — typically bowel rest ~7–14 days with parenteral (IV) nutrition
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes)
  • Supportive: IV fluids, correct acidosis/electrolytes, respiratory/circulatory support, treat DIC/thrombocytopenia; serial abdominal X-rays and examinations to detect deterioration/perforation
Surgical (Bell III)
  • For perforation or deterioration despite medical management
  • Laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel (± stoma); peritoneal drain in the very small/unstable
  • Pneumoperitoneum is an indication for surgery
  • Complications: perforation/peritonitis, sepsis/DIC, strictures (later), short bowel syndrome (after resection → long-term parenteral nutrition), neurodevelopmental impairment
Prevention
  • Breast milk (maternal or donor) — the single most important protective factor
  • Antenatal corticosteroids (if preterm delivery anticipated — gut maturation), cautious/standardised feeding protocols, and probiotics (increasingly used to reduce NEC in preterms)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Inflammatory/ischaemic bowel necrosis of the neonate; commonest neonatal GI emergency; leading cause of death in preterms.
Risk
PREMATURITY + very low birth weight + FORMULA feeding (breast milk PROTECTIVE); also IUGR, CHD, hypoxia, transfusion, sepsis. Usually weeks 2–4, after feeds started.
Presentation
Feeding intolerance + abdominal distension + BLOODY stools (± bilious vomiting, lethargy, temp instability); late → abdominal discolouration, perforation, peritonitis.
AXR
Dilated loops, bowel wall oedema, PNEUMATOSIS INTESTINALIS (intramural gas — classic), PORTAL VENOUS GAS; pneumoperitoneum + RIGLER’S SIGN = perforation.
Bloods
THROMBOCYTOPENIA, metabolic acidosis, raised CRP. Staged by Bell criteria.
Management
STOP feeds (bowel rest) + NG decompression + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics + parenteral nutrition + supportive; SURGERY (resection) for perforation/deterioration.
Complications
Perforation, sepsis/DIC, strictures, SHORT BOWEL SYNDROME.
Prevention
BREAST MILK, antenatal steroids, cautious feeding, probiotics.
PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding & Reflux:
Overview — infant feeding & reflux
Common feeding-related presentations in infancy — cow's milk protein allergy and gastro-oesophageal reflux.
The organising principle: physiological reflux (posseting, otherwise thriving) usually resolves by ~1yr; red flags (poor weight gain, distress, blood) suggest GORD or CMPA (an immune reaction to cow's milk protein).
ConditionClueManagement
Cow's milk protein intolerancevomiting, diarrhoea/blood in stool, eczema, poor weight gainexclude cow's milk (extensively hydrolysed formula / maternal dairy exclusion)
Infant reflux (GOR/GORD)effortless posseting; GORD = distress/faltering growthGOR: reassure; GORD: thickened feeds, alginates, PPI
Reflux with faltering growth, marked distress, haematemesis or respiratory symptoms is GORD (not simple posseting) — investigate/treat. Consider CMPA in refractory reflux + atopy.
What & Why

Cow’s milk protein allergy is an immune-mediated adverse reaction to the proteins in cow’s milk (mainly casein and whey), and one of the commonest food allergies of infancy (~1–3% of infants). It presents in young, formula-fed (or sometimes breastfed) babies with a confusing mix of GI, skin, and respiratory symptoms that overlap with reflux, colic, and infection; the management pathway (which formula to use) is a defined, examinable ladder; and it’s both over- and under-diagnosed.

A terminology note: strictly, “allergy” = an immune-mediated reaction (IgE or non-IgE) — what CMPA/CMPI usually refers to in infants. True “intolerance” normally means a non-immune reaction (e.g. lactose intolerance — an enzyme/sugar problem, a completely different entity).
The Decisive Fork — IgE-mediated vs Non-IgE-mediated
IgE-mediated (immediate)Non-IgE-mediated (delayed)
Timing<2 hours after ingestionAfter 4 hours (up to 24–48 h/days)
MechanismImmediate hypersensitivity (mast cell/IgE)Cell-mediated (delayed)
FeaturesUrticaria, wheeze, stridor, angioedema; acute; can → anaphylaxisRectal bleeding, mucus in stool, vomiting, diarrhoea; GI-predominant
TestingSkin prick / specific IgE (RAST) helpfulNo useful blood test — diagnosis is clinical (elimination + reintroduction)
ResolutionLater — ~by 5 yearsEarlier — ~by 3 years
Some infants have mixed IgE + non-IgE features.
Presentation
  • Onset: usually in the first 3 months of life, in formula-fed infants (can also occur in exclusively breastfed babies, from maternal dairy passing into breast milk)
  • GI: regurgitation/vomiting, diarrhoea, colic (irritability, crying), rectal bleeding/mucus (non-IgE), constipation, faltering growth
  • Skin: urticaria, atopic eczema, angioedema
  • Respiratory: wheeze, chronic cough, stridor (IgE)
  • Anaphylaxis — rare but possible in IgE-mediated disease
Investigations
  • Primarily a CLINICAL diagnosis — improvement on removing cow’s milk protein, and recurrence on reintroduction is the cornerstone (especially for non-IgE disease, where tests don’t help)
  • IgE-mediated: skin prick / patch testing; total IgE and specific IgE (RAST) to cow’s milk protein
  • Non-IgE-mediated: no reliable blood/allergy test — diagnosis is the elimination-and-reintroduction trial
  • Avoid unproven tests — e.g. food-specific IgG panels (not validated → cause overdiagnosis)
Management
📷 Image placeholder — The milk ladder — reintroduction rungs from baked milk (e.g. a malted-milk biscuit) upward, alongside the extensively-hydrolysed-formula-first → amino-acid-formula ladder
If severe (failure to thrive, anaphylaxis, severe symptoms): refer to paediatrics/allergy.
🍼 Formula-fed (the formula ladder)
  • First-line (mild–moderate): Extensively Hydrolysed Formula (EHF) — cow’s-milk protein broken down so it’s not recognised (tolerated by ~90%)
  • Amino Acid Formula (AAF): if SEVERE, or no response to EHF — fully non-allergenic; only ~10% need this
  • Do NOT use: soya formula (cross-reactivity, esp. <6 months) or other mammalian milks (goat/sheep — cross-react)
🤱 Breastfed
  • Continue breastfeeding — breast milk is optimal
  • Eliminate cow’s milk protein from the MATERNAL diet + give the mother calcium (± vitamin D)
  • When breastfeeding stops → use EHF, until ~12 months of age and for at least 6 months
  • Dietitian involvement — ensure nutritional adequacy (calcium/vitamin D), avoid hidden allergens, prevent unnecessary long-term restriction
  • The “milk ladder” — planned reintroduction in stages, starting with small amounts of BAKED milk (e.g. malted-milk biscuit) → progressing up — to confirm resolution + build tolerance (for non-IgE/lower-risk; supervised/specialist for IgE-mediated)
  • Most children outgrow it (non-IgE ~3 yrs, IgE ~5 yrs)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Immune reaction to cow’s-milk protein; commonest in first 3 months, formula-fed (or breastfed via maternal dairy).
IgE-mediated
Immediate (<2 h): urticaria, wheeze, stridor, angioedema, ± anaphylaxis; skin prick/specific IgE useful; resolves ~5 yrs.
Non-IgE-mediated
Delayed (>4 h–days): vomiting, diarrhoea, rectal bleeding/mucus, eczema, colic; NO useful blood test (clinical dx); resolves ~3 yrs.
Diagnosis
Clinical (elimination + reintroduction); avoid unproven IgG panels.
Formula-fed
EHF first-line (mild-mod) → AAF if severe/no response. Avoid soya & other mammalian milks.
Breastfed
Continue breastfeeding + remove cow’s milk from mother’s diet + maternal calcium; EHF when breastfeeding stops (to ~12 months, ≥6 months).
Reintroduction
Dietitian input; reintroduce via the MILK LADDER (baked milk first).
Distinguish
From LACTOSE intolerance (non-immune, enzyme/sugar problem — a different entity).
What & Why

Gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) is the passage of stomach contents up into the oesophagus — in babies, effortless posseting/regurgitation of milk after feeds. It’s extremely common and physiological (≥40% of infants) and, in a thriving baby, needs only reassurance, not treatment — yet it’s frequently over-medicalised. The key skill is distinguishing benign GOR from GORD (reflux disease) and from serious mimics (pyloric stenosis, obstruction, CMPA).

Why it’s so common in babies: infants have a short, narrow oesophagus, a relatively incompetent/immature lower oesophageal sphincter, a large fluid milk volume, and spend a lot of time lying flat → milk easily flows back up. As the baby matures, sits up, and takes solids, it resolves — ~90% by 12 months.
The Decisive Fork — GOR vs GORD
GOR (physiological)GORD (reflux disease)
NatureNormal, effortless regurgitationReflux causing symptoms/complications
BabyWell, thriving, “happy spitter”Distressed / unwell / faltering
FeaturesPosseting after feeds, otherwise contentFaltering growth, feed refusal, marked distress/pain, oesophagitis, chronic cough/wheeze (aspiration), recurrent chest infections
ActionReassure; no treatmentStepped-care treatment ± investigation/referral
Key teaching point: GOR does NOT cause crying/irritability in an otherwise healthy, thriving infant. If a baby is genuinely distressed or not growing, think GORD or an alternative diagnosis — not “just reflux”.
Clinical Features of GORD
  • Regurgitation/vomiting WITH poor weight gain / faltering growth
  • Feeding difficulties — refusal, pulling off the feed, distress/pain during feeds
  • Marked, unexplained irritability/crying (especially with arching)
  • Sandifer syndrome — episodic dystonic posturing: torticollis (neck twisting) + back arching (can be mistaken for seizures)
  • Respiratory: chronic cough, wheeze (aspiration), recurrent chest infections, apnoea/BRUE; oesophagitis (haematemesis, pain), dental erosion (older children)
Red Flags — NOT Reflux, Investigate/Refer
  • BILIOUS (green) vomiting → intestinal obstruction (e.g. malrotation/volvulus) — urgent, same-day surgical referral (never ignore green vomit)
  • Projectile, non-bilious vomiting in a 2–8-week-old → pyloric stenosis
  • Haematemesis/melaena, abdominal distension/tenderness, bulging fontanelle/altered consciousness (raised ICP), blood in stool
  • Onset of regurgitation AFTER 6 months, or persisting beyond 1 year (atypical for simple GOR)
  • Fever/lethargy (infection, incl. UTI/meningitis), faltering growth, chronic diarrhoea
  • Consider CMPA — eczema, family history of atopy, other GI symptoms → CMPA can present as/with reflux
Investigations
  • Usually a CLINICAL diagnosis — investigations rarely needed
  • Consider urinalysis (exclude UTI if faltering growth/late onset); further tests only if diagnostic doubt/complications/red flags:
  • pH/impedance monitoring (quantify acid/non-acid reflux), upper GI endoscopy (suspected oesophagitis/other diagnosis), contrast study (if anatomical/obstruction suspected)
Management (NICE NG1, stepped care)
📷 Image placeholder — Stepped-care flowchart — separate breastfed vs formula-fed arms: feeding review → (breastfed) alginate / (formula) thickened feed → alginate → PPI/H2RA only for distress, faltering growth or oesophagitis
GOR (well, thriving infant): REASSURE — no treatment. Explain it’s common and resolves (usually by ~1 year); return if red flags/faltering growth develop.
  • 1. Feeding review — assess technique/volume; avoid overfeeding (smaller, more frequent feeds); breastfeeding assessment if breastfed
  • 2. Breastfed: breastfeeding assessment → if persists, trial of alginate (Gaviscon Infant) for 1–2 weeks
  • 3. Formula-fed: review feed volumes → thickened (anti-reflux) formula → if unsuccessful, stop thickener and trial alginate for 1–2 weeks
  • 4. Acid suppression — only if specific indications: do NOT offer PPI/H2RA for overt regurgitation alone in an otherwise-well infant. Consider a PPI (or H2RA) trial only if unexplained feeding difficulties, distressed behaviour, or faltering growth with suspected acid reflux/oesophagitis
  • 5. Endoscopy-proven reflux oesophagitis → PPI/H2RA treatment; do NOT use prokinetics (metoclopramide/domperidone/erythromycin) without specialist advice
  • 6. Specialist referral / fundoplication — for severe, intractable GORD unresponsive to medical treatment, or complications
Safe sleep caveat: do NOT use positional (head-up/prone/side) management to treat reflux in sleeping infants — babies must be placed on their BACK to sleep (SIDS prevention overrides reflux positioning).
Exam Pearls
GOR
Normal, effortless regurgitation in a WELL, thriving infant (≥40% of babies) → REASSURE, resolves by ~1 year (~90%). No treatment.
GORD
Reflux causing complications: faltering growth, feed refusal, marked distress/pain, oesophagitis, cough/wheeze (aspiration).
Key point
GOR does NOT cause crying/irritability in a healthy thriving baby — if distressed/not growing, think GORD or another cause.
Red flags
BILIOUS (green) vomiting → obstruction (urgent); projectile non-bilious at 2–8 wks → pyloric stenosis; onset >6 months/persisting >1 yr; haematemesis; bulging fontanelle. Consider CMPA (eczema/atopy).
Sandifer
Torticollis + back arching (mimics seizures).
Stepped care
Feeding review → (breastfed) alginate; (formula) thickened feed → alginate → PPI/H2RA ONLY for distress/faltering growth/oesophagitis (NOT overt regurgitation alone).
Safe sleep
Do NOT position babies for reflux in sleep — BACK to sleep (SIDS). Avoid prokinetics without specialist advice; fundoplication for severe intractable GORD.
PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medicine:
Overview — neonatal medicine
Core neonatal problems — respiratory, metabolic, infective and neurological — in the term and preterm baby.
The organising principle: prematurity and perinatal events drive most neonatal illness. Approach by system: breathing (RDS, meconium aspiration), metabolic (jaundice, hypoglycaemia), infection (sepsis) and brain (HIE).
ConditionKey points
Neonatal RDSpreterm surfactant deficiency; grunting, ground-glass X-ray; antenatal steroids, surfactant, CPAP
Meconium aspiration syndrometerm/post-term, meconium-stained liquor; respiratory distress; supportive/ventilation
Neonatal jaundice<24h = always pathological (haemolysis/sepsis); phototherapy/exchange by threshold; kernicterus risk
Neonatal sepsisnon-specific (temperature instability, poor feeding); cultures + empirical antibiotics promptly
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)perinatal hypoxia; encephalopathy; therapeutic cooling within 6h
Neonatal hypoglycaemiajittery, poor feeding, seizures; at-risk (IUGR, IDM, preterm); feed / IV dextrose
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological (urgent bilirubin; exclude haemolysis/sepsis). Treat suspected neonatal sepsis empirically without delay; offer cooling for moderate–severe HIE within 6 hours.
What & Why

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) — also called surfactant deficient lung disease, and historically hyaline membrane disease — is an acute lung disease of the newborn caused by insufficient pulmonary surfactant, leading to alveolar collapse and stiff, poorly-inflated lungs. It matters because it’s the commonest cause of respiratory distress in premature infants, its incidence rises steeply the more preterm the baby is, and it’s one of the great preventable/treatable neonatal conditions — antenatal corticosteroids and exogenous surfactant have transformed survival.

The core mechanism: surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes (which mature ~weeks 24–34 of gestation). In prematurity, insufficient surfactant + structural lung immaturity → high alveolar surface tension → alveoli collapse (atelectasis) → the lungs are stiff/non-compliant, and blood passing collapsed alveoli isn’t oxygenated (intrapulmonary shunt) → hypoxaemia + increased work of breathing. Surfactant’s job is to lower surface tension and stop alveoli collapsing — so its absence is the whole disease.
Risk Factors
  • Prematurity — the biggest; risk is inversely proportional to gestational age (very common <28 weeks, uncommon at term)
  • Male sex
  • Maternal diabetes — fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production (a key link)
  • Caesarean section (especially without labour — less stress-hormone surge)
  • Also: second twin, perinatal asphyxia/hypothermia, family history
Clinical Features
  • Onset within minutes–hours of birth (typically <4 hours), worsening over the first ~48–72 h
  • Signs of respiratory distress — the common newborn picture:
  • — Tachypnoea
  • — Intercostal (± subcostal) recession
  • — Expiratory grunting (grunting = auto-PEEP against a closed glottis to keep alveoli open)
  • — Cyanosis; nasal flaring, apnoea (in the very preterm)
Investigations
  • Chest X-ray — “ground-glass” appearance with an indistinct heart border: diffuse fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) shadowing + air bronchograms + reduced lung volumes, obscuring the cardiac/diaphragmatic borders (from widespread atelectasis)
  • Blood gas: hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, respiratory ± metabolic acidosis
  • Screen for/exclude sepsis (blood culture, FBC, CRP) — congenital pneumonia (e.g. Group B Strep) can look identical
  • (Antenatally: lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio on amniotic fluid indicates lung maturity — historical)
Management
Guideline-verified — prevention plus a stepwise respiratory-support ladder.
Prevention (antenatal)
  • Maternal (antenatal) corticosteroids to induce fetal lung maturation
  • Give to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (e.g. <34–36 weeks) → accelerates surfactant production
  • Reduces RDS, intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH), and neonatal death
Postnatal (respiratory-support ladder)
  • CPAP is first-line respiratory support (keeps alveoli open, often avoids intubation), escalating to mechanical ventilation if needed
  • Exogenous surfactant via an endotracheal tube — replaces the missing surfactant; increasingly given by minimally invasive techniques (LISA/MIST — a thin catheter without full intubation)
  • Supportive: thermoregulation, fluids/nutrition, treat sepsis, gentle handling
Complications
  • Pneumothorax / air leak (stiff lungs + positive-pressure ventilation)
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD / chronic lung disease of prematurity) — oxygen requirement persisting beyond 36 weeks corrected age (from lung injury + oxygen/ventilation)
  • Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH), patent ductus arteriosus, retinopathy of prematurity, necrotising enterocolitis (the wider prematurity complications), infection
Exam Pearls
What it is
Surfactant deficient lung disease / hyaline membrane disease = insufficient surfactant → alveolar collapse → stiff lungs + hypoxaemia. Surfactant made by TYPE II PNEUMOCYTES (mature ~24–34 wks).
Risk
PREMATURITY (biggest — inverse to gestation), male, MATERNAL DIABETES (fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant), C-section.
Presentation
Within hours of birth: tachypnoea, intercostal recession, expiratory GRUNTING, cyanosis, nasal flaring.
CXR
Diffuse “GROUND-GLASS” reticulogranular shadowing + air bronchograms + indistinct heart border.
Prevention
ANTENATAL CORTICOSTEROIDS (mother at risk of preterm birth) — reduces RDS/IVH/death.
Treatment
CPAP (first-line) ± ventilation + EXOGENOUS SURFACTANT (endotracheal/LISA) + oxygen + supportive.
Complications
Pneumothorax/air leak, BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA (O2 need beyond 36 wks), IVH, patent ductus arteriosus, retinopathy of prematurity.
Differentials
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN — term/C-section, self-resolves ~24–48h) and congenital pneumonia (Group B Strep).
What & Why

Meconium aspiration syndrome is respiratory distress in a newborn caused by aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid (MSAF) into the lungs. It matters because it’s an important cause of respiratory distress in TERM and POST-TERM infants (the opposite end of the gestational spectrum to RDS), because it causes disease through multiple mechanisms at once (obstruction + inflammation + surfactant inactivation), and because it’s strongly linked to the feared complication persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

The core sequence: fetal distress/hypoxia (or maturity) → the fetus passes meconium into the amniotic fluid AND gasps → meconium is inhaled into the airways.
Once in the lungs, meconium causes disease four ways
  • Airway obstruction — meconium plugs airways; a “ball-valve” effect → air trapping/hyperinflation → risk of pneumothorax/air leak (some areas), and atelectasis (others)
  • Chemical pneumonitis / inflammation (meconium is irritant)
  • Surfactant inactivation (free fatty acids/bile acids inactivate surfactant → collapse)
  • Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) — hypoxia → pulmonary vasoconstriction → the circulation reverts to a right-to-left shunt (fetal-type) → refractory hypoxaemia
Risk Factors
  • Post-term / post-maturity — the classic (mature gut passes meconium more readily); MSAF is common beyond term
  • Fetal distress / intrapartum hypoxia-asphyxia — the single most important risk factor (hypoxia → meconium passage + gasping)
  • Small-for-gestational-age / IUGR, placental insufficiency, difficult/prolonged labour
  • MSAF is rare in preterm labour — if present, think chorioamnionitis/infection or cord compression (a useful point)
Clinical Features
  • Onset immediately/soon after birth, in a term/post-term baby
  • Meconium-stained (green) liquor and meconium staining of the skin/nails/cord (green-yellow)
  • Respiratory distress — tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, recession, cyanosis; often a barrel/hyperinflated chest (air trapping); crackles/rhonchi
  • Signs of the underlying insult — may be depressed/asphyxiated at birth (low Apgars)
  • Watch for PPHN — severe/labile hypoxaemia out of proportion to lung findings
Investigations
  • Chest X-ray — patchy infiltrates and atelectasis, with hyperinflation and areas of consolidation/collapse; ± pneumothorax/air leak (look for it)
  • Blood gas: hypoxaemia, ± hypercapnia, acidosis
  • Pre-/post-ductal saturations + echocardiography if PPHN suspected (right-to-left shunt)
  • Sepsis screen (MAS mimics/co-exists with congenital pneumonia)
Management
Delivery-room change (high-yield): routine deep endotracheal suctioning of meconium-stained babies is NO LONGER recommended — even NON-VIGOROUS infants: follow normal neonatal resuscitation (airway, breathing). Suction only if the airway is obstructed (the old “always intubate and suction” teaching is outdated).
Postnatal (supportive — the mainstay)
  • Oxygen and respiratory support — CPAP/mechanical ventilation as needed (careful — air trapping + atelectasis makes ventilation tricky); high-frequency (HFOV) ventilation in severe cases
  • Exogenous surfactant (meconium inactivates surfactant) and/or surfactant lavage — used in moderate–severe MAS
  • Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) — for PPHN (pulmonary vasodilator); ECMO as rescue in refractory PPHN/respiratory failure
  • Supportive: antibiotics (can’t exclude infection), thermoregulation, fluids, treat air leaks (chest drain for pneumothorax), monitor for hypoxic-ischaemic injury
Exam Pearls
What it is
Respiratory distress from aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid; TERM/POST-TERM infants (contrast RDS = preterm).
Risk factors
POST-MATURITY + fetal distress/HYPOXIA-ASPHYXIA (most important) + IUGR/SGA. MSAF in preterm → think infection/cord compression.
Four mechanisms
Airway obstruction (ball-valve → air trapping/pneumothorax + atelectasis), chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation, and PPHN.
Presentation
At/soon after birth: meconium-stained liquor/skin, respiratory distress, hyperinflated chest.
CXR
Patchy infiltrates + atelectasis + hyperinflation ± pneumothorax.
Delivery room
Routine endotracheal suctioning NO LONGER recommended (even non-vigorous babies) — normal resuscitation; suction only if airway obstructed.
Treatment
Supportive — O2/ventilation (± HFOV), surfactant, antibiotics; iNO ± ECMO for PPHN.
Complications
PPHN and air leak (pneumothorax).
What & Why

Neonatal jaundice is yellow discolouration of the skin/sclera from raised bilirubin (hyperbilirubinaemia) in a newborn. It matters because it’s extremely common (>50% of term, most preterm babies) — usually benign and physiological — but a minority is pathological and dangerous, because severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause KERNICTERUS (permanent brain injury), and because the whole clinical skill is using the TIMING to separate benign from serious.

The core physiology (why newborns get jaundiced): newborns have a high red-cell mass with a short lifespan (rapid breakdown of fetal Hb → more bilirubin) + an immature liver (low UGT enzyme activity → can’t conjugate it fast enough) + increased enterohepatic circulation. So a mild rise is normal; the job is spotting when it’s too early, too high, or too prolonged.
The Decisive Fork — the TIMING of Onset
📷 Image placeholder — Neonatal jaundice timeline — <24h (always pathological, haemolytic) vs day 2–14 (physiological) vs >14 days (prolonged → biliary atresia/hypothyroidism)

This framework is the entire clinical approach:

TimingInterpretationKey causes
<24 hoursALWAYS PATHOLOGICAL — usually haemolysisRhesus & ABO haemolytic disease, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency; congenital infection/sepsis
~Day 2–14 (peaks 3–5)Usually PHYSIOLOGICAL (or breast-milk/breastfeeding jaundice) — unconjugated, benignPhysiological, breastfeeding/breast-milk jaundice, bruising/cephalohaematoma, polycythaemia, sepsis
>14 days (prolonged; >21 days if preterm)PATHOLOGICAL until proven otherwise → JAUNDICE SCREENBiliary atresia, hypothyroidism, galactosaemia, UTI, breast-milk jaundice, prematurity
<24 Hours — Always Pathological
  • Jaundice in the first 24 hours is NEVER physiological
  • Must urgently check serum bilirubin (within ~2 hours) — risk of severe hyperbilirubinaemia
  • Usually HAEMOLYTIC: Rhesus haemolytic disease, ABO incompatibility, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency — plus congenital infection/sepsis (TORCH)
Physiological Jaundice (day 2–14)
  • Unconjugated, appears after 24 hours, peaks ~day 3–5, resolves by ~day 10–14; the baby is WELL and feeding. A diagnosis of exclusion
  • Breastfeeding jaundice (early, from suboptimal intake/dehydration → more enterohepatic circulation) vs breast-milk jaundice (later/prolonged, benign, from breast-milk factors — a common cause of prolonged jaundice in a thriving baby)
  • Prematurity exaggerates and prolongs physiological jaundice (immature liver + shorter red-cell survival)
Prolonged Jaundice (>14 days)
  • Any term baby jaundiced beyond 14 days (preterm >21 days) → a “jaundice screen”: conjugated + unconjugated (split) bilirubin, Coombs (DAT), TFTs, FBC (± film), urine MC&S, U&E, LFTs (+ blood group, G6PD, infection/metabolic screen)
  • The split bilirubin is the key branch point:
  • — CONJUGATED (>~25 µmol/L or >20%) → pathological → BILIARY ATRESIA until proven otherwise (pale stools/dark urine), neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, metabolic
  • — Unconjugated → hypothyroidism, UTI/infection, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis, galactosaemia
  • Causes: biliary atresia, hypothyroidism, galactosaemia, UTI, breast-milk jaundice, prematurity
Investigations
  • Bilirubin measurement: transcutaneous bilirubinometer (screening, ≥35 weeks & >24h) → serum bilirubin (SBR) to confirm/if high-risk; always SBR if <24 hours old or <35 weeks
  • Plot the SBR on the gestational-age-specific treatment threshold chart (NICE) — this decides treatment
  • Cause work-up: blood group + DAT/Coombs (haemolysis), FBC/film, G6PD, split bilirubin, sepsis/TORCH, TFTs, metabolic (as above)
Management
  • Plot SBR against age (hours) on the NICE threshold graph → treatment is guided by how the level compares to the phototherapy and exchange lines. Support feeding/hydration
  • Phototherapy — first-line: blue light (~450 nm) converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin to water-soluble isomers excreted without conjugation. Escalate to multiple/intensified phototherapy if rising fast or nearing exchange threshold
  • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) — adjunct in Rhesus/ABO haemolytic disease when bilirubin keeps rising despite intensive phototherapy
  • Exchange transfusion — for very high/rapidly rising bilirubin (above the exchange line, or signs of bilirubin encephalopathy) — removes bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells; prevents kernicterus
  • Treat the cause (antibiotics for sepsis/UTI, thyroxine for hypothyroidism, surgery for biliary atresia, etc.)
Kernicterus (the reason it matters)
📷 Image placeholder — Kernicterus — unconjugated bilirubin crossing the blood–brain barrier to the basal ganglia; acute encephalopathy signs and chronic sequelae (choreoathetoid CP, sensorineural deafness)
Only UNCONJUGATED bilirubin causes kernicterus (conjugated is water-soluble, doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier) — which is why the split matters and why we treat unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia aggressively.
  • Unconjugated (fat-soluble) bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier → deposits in the basal ganglia → bilirubin encephalopathy
  • Acute: lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia → then irritability, hypertonia, arching (opisthotonos), high-pitched cry, seizures
  • Chronic (permanent): choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upward-gaze palsy, dental enamel dysplasia, learning difficulty
Exam Pearls
What it is
Raised bilirubin; very common; mostly physiological but a minority pathological. Newborns predisposed: high red-cell turnover + immature liver (low UGT).
TIMING
<24 h = ALWAYS pathological (HAEMOLYSIS — Rhesus/ABO/spherocytosis/G6PD; check SBR urgently). Day 2–14 = usually physiological/breast-milk (well baby). >14 days (>21 preterm) = prolonged → JAUNDICE SCREEN.
Prolonged
SPLIT bilirubin — CONJUGATED → BILIARY ATRESIA until proven otherwise (pale stools/dark urine); unconjugated → hypothyroid, UTI, breast-milk, haemolysis, galactosaemia.
Investigations
Transcutaneous bilirubin (screen) → SERUM bilirubin; always SBR if <24 h or preterm; plot on NICE threshold chart; DAT/Coombs, blood group, G6PD, FBC.
Management
Threshold-driven: PHOTOTHERAPY (converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers) → IVIG (Rhesus/ABO) → EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION for very high/rising levels.
Kernicterus
Unconjugated bilirubin crosses blood-brain barrier → basal ganglia → choreoathetoid CP, sensorineural deafness, gaze palsy. Only UNCONJUGATED bilirubin causes it.
What & Why

Neonatal sepsis is a systemic bacterial infection in the first 28 days of life — a medical emergency because newborns have an immature immune system, deteriorate rapidly, and present with vague, non-specific signs that can be catastrophic if missed. It matters because it’s a major cause of neonatal death and disability, because Group B Streptococcus and E. coli are the leading organisms, and because the whole clinical approach is “have a low threshold — treat first, ask questions later”: identify risk factors and red flags, take cultures, and start antibiotics within 1 hour.

The Decisive Fork — Early-Onset vs Late-Onset

This determines the organisms, source, and antibiotics:

Early-onset sepsisLate-onset sepsis
Timing<72 hours (often <24 h) of life>72 hours – 28 days
SourceVertical — acquired from the mother (birth canal/ascending infection)Environmental/nosocomial (hands, lines, ventilators)
OrganismsGroup B Strep + E. coli (also Listeria)Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (esp. lines), Staph aureus, Gram-negatives, Group B Strep, fungal (Candida)
Risk groupMaternal risk factorsPreterm, low birth weight, indwelling lines/devices, prolonged neonatal-unit stay
Risk Factors (early-onset)
These trigger the assessment/antibiotics — high-yield.
  • Maternal Group B Strep — colonisation, Group B Strep bacteriuria, or a previous baby with invasive Group B Strep disease
  • Prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM, >18–24 h); preterm labour / prematurity
  • Chorioamnionitis / maternal intrapartum fever (>38°C) or confirmed maternal infection
  • A previous baby with Group B Strep disease
  • NICE “red flag” risk factors (e.g. suspected/confirmed infection in a co-twin) → prompt immediate treatment
Clinical Features

Non-specific — the septic neonate looks non-specifically unwell:

  • Respiratory: grunting, tachypnoea, apnoea, increased O2 requirement, cyanosis
  • Temperature instability — fever OR (more commonly in neonates) HYPOthermia
  • Feeding/GI: poor feeding, vomiting, abdominal distension
  • Neuro: lethargy, irritability, hypotonia, seizures (→ meningitis), a bulging fontanelle
  • Circulatory: tachy-/bradycardia, poor perfusion/mottling, hypotension, prolonged capillary refill
  • Other: jaundice (especially <24 h), hypo-/hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, DIC/bleeding
  • “Red flag” signs (NICE) → treat immediately: signs of shock, seizures, need for mechanical ventilation, respiratory distress starting >4 h after birth
Investigations
Guideline-verified — NICE NG195.
  • Blood culture — BEFORE the first antibiotic dose (the key investigation; don’t delay antibiotics for it)
  • FBC (neutropenia or neutrophilia, thrombocytopenia), CRP (at baseline and repeated ~18–24 h — trend guides duration)
  • Lumbar puncture — if strong clinical suspicion / meningitis signs / culture-positive (neonatal meningitis is common with sepsis)
  • Blood gas (acidosis), glucose, U&E; surface/urine cultures, CXR as indicated; late-onset → sample lines
Management
Time-critical — start empirical IV antibiotics WITHIN 1 HOUR of deciding to treat; don’t wait for results (NICE NG195).
Empirical antibiotics
  • Early-onset: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin (the standard UK regimen — covers Group B Strep, E. coli, Listeria)
  • Late-onset (on the neonatal unit): flucloxacillin + gentamicin (or per local policy — cover coagulase-negative staph/line infection; add Gram-negative/Listeria cover as needed)
Supportive + review
  • Supportive: respiratory support (O2/ventilation), fluids/inotropes for shock, glucose, correct acidosis/coagulopathy (DIC), thermoregulation
  • Review at ~36 hours: stop antibiotics if the baby is well, blood cultures are negative, and CRP is normal/falling
  • Continue (≥7 days, longer for meningitis) if culture-positive or ongoing suspicion
Prevention
  • Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) — IV benzylpenicillin in labour for at-risk mothers (Group B Strep colonisation/bacteriuria, previous Group B Strep baby, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, intrapartum fever) → reduces early-onset Group B Strep disease
Exam Pearls
What it is
Systemic infection in the first 28 days; emergency; non-specific signs; Group B Strep + E. coli lead.
Early vs late
Early-onset (<72 h): vertical from mother; Group B Strep/E. coli/Listeria. Late-onset (>72 h): environmental/nosocomial; coag-neg staph (lines), Gram-negatives, Candida.
Risk factors (early)
Maternal Group B Strep, prolonged rupture of membranes >18–24 h, preterm labour, chorioamnionitis/maternal fever, previous Group B Strep baby.
Signs
Respiratory distress, temperature instability (often HYPOthermia), poor feeding, lethargy/irritability, seizures, poor perfusion, jaundice <24 h.
Investigations
BLOOD CULTURE before antibiotics; FBC + CRP (repeat at ~18–24 h); lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected/culture positive.
Treatment
Start IV antibiotics WITHIN 1 HOUR — early-onset: BENZYLPENICILLIN + GENTAMICIN; late-onset: flucloxacillin + gentamicin.
Review
At 36 h: stop if well + cultures negative + CRP normal; continue ≥7 days if positive/meningitis.
Prevention
Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IV benzylpenicillin) for at-risk mothers.
What & Why

Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is neonatal brain injury caused by insufficient oxygen and blood flow to the brain (perinatal asphyxia), usually around the time of birth. It matters because it’s a major cause of neonatal death and of long-term neurodisability (especially cerebral palsy, epilepsy, cognitive/sensory impairment), because it’s a time-critical treatable emergency — therapeutic hypothermia (cooling), started within 6 hours, is the one intervention proven to reduce death and disability — and because recognising and grading it (Sarnat) drives that decision.

The core mechanism — the “two-phase” injury (why the 6-hour window exists): Primary energy failure — during the hypoxic-ischaemic insult, cells can’t make ATP → ion pumps fail → cell death. Then a latent phase (~6 hours) as circulation is restored — the therapeutic window. Then secondary energy failure (~6–48 h) — a cascade of excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis causes delayed neuronal death. Cooling works by slowing this secondary cascade — which is why it must start within ~6 hours, before secondary injury takes hold.
Causes

Anything compromising placental/cerebral oxygen delivery around birth:

  • Antepartum/intrapartum events: placental abruption, cord prolapse/compression, uterine rupture, shoulder dystocia, maternal hypotension/shock, prolonged/obstructed labour
  • Failure to breathe at birth, severe anaemia (e.g. feto-maternal haemorrhage), maternal hypoxia
  • Meconium aspiration (a shared asphyxia trigger)
Clinical Features & Diagnosis

The diagnosis combines evidence of an asphyxial insult + encephalopathy:

  • Evidence of perinatal asphyxia: low Apgar scores (≤5 at 10 min), need for prolonged resuscitation, and metabolic acidosis (cord pH <7.0 or base deficit ≥16)
  • Encephalopathy (within the first hours–days): altered consciousness (irritability → lethargy → coma), abnormal tone (hypo-/hypertonia), poor feeding/weak suck, abnormal/primitive reflexes, seizures, apnoea, abnormal posturing/movements
  • Multi-organ involvement supports it (hypoxia hits other organs too): acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction (deranged LFTs), cardiac dysfunction, DIC
Sarnat Staging (grades severity → guides prognosis & cooling)

Investigations
  • Cord/arterial blood gas (acidosis: pH, base deficit), glucose, U&E, LFTs, FBC, coagulation (multi-organ screen)
  • aEEG / EEG — background activity + detect (often subclinical) seizures; also prognostic
  • MRI brain (usually days 5–14) — defines the pattern/extent of injury and gives prognostic information (e.g. basal ganglia/thalamus, watershed)
  • Cranial ultrasound (bedside), and monitoring for the systemic complications
Management
Time-critical — guideline-verified.
Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) — the key intervention
  • Cool to ~33–34°C for 72 hours, started WITHIN 6 HOURS of birth
  • For moderate–severe (Sarnat 2–3) HIE in infants ≥36 weeks
  • Reduces death and disability (TOBY/NICHD trials). Then rewarm slowly
Supportive intensive care (the mainstay alongside cooling)
  • Respiratory: ventilation as needed; maintain normal oxygenation/CO2
  • Treat seizures (e.g. phenobarbital first-line)
  • Maintain normoglycaemia, normal BP/perfusion, fluid/electrolyte balance; treat multi-organ dysfunction (acute kidney injury, coagulopathy, cardiac)
  • Avoid hyperthermia (worsens injury), monitor for infection

Neurodevelopmental follow-up — all HIE survivors need long-term follow-up.

Prognosis
  • Depends on severity (Sarnat grade): Grade 1 usually normal; Grade 2 variable (a significant minority have sequelae); Grade 3 high mortality/severe disability
  • Sequelae: cerebral palsy (especially dyskinetic/spastic quadriplegic), epilepsy, learning disability, sensorineural hearing loss, visual impairment
Exam Pearls
What it is
Neonatal brain injury from perinatal asphyxia (hypoxia + ischaemia); major cause of death and cerebral palsy.
Two-phase injury
Primary energy failure → ~6-hour LATENT window → secondary energy failure (delayed neuronal death) — cooling targets the secondary phase, so it must start within 6 hours.
Causes
Abruption, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, shoulder dystocia, maternal hypotension, failure to breathe, meconium aspiration.
Diagnosis
Asphyxia (low Apgars ≤5 at 10 min, prolonged resuscitation, cord pH <7.0 / base deficit ≥16) + ENCEPHALOPATHY (altered consciousness, tone, seizures) ± multi-organ dysfunction.
Sarnat staging
1 mild (good), 2 moderate (variable, cool), 3 severe (poor, cool). Grades 2–3 → cooling.
Management
THERAPEUTIC HYPOTHERMIA (33–34°C, 72h, start <6h, ≥36 wks, Sarnat 2–3) + supportive intensive care + treat seizures (phenobarbital) + maintain glucose/BP; avoid hyperthermia.
Investigations
Blood gas/multi-organ screen, aEEG/EEG (seizures + prognosis), MRI (days 5–14, prognostic).
Sequelae
Cerebral palsy, epilepsy, learning disability, hearing/vision loss.
What & Why

Neonatal hypoglycaemia is a low blood glucose in the newborn — the commonest metabolic problem in neonates. It matters because transient, mild hypoglycaemia in the first hours of life is common and usually benign (the newborn is transitioning from a constant placental glucose supply to intermittent feeds), but persistent or symptomatic hypoglycaemia can cause permanent brain injury (the brain depends on glucose), so the skill is identifying at-risk babies, screening them, and treating promptly.

The core physiology: at birth, the placental glucose supply is suddenly cut off → the newborn must mobilise its own glucose (glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis) and establish feeding. A transient dip is normal and self-corrects. Problems arise when demand outstrips supply — e.g. infants of diabetic mothers (fetal hyperinsulinaemia from maternal hyperglycaemia persists after birth → the baby keeps over-secreting insulin) — or when glycogen stores are low (preterm, IUGR) or consumption is high (sepsis, hypothermia).
Causes / At-Risk Groups
Transient (first hours) — common and benign. The list below is the persistent / at-risk group to screen.
  • Maternal diabetes (infant of a diabetic mother) — fetal hyperinsulinaemia (the classic)
  • Prematurity (low glycogen stores)
  • IUGR / small-for-gestational-age (low stores); large-for-dates
  • Hypothermia (increased glucose consumption)
  • Neonatal sepsis
  • Perinatal asphyxia/stress, polycythaemia
  • Inborn errors of metabolism, congenital hyperinsulinism (nesidioblastosis), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, endocrine (hypopituitarism, cortisol/growth hormone deficiency)
Clinical Features

The autonomic / neuroglycopenic split:

  • May be ASYMPTOMATIC — hence the need to screen at-risk babies
Autonomic (sympathetic activation)
  • Jitteriness — a classic sign (the common word used in exam questions)
  • Irritability, tachypnoea, pallor, sweating
Neuroglycopenic (brain glucose deprivation)
  • Poor feeding/sucking, weak/high-pitched cry, drowsiness/lethargy, hypotonia
  • Seizures, apnoea, coma (severe)
Investigations
  • Blood glucose measurement — screen at-risk infants (pre-feed capillary glucose); confirm low readings with a laboratory glucose (bedside glucometers are unreliable at low values)
  • Operational threshold: treat/act at <2.6 mmol/L in at-risk/symptomatic babies (commonly used UK/BAPM threshold); symptomatic or very low → urgent action
  • Persistent/severe hypoglycaemia → a “hypoglycaemia screen” (taken WHEN glucose is low): insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, free fatty acids, lactate, ammonia, and metabolic/acylcarnitine studies — to identify hyperinsulinism (nesidioblastosis), endocrine deficiency, or an inborn error of metabolism
Management
  • Asymptomatic / mildly low: encourage normal/early feeding and monitor blood glucose — frequent feeds (breast/formula), keep warm, recheck pre-feeds
  • Add buccal (40%) dextrose gel — massaged into the cheek alongside feeding for asymptomatic at-risk hypoglycaemia — reduces neonatal-unit admissions and supports breastfeeding (now a standard first-line adjunct)
  • Symptomatic or very low glucose: admit to the neonatal unit + IV 10% dextrose — glucose infusion (bolus then maintenance); escalate concentration/rate as needed
  • Refractory/persistent: investigate the cause (screen above); hyperinsulinism → diazoxide (± octreotide); treat endocrine deficiency; specialist metabolic/endocrine input
  • Aim: maintain glucose in a safe range and avoid recurrent/prolonged hypoglycaemia (neuroprotection)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest metabolic problem; TRANSIENT mild dip in first hours common/benign; persistent/symptomatic → brain injury risk.
At-risk
Infant of DIABETIC MOTHER (fetal hyperinsulinaemia), preterm, IUGR/SGA, large-for-dates, hypothermia, sepsis, asphyxia, Beckwith-Wiedemann, hyperinsulinism (nesidioblastosis), inborn errors.
Features
Often ASYMPTOMATIC → screen. Autonomic: JITTERINESS, irritability, tachypnoea, pallor. Neuroglycopenic: poor feeding, weak cry, drowsiness, hypotonia, SEIZURES.
Screening
Screen at-risk babies (pre-feed glucose); act at <2.6 mmol/L; confirm low bedside readings with lab glucose.
Management
Asymptomatic → feed + monitor + BUCCAL DEXTROSE GEL; symptomatic/very low → admit + IV 10% DEXTROSE.
Persistent
Hypoglycaemia screen (taken when low): insulin/cortisol/growth hormone/ketones/lactate/ammonia. Hyperinsulinism → diazoxide.
PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries:
Overview — birth injuries
Brachial plexus injuries sustained during delivery (often with shoulder dystocia), classified by the nerve roots involved.
The organising principle: the root level predicts the deformity. Upper roots (C5–6) = Erb's palsy → “waiter's tip”; lower roots (C8–T1) = Klumpke's → claw hand. Most recover with physiotherapy.
InjuryRootsFeatures
Erb's palsyC5–6arm adducted/internally rotated, pronated (“waiter's tip”); assoc. shoulder dystocia/macrosomia
Klumpke's palsyC8–T1claw hand ± Horner's; rarer
Most brachial plexus birth injuries recover spontaneously with physiotherapy — refer if no recovery by ~3 months. Associated with shoulder dystocia and large babies.
What & Why

Erb’s palsy is the commonest neonatal brachial plexus birth injury — paralysis of the upper arm and shoulder from injury to the C5–C6 nerve roots during delivery. It’s a classic exam picture (the “waiter’s tip” posture), the visible neurological consequence of shoulder dystocia, and its prognosis is generally good — most recover with conservative care, so recognition + physiotherapy referral matter more than any dramatic intervention.

The core mechanism: during a difficult delivery, excessive lateral traction / widening of the head-to-shoulder angle stretches (or, more severely, ruptures/avulses) the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6). These roots supply the shoulder abductors/external rotators + elbow flexors → the characteristic posture. The forearm and hand (C8–T1) are spared — which distinguishes it from Klumpke’s palsy.
The Decisive Fork — Erb’s (upper) vs Klumpke’s (lower)
