Risk Factors

All things that stretch the head-shoulder angle at delivery.

  • Shoulder dystocia — the classic cause
  • Macrosomia / large-for-dates baby (often maternal/gestational diabetes)
  • Instrumental delivery (forceps/ventouse); breech presentation
  • Prolonged/difficult labour, high maternal BMI; previous baby with brachial plexus injury
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Brachial plexus root map (C5–T1) — upper trunk (C5–6 = Erb’s) vs lower trunk (C8–T1 = Klumpke’s), with T1 sympathetic fibres to the eye explaining the Horner’s association
  • Noticed at or shortly after birth — the affected arm lies limp/motionless by the side
  • “Waiter’s tip” posture: shoulder adducted + internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist and fingers flexed (palm facing backward/outward)
  • Absent Moro reflex on the affected side; grasp reflex intact (C8–T1 spared)
  • Preserved hand movement/grip (distinguishes from Klumpke’s/total palsy); may have sensory loss over the lateral (outer) upper arm
  • Check for associated injuries: clavicle/humeral fracture (co-exist with shoulder dystocia), and phrenic nerve palsy (respiratory distress → hemidiaphragm paralysis on the same side)
Assessment / Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — inspection of posture + neurological examination of the limb
  • Examine for associated injuries — palpate the clavicle and humerus (fracture); assess respiratory effort (phrenic nerve / diaphragm)
  • Check for Horner’s syndrome — its presence suggests T1 involvement → worse prognosis / more extensive injury
  • Imaging (X-ray for suspected fracture); MRI / nerve conduction studies reserved for severe/non-recovering cases being considered for surgery
Management
Most cases are managed CONSERVATIVELY and recover.
  • Physiotherapy / occupational therapy — gentle passive range-of-movement exercises + positioning to prevent contractures and joint stiffness while the nerve recovers (usually started within the first weeks)
  • Parental education + support; early referral to a specialist multidisciplinary brachial plexus service
  • Watchful waiting — recovery is monitored; the rate of recovery in the first weeks predicts the final outcome
  • Surgery (nerve grafting/reconstruction, ~3–6 months) — reserved for the minority with no meaningful recovery by ~3 months (suggesting rupture/avulsion rather than a stretch); later secondary orthopaedic procedures (tendon transfers) for residual deformity
Prognosis & Prevention
  • Good overall — ~80–90% recover fully or nearly fully within the first year, especially milder (stretch/neurapraxia) injuries
  • Poorer prognosis markers: no recovery by 3 months, Horner’s syndrome (T1 involvement/avulsion), total plexus (C5–T1) involvement; permanent impairment in a minority (~3–25%)
Prevention (obstetric link): the injury is classically linked to excessive traction during shoulder dystocia — the correct response to shoulder dystocia is the McRoberts manoeuvre + suprapubic pressure, NOT traction on the fetal head.
Exam Pearls
What it is
C5–C6 (upper) brachial plexus birth injury → “WAITER’S TIP” posture (arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed).
Epidemiology
Commonest birth brachial plexus injury; associated with SHOULDER DYSTOCIA + macrosomia (diabetic mother).
Reflexes
Moro absent on that side; GRASP PRESERVED (C8–T1 spared) — distinguishes from Klumpke’s.
Klumpke’s contrast
C8–T1 (lower) → “claw hand” + grasp LOST + Horner’s syndrome.
Associated injuries
Check for clavicle/humerus fracture and phrenic nerve (diaphragm) palsy.
Management
Mostly CONSERVATIVE — physiotherapy (passive ROM, prevent contractures); surgery only if no recovery by ~3 months.
Prognosis
~80–90% recover in the first year. Horner’s / no recovery by 3 months = worse.
Prevention
Correct shoulder dystocia management (McRoberts + suprapubic pressure, NOT head traction).
What & Why

Klumpke’s palsy is a lower brachial plexus birth injury affecting the C8–T1 nerve roots, paralysing the intrinsic hand muscles and long finger flexors — the classic “claw hand”. It’s the rarer, more severe counterpart to Erb’s palsy, carries a worse prognosis (the lower roots are more often avulsed than stretched), and is the birth injury classically associated with Horner’s syndrome. Essence: C8–T1 → claw hand → grasp lost → check for Horner’s.

The core mechanism: Klumpke’s arises from traction on an ABDUCTED arm — classically the arm pulled upward/overhead (baby delivered with the arm extended above the head, or a difficult breech). This stretches/avulses the lower trunk (C8–T1), supplying the intrinsic hand muscles + finger/wrist flexors. T1 also carries sympathetic fibres to the head/eye — why lower-plexus avulsion can cause Horner’s syndrome.

Memory anchor: Klumpke’s = C8,T1 = Claw hand = grasp lost + Horner’s (Klumpke → “Claw”). Erb’s = C5,6 = waiter’s tip = grasp preserved.
Risk Factors
  • Traction on the arm in an abducted/hyperabducted position (arm pulled over the head)
  • Difficult breech delivery — a classic Klumpke’s mechanism (the arm extends overhead)
  • Shoulder dystocia, instrumental delivery; macrosomia (maternal/gestational diabetes), large-for-dates baby
Clinical Features
  • Noticed at/shortly after birth — the affected hand is the focus
  • “Claw hand” deformity — paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals/interossei) → hyperextension at the MCP joints + flexion at the IP joints; forearm may be supinated, wrist extended
  • Loss of grip / finger and wrist flexion; absent grasp reflex
  • Preserved shoulder and elbow movement (upper plexus intact — distinguishes from Erb’s/total palsy)
  • Sensory loss over the medial (ulnar) aspect of the forearm and hand (C8–T1 dermatomes)
  • Horner’s syndrome on the same side — ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (± enophthalmos) — indicates T1 root avulsion (a poor prognostic sign)
Assessment / Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — posture (claw hand), neurological exam, and look specifically for Horner’s syndrome (examine the eye/pupil/eyelid)
  • Check for associated injury — clavicle/humeral fracture; assess the whole plexus (is it a total C5–T1 palsy → flail arm?)
  • Imaging: X-ray for fracture; MRI + nerve conduction studies / EMG for severe/non-recovering cases (assess for root avulsion, plan surgery)
Management & Prognosis
  • Conservative first-line — physiotherapy/occupational therapy: gentle passive range-of-movement exercises, splinting, and positioning to prevent contractures while awaiting nerve recovery (wrist/hand splinting is particularly relevant given the claw deformity)
  • Early referral to a specialist brachial plexus MDT; parental education; monitor recovery (early recovery rate predicts outcome)
  • Surgery (nerve reconstruction/grafting, ~3–6 months) — more often needed than in Erb’s, because lower-plexus injuries are more likely to be avulsions (which don’t recover spontaneously); later tendon transfers for residual hand deformity
Worse than Erb’s palsy — the lower roots (especially T1) are more frequently avulsed, so spontaneous full recovery is less likely and surgery is more often required. Horner’s syndrome = a marker of severe injury (T1 avulsion) → poorer prognosis.
Exam Pearls
What it is
C8–T1 (lower) brachial plexus birth injury → “CLAW HAND” (intrinsic hand muscles + finger/wrist flexors paralysed).
Mechanism
Traction on an ABDUCTED/overhead arm (classically difficult breech).
Reflexes
Grasp reflex ABSENT (hand affected); shoulder/elbow preserved (distinguishes from Erb’s).
Sensory
Loss over the MEDIAL (ulnar) forearm/hand (C8–T1).
Horner’s
Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis = T1 avulsion → poor prognosis — the classic Klumpke’s association.
Severity
Rarer and MORE SEVERE than Erb’s; worse prognosis (more avulsions → more often needs surgery).
Management
Physiotherapy/splinting (prevent contractures) → surgery if no recovery by ~3 months.
Mnemonic
“KLumpke’s = CLaw + C8,T1 + Horner’s” vs “Erb’s = C5,6 + waiter’s tip + grasp preserved.”
PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exanthems (Rashes:
Overview — childhood exanthems (rashes)
The classic infectious childhood rashes (“exanthems”) — mostly viral — recognised by the rash pattern, prodrome and associated features.
The organising principle: pattern recognition. Measles (Koplik spots, descending rash, miserable); rubella (mild, post-auricular nodes); slapped cheek (parvovirus); roseola (high fever then rash); hand-foot-mouth (Coxsackie); scarlet fever (strep, sandpaper rash); chickenpox (vesicular crops).

Measles and scarlet fever are notifiable. Beware parvovirus in sickle-cell (aplastic crisis) and pregnancy (hydrops), and varicella/measles in the immunocompromised or a non-immune pregnant contact.
What & Why

Measles is a highly contagious acute viral infection caused by the measles virus (a paramyxovirus, RNA virus) — a prodrome (the “3 C’s”) followed by a characteristic maculopapular rash. It’s one of the most communicable diseases known (R₀ ~15), causes serious complications (pneumonia, encephalitis, the rare fatal SSPE), is vaccine-preventable (MMR) yet has resurged in the UK, and is a notifiable disease.

The core clinical rhythm: a prodrome of high fever + the “3 C’s” (Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis) → then Koplik spots (pathognomonic, in the mouth) → then the rash starting behind the ears/on the face and spreading down. Infectivity spans ~4 days before to 4 days after the rash.
The Decisive Fork — Measles or Another Exanthem?
📷 Image placeholder — Koplik spots (white spots on buccal mucosa) and the blotchy confluent measles rash spreading face-down — vs the milder, non-confluent viral exanthems
FeatureMeaslesOther exanthems
ProdromeProminent — high fever + 3 C’sUsually milder
Pathognomonic signKoplik spots (buccal mucosa)Rubella (post-auricular nodes), parvovirus (slapped cheek), roseola (rash after fever breaks)
RashMaculopapular, starts face/behind ears → spreads down, becomes confluentVaries
ChildMiserable, unwellOften well (e.g. rubella)
Clinical Features

Incubation: ~10 days (range 7–18) after exposure.

🤒 Prodrome (2–4 days before rash)
  • High fever (can spike >40°C as the rash appears)
  • The 3 C’s: Cough, Coryza (runny nose), Conjunctivitis
  • Malaise, miserable child
⚪ Koplik spots (pathognomonic)
  • Small white/bluish-white spots (2–3 mm) on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa (opposite the lower molars)
  • Appear 1–2 days before the rash, fade as it emerges
  • Pathognomonic but transient + easily missed — absence does NOT exclude measles
  • The rash: erythematous, maculopapular, blotchy; starts behind the ears / on the face → spreads cephalocaudally (to trunk + limbs) over 3–4 days, becomes confluent
  • Spares palms and soles (unlike secondary syphilis); may be harder to see on black/brown skin; fades after ~5 days (brownish staining/desquamation)
  • Immunocompromised patients may have an atypical rash or no rash
Investigations
  • Notify the local Health Protection Team by telephone the SAME DAY on clinical suspicion — do NOT wait for lab confirmation (statutory notifiable disease)
  • Confirm with an oral fluid (saliva) sample for measles-specific IgM/IgG and/or RNA (PCR) — reference lab; serum IgM is an alternative
  • Isolate immediately (side room, mask; don’t leave in a waiting room) — extremely contagious
Management
  • Supportive — most otherwise-healthy children recover: rest, fluids, antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen)
  • Isolation: exclude from school/nursery/work until at least 4 days after the onset of the rash, and avoid contact with susceptible people (pregnant, immunocompromised, infants)
  • Vitamin A — recommended (all admitted children, particularly under-2s / severe cases) — reduces morbidity + mortality
  • Antibiotics only for secondary bacterial infection (otitis media, pneumonia); admit if serious complications, dehydration, or high-risk
Post-exposure prophylaxis (susceptible contacts): MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure (if immunocompetent + not pregnant), OR human normal immunoglobulin (HNIG) within 6 days — for those in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated: pregnant women, immunocompromised, and infants.
Complications
  • Common: otitis media (commonest), diarrhoea, febrile convulsions
  • Pneumonia — the commonest cause of measles death
  • Encephalitis — ~1 in 1000 (acute post-infectious)
  • Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) — a rare, fatal, late complication (~7–10 years later) from persistent measles virus in the CNS → progressive behavioural/intellectual deterioration, myoclonus, seizures, death; higher risk if infected <2 years old
  • Keratoconjunctivitis / blindness (esp. with vitamin A deficiency)
  • In pregnancy: miscarriage, preterm birth, low birth weight (not classically teratogenic like rubella, but causes fetal loss/prematurity)
  • Transient immune suppression (“immune amnesia”) → susceptibility to other infections
Prevention — MMR Vaccine
  • Live attenuated MMR vaccine, two doses: 12 months and 18 months (UK schedule)
  • Live vaccine → contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromise
  • Two doses give ~99% protection; falling uptake underlies recent outbreaks; a measles-like rash 10–12 days post-MMR can occur (vaccine reaction, non-infectious)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Highly contagious paramyxovirus; prodrome (high fever + 3 C’s: Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis) → Koplik spots → rash.
Koplik spots
White spots on buccal mucosa = pathognomonic, appear 1–2 days before rash; absence doesn’t exclude it.
Rash
Maculopapular, starts behind ears/face → spreads DOWN → confluent; spares palms/soles.
Infectivity
4 days before to 4 days after rash; incubation ~10 days.
Notifiable
Phone the Health Protection Team the same day on suspicion (don’t wait for labs). Confirm with oral fluid IgM/PCR.
Management
Supportive (fluids, antipyretics) + isolate 4 days after rash + vitamin A; antibiotics only for bacterial complications.
PEP
MMR within 72 h OR HNIG within 6 days (HNIG for pregnant/immunocompromised/infants).
Complications
Otitis media (commonest), pneumonia (commonest cause of death), encephalitis (~1/1000), SSPE (rare, fatal, years later — worse if <2 yrs).
Prevention
MMR (live) at 12 months and 18 months; contraindicated in pregnancy/immunocompromise.
What & Why

Rubella (“German measles” / “three-day measles”) is a mild, self-limiting viral exanthem caused by the rubella virus (RNA virus, genus Rubivirus). It matters not for the childhood illness — usually trivial or asymptomatic — but for its devastating effect in pregnancy: congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). The whole public-health importance is protecting pregnant women through vaccination + rapid case identification. It’s a notifiable disease.

The key framing: in a child, rubella is a “so what?” illness — mild fever, a fleeting rash, big glands behind the ears. It’s on every curriculum because of the pregnant contact: a non-immune pregnant woman infected in early pregnancy → the fetus can suffer CRS. Every rubella question is really a pregnancy/vaccination question.
The Decisive Fork — Acquired vs Congenital Rubella
Acquired rubella (this note)Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)
WhoChild/adultFetus of a non-immune mother infected in early pregnancy
SeverityMild/self-limiting (often subclinical)Devastating, permanent
FeaturesMild rash + lymphadenopathySensorineural deafness + cataracts + congenital heart disease (PDA)
Risk window—Highest <12 weeks’ gestation (~85–90% affected)
Clinical Features (acquired rubella)

Incubation: ~14–21 days after exposure. ~25–50% of cases are asymptomatic/subclinical — important, because silent infection can still infect a pregnant contact.

  • Prodrome (mild; often minimal in young children, more prominent in adolescents/adults): low-grade fever (rarely >38°C), malaise, headache, mild coryza, sore throat, non-exudative conjunctivitis
  • Lymphadenopathy — the characteristic feature: postauricular (behind the ear), suboccipital, and posterior cervical nodes; precedes the rash (by days), persists ~1–2 weeks, tender (the classic discriminator)
  • The rash: pink/light-red, fine maculopapular; starts on the face → spreads to trunk + limbs, fainter + more transient than measles; lasts ~3 days (“three-day measles”); no palm/sole involvement
  • Forchheimer spots — petechiae on the soft palate (~20%) — supportive but not diagnostic
  • Arthralgia/arthritis — common in adults, especially women (a useful clue)
Investigations
  • Notifiable disease → notify the local Health Protection Team on clinical suspicion
  • Clinical diagnosis is unreliable (many rashes look alike) → confirm serologically: rubella-specific IgM (from ~4 days after rash), rising IgG or IgG avidity (low avidity = recent primary infection); oral fluid (saliva) used in UK surveillance
  • Pregnant woman exposed/symptomatic → urgent serology (IgM/IgG + avidity) and discuss with virology/Health Protection Team
Management
  • Supportive only — rest, fluids, antipyretics (paracetamol); self-limiting; no specific antiviral
  • Isolation: exclude from school/work until 4–5 days after the onset of the rash, and — crucially — keep away from pregnant women
In pregnancy: there is no treatment to prevent CRS once maternal infection occurs → management is counselling about fetal risk (very high if <12 weeks). Immunoglobulin does not reliably prevent CRS + is not routinely recommended. MMR is a LIVE vaccine → contraindicated in pregnancy; susceptible women are vaccinated postpartum (avoid pregnancy for ~1 month).
Complications & Prevention
  • Uncommon (rubella is usually benign): arthralgia/arthritis (adult women), thrombocytopenia, encephalitis (rare)
  • The overwhelming “complication” that matters = congenital rubella syndrome in a pregnant contact
  • Prevention: live attenuated MMR, two doses (12 months + 18 months); contraindicated in pregnancy/immunocompromise
  • The programme goal is herd immunity to protect pregnant women; antenatal rubella screening was stopped in the UK in April 2016 (herd immunity made individual screening low-value)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Mild viral exanthem; matters mainly for its effect in PREGNANCY (congenital rubella syndrome).
Characteristic sign
Tender POSTAURICULAR + suboccipital + posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (precedes rash).
Rash
Pink, fine, maculopapular, face → down, faint, lasts ~3 days (“three-day measles”).
Other clues
Forchheimer spots (soft palate petechiae, ~20%) — supportive not diagnostic; ~25–50% asymptomatic; arthralgia common in adult women; incubation 14–21 days.
Diagnosis
Notifiable; confirm with rubella IgM / IgG avidity / oral fluid (clinical diagnosis unreliable).
Management
Supportive; exclude until 4–5 days after rash; KEEP AWAY FROM PREGNANT WOMEN.
CRS
Deafness + cataracts + PDA; worst <12 weeks; no treatment → prevention via MMR (live, contraindicated in pregnancy → vaccinate postpartum).
Distinguish
From measles (Koplik spots, sicker, confluent rash) and parvovirus (slapped cheek).
What & Why

Hand, foot and mouth disease is a common, mild, self-limiting viral illness of young children, caused by enteroviruses — most often Coxsackievirus A16 — producing a characteristic combination of oral ulcers and a vesicular rash on the hands and feet. It’s very common + highly contagious (spreads rapidly through nurseries), a classic exam picture (the name tells you the distribution), and the teaching is all about reassurance + infection control — plus the rare severe variant (enterovirus 71) and the pregnancy caveat. It is completely unrelated to animal “foot-and-mouth disease”.

The core point: an enteroviral illness spread faeco-orally + by respiratory droplets/vesicle fluid → it’s about hygiene and it resolves on its own. No specific treatment; (UK) no need to exclude children from school once they feel well.
Organism
  • Coxsackievirus A16 — the commonest cause (the classic answer)
  • Enterovirus 71 (EV71) — associated with more severe disease + neurological complications (encephalitis, meningitis); important in Asian outbreaks
  • Coxsackievirus A6 — increasingly common; more extensive/atypical rash + later onychomadesis (nail shedding)
  • All are enteroviruses (Picornaviridae, RNA viruses)
Clinical Features
  • Age: mostly young children (<5–10 years); nursery/school outbreaks. Incubation ~3–7 days
  • Prodrome: mild — low-grade fever, sore throat, malaise, reduced appetite for a day or two
  • Oral lesions (herpangina-like): painful vesicles + ulcers on the tongue, buccal mucosa, palate → sore mouth, reduced eating/drinking (the main practical problem — dehydration risk in toddlers)
  • Rash: vesicular/papulovesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and often buttocks/perineum — small greyish blisters on an erythematous base; usually not itchy
  • Self-limiting — resolves in ~7–10 days
  • Onychomadesis (nail shedding) + desquamation of palms/soles can occur weeks later (especially Coxsackie A6) — benign
The Decisive Fork — HFMD vs Its Mimics
Hand, foot & mouthDifferentials
DistributionHands + feet + mouth (+ buttocks)—
LesionsOral ulcers + peripheral vesiclesChickenpox (widespread, central/trunk, crops of different stages); herpangina (mouth only — same virus family); herpes gingivostomatitis (mouth + gums, HSV)
The name is the diagnosis: ulcers in the mouth + vesicles on the hands and feet in a young child = HFMD. Chickenpox is more widespread + truncal; herpangina is mouth-only.
Investigations & Management
  • Clinical diagnosis — no investigations usually needed; viral swab/PCR (vesicle fluid, throat, stool) only if severe/atypical or for outbreak surveillance
  • Supportive only — no specific antiviral; it self-resolves: analgesia/antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) for fever + mouth pain
  • Encourage fluids — the priority is preventing dehydration (sore mouth → poor drinking); soft/cool foods, avoid acidic/salty foods
  • Good hand hygiene to limit spread; antibiotics NOT indicated (viral)
  • Safety-net — return if not drinking/passing urine (dehydration), high/persistent fever, drowsiness, or neurological signs
School/nursery exclusion is NOT required (UK) — children can attend once they feel well enough; exclusion doesn’t reduce spread (asymptomatic shedding in stool continues for weeks).
Complications
  • Dehydration (from painful oral ulcers → the commonest practical problem)
  • Secondary bacterial skin infection
  • Neurological (rare, mainly enterovirus 71): aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis
  • Onychomadesis (nail shedding) — benign, weeks later
  • In pregnancy: usually mild with no strong evidence of fetal harm, but infection around the time of delivery can rarely cause neonatal infection — advise good hygiene; reassure
Exam Pearls
What it is
Mild enteroviral illness; Coxsackievirus A16 (commonest); enterovirus 71 = severe/neurological.
Presentation
Young child, mild fever + PAINFUL ORAL ULCERS + VESICLES on hands, feet (± buttocks).
The name = the distribution
Distinguish from chickenpox (widespread/truncal, crops of different stages) and herpangina (mouth-only).
Course
Self-limiting (~7–10 days); clinical diagnosis, no tests needed.
Management
Supportive — analgesia + FLUIDS (prevent dehydration); hand hygiene. No antivirals, no antibiotics.
Exclusion
NO school exclusion needed (UK) — attend when well; virus shed in stool for weeks regardless.
Complications
Dehydration (commonest), rare neuro disease (EV71), onychomadesis (nail shedding) later.
Trap
Unrelated to animal “foot-and-mouth disease”.
What & Why

Slapped cheek syndrome (erythema infectiosum, “fifth disease”) is a common, usually mild childhood viral exanthem caused by parvovirus B19 — a bright red “slapped cheek” facial rash followed by a lacy body rash. Though trivial in a healthy child, B19 has two very serious complications in vulnerable groups: an aplastic crisis in chronic haemolytic anaemias (e.g. sickle cell) and hydrops fetalis / fetal loss in pregnancy. As with rubella, the exam value is in the at-risk contacts.

The core mechanism: parvovirus B19 targets and destroys erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow (binds the P antigen / blood group P on red-cell precursors). In a healthy person → only a brief harmless dip in red-cell production. But in someone who already depends on rapid red-cell turnover (haemolytic anaemia) or a fetus → shutting down erythropoiesis is catastrophic → aplastic crisis / severe fetal anaemia → hydrops. Everything dangerous about B19 flows from “it stops red-cell production”.
Clinical Features

Classically three phases:

1
Prodromeheadache + fever first — mild, non-specific, coryzal/flu-like
↓
2
“Slapped cheek” rashbright red, firm erythema on BOTH cheeks (appears days after prodrome); circumoral pallor (spares around the mouth)
↓
3
Lacy body rashspreads to proximal arms/extensor surfaces/trunk — lacy/reticular (net-like) erythema; waxes + wanes over 1–3 weeks, worse with heat/sun/exercise
  • Arthralgia/arthritis — common in adults, especially women (symmetrical small joints) — sometimes the only feature
  • “Gloves and socks” syndrome — papular-purpuric eruption on hands/feet (mainly adults)
  • Often asymptomatic/subclinical
Infectivity — the Key Practical Rule
  • Spread by respiratory droplets (and vertically / via blood products)
  • Infectious BEFORE the rash appears; once the “slapped cheek” rash is present, they are NO LONGER infectious
  • Consequence: no school exclusion is needed (past the contagious phase by the time they’re diagnosed)
  • Exception — aplastic crisis: patients in aplastic crisis (still viraemic, no rash) ARE infectious → isolate
The Decisive Fork — Healthy Host vs Vulnerable Host
This is the entire clinical importance of B19.
HostConsequence of B19
Healthy child/adultMild self-limiting rash ± arthralgia — reassure
Chronic haemolytic anaemia (sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia)Transient APLASTIC CRISIS — sudden severe anaemia + reticulocytopenia → may need transfusion
Immunocompromised (HIV, chemo, transplant)Chronic red-cell aplasia / persistent anaemia — may benefit from IVIG
Pregnant (non-immune)Fetal anaemia → HYDROPS FETALIS, fetal loss (esp. <20 weeks)
Investigations
  • Healthy child: clinical diagnosis; no tests needed
  • Confirm with parvovirus B19 serology: B19 IgM (recent infection) + IgG (past infection/immunity); PCR in the immunocompromised (may not mount antibodies)
  • Aplastic crisis: FBC (severe anaemia, low reticulocytes)
  • Pregnant exposure/infection: check B19 IgM/IgG; if acute infection → refer to fetal medicine for serial ultrasound + middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler to detect fetal anaemia
Management
  • Healthy host: supportive only — analgesia/antipyretics, fluids, rest; self-limiting; no antivirals; no exclusion needed
  • Aplastic crisis: supportive + blood transfusion for symptomatic severe anaemia; isolate (infectious)
  • Immunocompromised with chronic anaemia: IVIG (contains anti-B19 antibodies)
  • Pregnancy: no treatment prevents infection; management is fetal surveillance — if hydrops/severe fetal anaemia develops → intrauterine (fetal) blood transfusion; many hydrops cases resolve
Exam Pearls
What it is
“Slapped cheek” (erythema infectiosum / fifth disease); targets erythroid precursors (binds P antigen → stops red-cell production).
Three phases
Prodrome (fever/headache) → bright red “slapped cheek” → lacy/reticular body rash (worse with heat/sun).
Infectivity
Infectious BEFORE the rash; NOT infectious once the rash appears → NO school exclusion needed (except aplastic crisis).
Adults
Arthralgia/arthritis (esp. women) ± gloves-and-socks syndrome.
Aplastic crisis
In chronic haemolytic anaemia (sickle cell, spherocytosis, thalassaemia) — severe anaemia + low reticulocytes → transfusion.
Immunocompromised
Chronic red-cell aplasia → IVIG.
Pregnancy
Hydrops fetalis / fetal anaemia / loss (esp. <20 wks) → fetal medicine, MCA Doppler, intrauterine transfusion. Commonest infective cause of non-immune hydrops.
Diagnosis
B19 IgM/IgG (PCR if immunocompromised); FBC + reticulocytes in crisis.
What & Why

Scarlet fever is an acute bacterial illness caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, “Strep A”) — strains producing erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxins — with a sore throat, fever, a characteristic sandpaper rash, and strawberry tongue. It’s common in school-age children, has resurged dramatically in the UK (with a rise in severe invasive Strep A), is a notifiable disease, and — though easily treated with penicillin — can cause serious post-streptococcal complications if untreated.

The core mechanism: scarlet fever is essentially Strep A pharyngitis (strep throat) PLUS a toxin. Only GAS strains releasing erythrogenic exotoxins (superantigens) cause the rash — driving the diffuse erythema, sandpaper texture, and strawberry tongue. So scarlet fever = “strep throat with a rash-producing toxin”.
The Decisive Fork — Strep A or a Viral Exanthem?
📷 Image placeholder — Fine “sandpaper” scarlet-fever rash with circumoral pallor and a red “strawberry tongue” vs a smooth macular viral rash
Scarlet fever (GAS)Viral exanthems
Rash textureSandpaper (fine, rough)Usually macular/smooth
TongueStrawberry tongueNormal
ThroatExudative pharyngitis/tonsillitisUsually not
Cough/coryzaAbsent (favours bacterial)Often present
Key mimics—Kawasaki (strawberry tongue too — but ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, cracked lips, <5 yrs), measles, drug eruption, toxic shock
Clinical Features
  • Age: typically children 5–15 years; incubation 2–4 days
  • Prodrome: sudden fever, sore throat (pharyngitis/tonsillitis), headache, malaise, nausea/vomiting, tender cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Rash (~12–48 h after symptoms): fine, blanching, erythematous, “sandpaper” texture (often easier to feel than see); starts on the trunk → spreads outward
  • Circumoral pallor — flushed cheeks but pale around the mouth; Pastia’s lines — rash accentuated (deeper red) in skin creases (antecubital fossa, axillae, groin)
  • Strawberry tongue: initially white coating with red papillae (“white strawberry tongue”) → coating peels → red, swollen tongue with prominent papillae (“red strawberry tongue”)
  • Desquamation — as the rash fades (~1 week), the skin peels, classically on the fingertips, palms, and soles (a late clue)
Investigations
  • Primarily a clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for confirmation to start treatment
  • Throat swab (culture) or rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for GAS — to confirm, especially in outbreaks/atypical cases
  • ASO titre (anti-streptolysin O) — evidence of recent strep (retrospective; used in suspected rheumatic fever/GN)
  • Notifiable disease → notify UKHSA / the local Health Protection Team on clinical suspicion
Management
  • First-line: oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 10 days
  • Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin (or azithromycin/erythromycin) — a 5-day course. (Amoxicillin is an alternative if penicillin V isn’t tolerated)
  • Supportive: antipyretics/analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen), fluids, rest
  • School/nursery exclusion: until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics (and until well)
  • Why treat: antibiotics shorten illness, reduce transmission, and reduce suppurative + non-suppurative complications (especially rheumatic fever)
Complications
🔥 Suppurative (direct spread)
  • Otitis media (commonest), sinusitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), cervical lymphadenitis, pneumonia
  • Invasive Group A Strep (iGAS) — necrotising fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, bacteraemia — rare but life-threatening (rising incidence)
🛡️ Non-suppurative (immune-mediated)
  • Acute rheumatic fever (2–4 weeks later) — autoimmune; carditis/valve disease, arthritis, chorea (antibiotics prevent it)
  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (1–3 weeks later) — haematuria, oedema, hypertension
Exam Pearls
What it is
Group A Strep (S. pyogenes) producing erythrogenic exotoxin → “strep throat + toxin rash”.
Presentation
Child 5–15; fever + sore throat, then SANDPAPER rash (trunk → out), CIRCUMORAL PALLOR, Pastia’s lines (creases), STRAWBERRY TONGUE.
Late clue
Desquamation of fingers/palms/soles as it resolves. No cough/coryza (favours bacterial).
Diagnosis
Clinical (don’t wait to treat); throat swab confirms; NOTIFIABLE → inform UKHSA.
Treatment
1st-line penicillin V 10 days; clarithromycin 5 days if penicillin-allergic.
Exclusion
Until 24 h after starting antibiotics.
Complications
Suppurative (otitis media, quinsy, iGAS/nec fasc/toxic shock) + non-suppurative (rheumatic fever, post-strep glomerulonephritis).
Mimic
Kawasaki disease (strawberry tongue too, but ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, cracked lips, <5 yrs).
What & Why

Chickenpox is the primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a herpesvirus — a widespread, intensely itchy vesicular rash with fever. It’s a common, usually mild childhood illness, but dangerous in neonates, pregnant women, and the immunocompromised, and VZV stays dormant and can reactivate later as shingles (incl. Ramsay Hunt syndrome).

The core biology: VZV is highly contagious (respiratory droplets + direct vesicle contact). After primary infection it becomes latent in the dorsal root/cranial nerve ganglia and can reactivate decades later as shingles. Chickenpox and shingles are the same virus — primary vs reactivation.
Clinical Features
  • Age: most children by ~10 years; incubation ~14 days (10–21). Prodrome: mild fever, malaise, headache, anorexia (more marked in older children/adults)
  • The rash: starts on the face/trunk (central) → spreads to limbs (centripetal, denser on the trunk)
  • Evolves: macules → papules → vesicles (“dewdrop on a rose petal”) → pustules → crusts
  • Lesions appear in successive “crops” → lesions of DIFFERENT stages present at the same time (a key distinguishing feature)
  • Intensely itchy (pruritic); can involve mucous membranes (mouth, genitals); self-limiting in healthy children (~1 week)
Infectivity: infectious from ~2 days BEFORE the rash until ALL lesions have crusted over (~5 days after onset). Spread by respiratory droplets + direct contact. School exclusion until all lesions have crusted. Shingles can transmit VZV (→ chickenpox in a non-immune contact), but is less contagious.
The Decisive Fork — Healthy Host vs High-Risk Host
HostApproach
Healthy child (>1 month)Supportive only — do NOT routinely give aciclovir (mild, self-limiting)
Adolescents/adultsHigher complication rate → consider oral aciclovir (if within 24 h of rash)
ImmunocompromisedIV aciclovir (risk of severe disseminated/haemorrhagic varicella)
Neonate / <1 monthIV aciclovir ± VZIG (high mortality)
PregnantSpecialist input — aciclovir, VZIG; risk of maternal pneumonia + fetal effects
Management
🧴 Healthy child — supportive
  • Do NOT routinely give aciclovir (>1 month; mild, self-limiting)
  • Antipyretics — paracetamol (avoid ibuprofen/NSAIDs — linked to severe skin/soft-tissue infection in chickenpox)
  • Calamine / chlorphenamine (antihistamine) for itch, keep cool, nails short, hydration
  • AVOID ASPIRIN in under-16s → Reye’s syndrome (encephalopathy + liver failure)
💊 Aciclovir (antiviral)
  • Works only if started within ~24 hours of rash onset
  • Oral aciclovir: consider in adolescents/adults presenting within 24 h
  • IV aciclovir: immunocompromised, neonates, severe/complicated disease (pneumonia, encephalitis)
Post-exposure (susceptible high-risk contacts): check immunity (VZV IgG); if susceptible → prophylactic antivirals (aciclovir/valaciclovir), typically days 7–14 post-exposure (now first-line PEP), OR VZIG where antivirals are unsuitable (up to ~10 days post-exposure).
Complications & Prevention
  • Secondary bacterial skin infection — the commonest (Group A Strep / Staph aureus); can progress to necrotising fasciitis / invasive GAS — worsened by NSAIDs
  • Dehydration; varicella pneumonia (adults, smokers, pregnant, immunocompromised)
  • Encephalitis — classically cerebellitis (ataxia) in children (usually self-limiting); hepatitis (usually subclinical); Reye’s (with aspirin); haemorrhagic/disseminated varicella (immunocompromised)
  • In pregnancy: congenital varicella syndrome (<28 weeks) + neonatal varicella (perinatal); later: shingles from reactivation (incl. Ramsay Hunt)
  • Prevention: varicella vaccine (live attenuated) — being added to the routine UK childhood schedule (via MMRV) following JCVI; live → contraindicated in pregnancy/immunocompromise. “Breakthrough varicella” = mild disease despite vaccination
Exam Pearls
What it is
Primary VZV; highly contagious; itchy vesicular rash starting centrally, in CROPS → lesions of DIFFERENT stages at once (macule→papule→vesicle→crust).
Infectivity
Infectious from 2 days before rash until ALL lesions crusted → exclude from school until crusted.
Healthy child
Supportive only (do NOT routinely give aciclovir); paracetamol NOT NSAIDs; NO aspirin (Reye’s).
Aciclovir
Oral for adults/adolescents within 24 h; IV for immunocompromised/neonates/severe.
High-risk
Pregnant/immunocompromised/neonate → specialist input; PEP with antivirals (day 7–14) or VZIG.
Complications
Bacterial superinfection (GAS/Staph — worse with NSAIDs → nec fasc), pneumonia (adults), encephalitis/cerebellitis (ataxia), Reye’s (aspirin), haemorrhagic varicella (immunocompromised).
Latency
VZV stays latent → reactivates as SHINGLES (incl. Ramsay Hunt).
Vaccine
Varicella vaccine (live) being added to UK schedule; contraindicated in pregnancy/immunocompromise.
What & Why

Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, “sixth disease”) is a common, benign viral illness of infants caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) (less often HHV-7), with a distinctive two-phase course: several days of high fever, then — as the fever suddenly breaks — a rash. It’s a very common cause of high fever (and febrile convulsions) in infants, and the “fever first, rash after the fever goes” pattern is a classic exam discriminator.

The core rhythm (the whole diagnosis): high fever for ~3 days → the fever suddenly resolves → THEN a rash appears. In most exanthems the rash comes with the fever; in roseola the rash is the “all-clear” sign that appears after the fever has gone. “Exanthem subitum” = “sudden rash”; also called “three-day fever”.
Clinical Features

Age: 6 months – 2 years (peak ~9–12 months); >90% before age 2 (maternal antibodies protect <6 months). Incubation ~5–15 days.

🌡️ Phase 1 — the fever
  • Abrupt-onset HIGH fever (often up to ~40°C), lasting ~3–5 days
  • The child is often relatively well / alert despite the high temperature (reassuring) — though may be irritable
  • Mild: coryza, cough, cervical/occipital lymphadenopathy, mild diarrhoea, periorbital/palpebral oedema, Nagayama spots (papules on the soft palate/uvula)
🌸 Phase 2 — the rash (as fever breaks)
  • The fever resolves suddenly → THEN a rash appears (~12–24 h later)
  • Rose-pink macules and papules, often with pale halos
  • Starts on the TRUNK → spreads to neck/limbs; typically NON-itchy + NON-tender; blanching; fades in 1–2 days, no desquamation
  • By the time the rash appears, the child is recovering (the rash marks the end of the illness)
The Decisive Fork — Roseola vs Measles
📷 Image placeholder — Rose-pink truncal roseola appearing AFTER the fever breaks in a well infant vs the confluent face-down measles rash appearing DURING fever in a miserable child
RoseolaMeasles

The one-liner: high fever in a well-ish infant → fever suddenly breaks → then a rose-pink truncal rash = roseola. If the child looks toxic or the rash came with the fever, think again.
Investigations & Management
  • Clinical diagnosis — no tests usually needed; the fever-then-rash course is characteristic (HHV-6 serology/PCR only in atypical/immunocompromised cases; bloods may show leukopenia)
  • The main clinical challenge is during the fever phase (before the rash) — a high-fever infant must be assessed for serious bacterial infection (the rash, once it appears, is reassuring)
  • Supportive only — benign + self-limiting: antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen), fluids/hydration, rest, reassurance; no antivirals in the healthy child
  • Immunocompromised: HHV-6 can cause severe disease/reactivation (encephalitis, marrow suppression) → may need antivirals (ganciclovir/foscarnet); specialist input
  • No school exclusion specifically required once well
Complications
  • Febrile convulsions — the commonest complication (roseola is a classic trigger, due to the high fever in the vulnerable age group); usually benign/self-limiting
  • Rare: encephalitis/meningoencephalitis, hepatitis (esp. immunocompromised)
  • HHV-6 latency — like other herpesviruses it persists and can reactivate (mainly a problem in the immunocompromised/transplant patients)
Exam Pearls
What it is
HHV-6 (± HHV-7); infants 6 months – 2 years.
The rhythm
HIGH fever ~3 days in a relatively WELL child → fever suddenly BREAKS → THEN a rose-pink, non-itchy, TRUNCAL rash (“exanthem subitum” = sudden rash; “three-day fever”).
Key contrast
The rash marks RECOVERY (appears after the fever goes) — vs measles (rash with fever, ill child).
Other signs
Nagayama spots (palate/uvula papules); periorbital oedema; cervical nodes.
Complication
Febrile convulsions = commonest complication (classic roseola association).
Management
Clinical diagnosis; supportive (antipyretics, fluids); benign + self-limiting.
Pitfall
During the febrile phase (pre-rash), exclude serious bacterial infection.
PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Cancers:
Overview — paediatric cancers
The commonest childhood malignancies — leukaemia (commonest overall) plus the classic solid tumours neuroblastoma, Wilms' and retinoblastoma.
The organising principle: presentation by tumour. ALL = marrow failure (pallor, bruising, infection) ± bone pain; abdominal mass in a young child → Wilms' (renal) or neuroblastoma (adrenal/sympathetic chain); white pupillary reflex → retinoblastoma.
CancerOriginClue
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemiabone marrowpallor, bruising/petechiae, infections, bone pain; commonest childhood cancer
Neuroblastomaneural crest (adrenal/sympathetic)abdominal mass crossing midline, <5yr; ↑catecholamines

Unexplained pallor/bruising/persistent bone pain → check FBC + blood film for leukaemia. A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) or new squint → urgent ophthalmology for retinoblastoma.
What & Why

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is a malignant proliferation of immature lymphoid precursor cells (lymphoblasts) in the bone marrow. It matters because it’s the commonest childhood cancer (~80% of childhood leukaemias), because its presentation is a bone-marrow-failure picture that every clinician must recognise (an unwell child with pallor, bruising, and infections), and because — remarkably — it’s one of oncology’s great success stories, with cure rates now ~90% in children with modern protocols.

The core mechanism: a lymphoid precursor acquires mutations → clonal proliferation of lymphoblasts that crowd out normal haematopoiesis in the marrow. Everything follows: failure of the three normal cell lines (→ anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) plus infiltration of other tissues (bone, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, central nervous system, testes). Most childhood ALL is B-cell precursor (B-ALL); a minority is T-cell (T-ALL).
Epidemiology
  • The most common malignancy affecting children (~80% of childhood leukaemias)
  • Peak incidence 2–5 years
  • Associations: Down syndrome (markedly increased risk), other genetic syndromes (Fanconi anaemia, ataxia-telangiectasia, Li-Fraumeni), ionising radiation
Clinical Features

Symptoms reflect marrow failure + tissue infiltration:

Marrow failure — the triad
  • Anaemia → lethargy, pallor (± breathlessness)
  • Neutropenia → frequent or severe infections
  • Thrombocytopenia → easy bruising, petechiae (± bleeding, e.g. epistaxis)
Infiltration & systemic
  • Bone pain — marrow infiltration (a child who won’t weight-bear/limps)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
  • Fever — in up to 50% of new cases
  • Testicular enlargement, central nervous system involvement (headache, cranial nerve palsies), mediastinal mass (especially T-ALL → superior vena cava obstruction/respiratory distress)
Red-flag rule: unexplained pallor + bruising/petechiae + recurrent infection ± bone pain + hepatosplenomegaly → urgent very urgent FBC within 48h (NICE NG12) + blood film + specialist referral. NICE: any child with unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly warrants immediate referral.
Investigations
  • FBC — anaemia, thrombocytopenia; WCC may be low, normal, or very high; often pancytopenia with circulating blasts
  • Blood film — lymphoblasts (the key finding)
  • Bone marrow aspirate & trephine biopsy — the diagnostic test: >20% blasts confirms acute leukaemia; sent for immunophenotyping (flow cytometry), cytogenetics/molecular studies
  • Cytogenetics/molecular — for risk stratification & prognosis: hyperdiploidy and ETV6-RUNX1 t(12;21) = good; Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) BCR-ABL, KMT2A (MLL) rearrangement, hypodiploidy = poor
  • Lumbar puncture — assess central nervous system involvement (blasts in CSF)
  • Blood chemistry — urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium, renal function (baseline for tumour lysis); LDH; coagulation; LFTs. CXR — mediastinal mass (T-ALL)
Management
Refer immediately to a paediatric oncology (principal treatment) centre. Care is protocol-based (UK: UKALL trials). Stabilise emergencies first.
Stabilise emergencies first
  • Neutropenic sepsis → immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (within 1 hour) — a medical emergency
  • Tumour lysis syndrome → hyperhydration + allopurinol or rasburicase, monitor/correct ↑potassium, ↑phosphate, ↑urate, ↓calcium (risk of acute kidney injury/arrhythmia as blasts lyse)
  • Transfuse (packed cells/platelets) as needed; correct coagulopathy
  • Chemotherapy — the mainstay, in phases over ~2–3 years: induction (achieve remission) → consolidation/intensification → central-nervous-system-directed therapy (intrathecal chemotherapy ± cranial irradiation — the central nervous system/testes are “sanctuary sites”) → maintenance (prolonged, lower-intensity)
  • Philadelphia-positive ALL → add a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib/dasatinib)
  • Newer therapies: immunotherapy — blinatumomab (bispecific), inotuzumab, and CAR-T cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel) for relapsed/refractory disease
  • Allogeneic stem cell transplant — for high-risk/relapsed disease; minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring guides risk and treatment intensity
  • Supportive care: infection prophylaxis (e.g. co-trimoxazole for PCP), antiemetics, nutrition, psychological/family support
Prognosis
  • Childhood ALL cure rate ~90% — one of the best in oncology
  • Good prognostic factors: age 2–10 years, low WCC at diagnosis, B-cell precursor, favourable cytogenetics (hyperdiploidy, ETV6-RUNX1), rapid response/low MRD, no central-nervous-system disease
  • Poor prognostic factors: age <1 or >10, high WCC (>50), T-cell, Philadelphia chromosome/hypodiploidy/KMT2A, central-nervous-system involvement at diagnosis, slow response/high MRD, male sex
Exam Pearls
What it is
Malignant lymphoblast proliferation; COMMONEST childhood cancer; peak age 2–5; associated with Down syndrome.
Presentation
Marrow failure: ANAEMIA (pallor/lethargy) + NEUTROPENIA (infections) + THROMBOCYTOPENIA (bruising/petechiae) + BONE PAIN + HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY + fever (~50%).
Red flag
Unexplained pallor + bruising + infections ± bone pain → very urgent FBC within 48h (NICE NG12) + blood film + urgent referral.
Diagnosis
Blood film (blasts) → bone marrow (>20% blasts) + immunophenotyping + cytogenetics.
Cytogenetics
Hyperdiploidy/ETV6-RUNX1 = good; Philadelphia t(9;22)/hypodiploidy/KMT2A = poor.
Emergencies
Neutropenic sepsis (IV antibiotics <1 hr) + tumour lysis syndrome (hydration + rasburicase/allopurinol; ↑K/↑phosphate/↑urate/↓calcium).
Treatment
Multi-phase chemo (induction → consolidation → CNS-directed → maintenance, ~2–3 yrs); tyrosine kinase inhibitor if Philadelphia+; CAR-T/blinatumomab for relapse.
Prognosis
Cure rate ~90%. Poor: age <1 or >10, WCC >50, T-cell, Philadelphia chromosome, CNS disease.
What & Why

Neuroblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumour of the sympathetic nervous system, arising from primitive neural crest cells. It matters because it’s the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the commonest cancer in infancy, because it’s a classic exam contrast with Wilms tumour (both present as an abdominal mass in a young child), and because it has an extraordinary biological spectrum — from tumours that spontaneously regress in infants to aggressive, treatment-resistant disease in older children.

The core mechanism: neural crest cells normally form the sympathetic chain, adrenal medulla, and paraganglia. Malignant transformation → a tumour that can arise anywhere sympathetic tissue exists — most commonly the adrenal medulla (~50%), but also the paravertebral sympathetic chain (neck→pelvis). Because these cells are catecholamine-producing, the tumour often secretes catecholamines → raised urinary breakdown products (VMA/HVA), the diagnostic hallmark.
The Decisive Fork — Neuroblastoma vs Wilms Tumour
📷 Image placeholder — Neuroblastoma (irregular hard mass crossing the midline, unwell child) vs Wilms tumour (smooth mass confined to one flank, not crossing the midline, well child)
NeuroblastomaWilms tumour (nephroblastoma)
OriginSympathetic chain / adrenal medulla (neural crest)Kidney (metanephric blastema)
Age<5 yr; median ~18 months (commonest in infancy)Peak 3–4 yr
MassIrregular, hard, CROSSES the midlineSmooth, confined to one side, rarely crosses midline
MarkersRaised urinary catecholamines (VMA/HVA)Usually none
Key geneticsMYCN amplification (poor prognosis)WT1/WT2; WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann
Unwell?Often systemically unwell (metastatic at diagnosis in ~50–60%)Often well child
The exam one-liner: an unwell young child with a hard abdominal mass crossing the midline + bone pain + raised urinary VMA → neuroblastoma; a well child with a smooth flank mass not crossing the midline → Wilms.
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Neuroblastoma metastatic signs — periorbital bruising and proptosis (“raccoon eyes”) from orbital/skull deposits

Depend on site, metastases, and catecholamine secretion:

  • Abdominal mass — the commonest presentation; firm, irregular, non-tender, may cross the midline
  • Systemic: weight loss, malaise, fever, pallor — often looks unwell
  • Bone pain, limp, pancytopenia — from bone-marrow metastases (common; can mimic leukaemia)
  • Periorbital bruising (“raccoon eyes”) and proptosis — orbital/skull metastases (a classic sign)
  • Hepatomegaly (liver metastases), subcutaneous skin nodules (“blueberry muffin” in infants)
  • Thoracic tumour → respiratory symptoms; paraspinal tumour → cord compression (dumbbell extension through the intervertebral foramen); cervical tumour → Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
  • Catecholamine effects: hypertension, sweating, flushing, secretory diarrhoea (VIP)
Paraneoplastic syndromes (classic exam pointers)
  • Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia (“dancing eyes, dancing feet”) — chaotic eye movements + myoclonic jerks + ataxia (immune-mediated; paradoxically good tumour prognosis)
  • VIP secretion → intractable watery diarrhoea
Investigations
  • Urinary catecholamine metabolites — VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) and HVA (homovanillic acid) raised in ~90% — the key biochemical test
  • Imaging: ultrasound (initial abdominal mass) → CT/MRI (extent, staging); MIBG scan (meta-iodobenzylguanidine — taken up by sympathetic/catecholaminergic tissue) for the tumour and metastases
  • Tumour biopsy — diagnostic (histology: small round blue cells, ± Homer-Wright rosettes), with molecular testing including MYCN amplification, ALK, and chromosomal changes (1p/11q loss)
  • Bone marrow aspirate/trephine (marrow involvement — common)
  • Bloods: FBC (cytopenias if marrow disease), LDH, ferritin (raised = adverse)
Management
  • Refer to a paediatric oncology centre; treatment is risk-stratified (INRG: age, stage, histology, MYCN, ploidy)
  • Low-risk / infant disease → observation — may spontaneously regress (especially stage 4S infants); or surgery alone
  • Intermediate-risk → surgery + moderate chemotherapy
  • High-risk (e.g. MYCN-amplified, metastatic, older child) → intensive multimodal therapy: induction chemotherapy → surgery → high-dose chemo + autologous stem cell rescue → radiotherapy → maintenance with immunotherapy (anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody, e.g. dinutuximab) + retinoic acid
Prognosis
  • Highly variable — biology-dependent
  • Good: infants <18 months, localised disease, favourable histology, hyperdiploidy, no MYCN amplification, opsoclonus-myoclonus
  • Poor: MYCN amplification, age >18 months, metastatic (high-risk) disease, 1p/11q loss — high-risk long-term survival only ~50% despite intensive therapy
  • Unique feature: some infant tumours (stage 4S) regress spontaneously without treatment
Exam Pearls
What it is
Malignant neural-crest tumour of the sympathetic nervous system (adrenal medulla ~50% / sympathetic chain); COMMONEST extracranial solid tumour of childhood & commonest cancer in infancy; median ~18 months.
Classic mass
Abdominal mass that CROSSES the midline in an UNWELL young child (vs Wilms = smooth, one side, well child).
Investigations
Raised urinary catecholamines (VMA & HVA); MIBG scan; biopsy shows small round blue cells; MYCN amplification = poor prognosis.
Metastases
Metastatic at diagnosis in ~50%: bone pain/marrow (mimics leukaemia), periorbital bruising/proptosis (“raccoon eyes”).
Paraneoplastic
Opsoclonus-myoclonus (“dancing eyes/feet”) — good prognosis; VIP → watery diarrhoea. Cervical → Horner’s; paraspinal → cord compression.
Management
Risk-stratified: observation/spontaneous regression (infants) → surgery → intensive multimodal (chemo + stem cell rescue + anti-GD2 immunotherapy) for high-risk.
Prognosis
Biology-dependent: MYCN amplification = poor; infants/stage 4S may spontaneously regress.
What & Why

Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is a malignant embryonal tumour of the kidney, arising from primitive metanephric blastema (the embryonic tissue that forms the kidney). It matters because it’s the commonest renal malignancy of childhood (and the commonest paediatric abdominal cancer), because it’s the classic exam contrast with neuroblastoma, and because — like ALL — it’s a modern oncology success story with cure rates >85–90%.

The core mechanism: during kidney development, metanephric blastema differentiates into nephrons. In Wilms tumour this tissue fails to differentiate and proliferates, producing a triphasic tumour (blastemal + epithelial + stromal elements). Mutations in WT1/WT2 (chromosome 11) underlie the syndromic forms.
Epidemiology & Associations
  • Commonest paediatric renal malignancy
  • Typically <5 years; peak 3–4 years (slightly older than neuroblastoma)
  • Usually unilateral; bilateral in ~5–10%
  • WAGR syndrome — Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, Retardation (intellectual disability); WT1 deletion
  • Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — overgrowth: macrosomia, macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycaemia
  • Hemihypertrophy (isolated); Denys-Drash syndrome — nephropathy + genitourinary malformation + Wilms (~90% develop Wilms)
The Decisive Fork — Wilms vs Neuroblastoma
Wilms (nephroblastoma)Neuroblastoma
OriginKidney (metanephric blastema)Sympathetic chain/adrenal medulla
AgePeak 3–4 yrMedian ~18 mo (younger)
ChildUsually WELL (incidental mass)Often unwell (metastatic)
MassSmooth, unilateral, does NOT cross midlineIrregular, crosses midline
MarkersNone specificRaised urinary VMA/HVA
HaematuriaCan occur (painless)No
Clinical Features
  • The classic stem: an asymptomatic abdominal mass discovered incidentally (by a parent bathing the child, or on routine exam) — the key clue
  • Abdominal mass — large, smooth, firm, unilateral, does not cross the midline
  • Painless haematuria; flank/abdominal pain
  • Anorexia, fever, malaise
  • Hypertension — from renin secretion/renal artery compression (a classic exam feature)
  • Rarely: rapid enlargement/pain after minor trauma (haemorrhage into tumour)
Referral
A child with an unexplained enlarged abdominal mass → paediatric review within 48 hours (NICE NG12).
Investigations
  • Abdominal ultrasound — the initial investigation (confirms a renal-origin mass)
  • CT/MRI abdomen & chest — staging (local extent, contralateral kidney, lung metastases — the commonest site)
  • Biopsy/histology — triphasic: epithelial tubules, immature glomerular structures, stroma with spindle cells, and small-cell blastematous tissue resembling metanephric blastema, ± areas of necrosis. (In the European/SIOP approach, chemotherapy is often given before biopsy/surgery based on imaging; biopsy practice varies)
  • Bloods: FBC, U&Es, urinalysis (haematuria); blood pressure
Management
  • Refer to a paediatric oncology centre; risk-stratified by stage and histology
  • Nephrectomy — surgical removal of the tumour and affected kidney is the mainstay
  • Chemotherapy — often neoadjuvant (before surgery) to shrink the tumour (standard in the European/SIOP protocol), and/or adjuvant after surgery
  • Radiotherapy — for advanced/higher-stage or unfavourable-histology disease
  • Bilateral disease → nephron-sparing surgery where possible
Prognosis
  • Excellent — overall survival >85–90% (favourable histology, localised)
  • Worse with anaplastic (unfavourable) histology, higher stage, or metastatic disease
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest childhood renal malignancy; from metanephric blastema; peak age 3–4; usually unilateral.
Classic stem
A WELL child with an incidental, smooth, unilateral abdominal mass that does NOT cross the midline (vs neuroblastoma = unwell, irregular, crosses midline).
Also
Painless haematuria, flank pain, hypertension, anorexia/fever.
Associations
WAGR (Wilms, Aniridia, GU malformation, Retardation), Beckwith-Wiedemann, hemihypertrophy, Denys-Drash.
Referral
Unexplained abdominal mass in a child → paediatric review within 48 hours.
Investigation
Abdominal ULTRASOUND first → CT/MRI staging; histology triphasic (blastemal/epithelial/stromal).
Management
NEPHRECTOMY ± chemotherapy (often neoadjuvant) ± radiotherapy for advanced disease.
Prognosis
Excellent (>85–90% survival).
What & Why

Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumour of the developing retina — the commonest intraocular/ocular malignancy of childhood. It matters because it’s the classic paradigm of the “two-hit hypothesis” of tumour-suppressor genes, because its hallmark sign — leukocoria (a white pupil / absent red reflex) — is detectable on the routine newborn/infant red-reflex check (so early detection saves sight and life), and because the hereditary form predisposes to bilateral disease and second cancers.

The core mechanism: RB1 (chromosome 13q14) is a tumour-suppressor gene whose protein (pRb) restrains the cell cycle. Retinoblastoma requires inactivation of BOTH copies of RB1 — Knudson’s “two-hit” hypothesis: Hereditary (~40%) — a germline RB1 mutation is inherited (the “first hit” is in every cell) → only one further somatic hit is needed → tumours arise early, bilaterally, and multifocally, with lifelong risk of second malignancies (especially osteosarcoma). Sporadic (~60%) — both hits are somatic in a single retinal cell → usually unilateral, unifocal, later onset.
Epidemiology & Genetics
  • Commonest ocular malignancy in children
  • Average age at diagnosis ~18 months; nearly all <5 years (bilateral present earlier, ~1 yr; unilateral ~2 yr)
  • RB1 tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 13 (13q14)
  • Hereditary form is autosomal dominant (germline mutation, high penetrance) — all bilateral (and multifocal) cases are hereditary
  • Unilateral (~60%) vs bilateral (~40%)
“Autosomal dominant” refers to the hereditary form — the germline mutation is inherited dominantly with high penetrance, even though tumour formation itself is “recessive at the cellular level” (needing both alleles hit).
Clinical Features
  • Leukocoria — a white pupillary reflex / ABSENT (or white) red reflex — the commonest and most important sign; often first noticed as a white pupil in flash photographs
  • Strabismus (squint) — the second commonest presentation (tumour impairs vision → the eye deviates). Any child with a new squint needs fundoscopy to exclude retinoblastoma
  • Deteriorating/loss of vision, a red or painful eye, or a change in eye appearance
  • Advanced: proptosis, orbital inflammation, buphthalmos (enlarged eye)
  • May be picked up on routine red-reflex screening (newborn & 6-week checks) or family screening (if hereditary)
Investigations
  • Examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with dilated fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist — the key assessment (see the tumour directly). Biopsy is AVOIDED (risk of seeding tumour outside the eye) — diagnosis is clinical/imaging-based when confined to the eye
  • Ocular ultrasound (often shows calcification) and MRI (extent, optic nerve/central-nervous-system involvement — avoid CT to limit radiation, especially in hereditary cases)
  • RB1 genetic testing — essential to identify hereditary disease → screen the child’s siblings/relatives and future offspring, and guide surveillance
Management
Refer to a specialist retinoblastoma centre. Aim, in order of priority: save life → save the eye → preserve vision.
  • Focal/local therapies (small tumours): laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, thermotherapy, plaque brachytherapy
  • Chemotherapy — systemic (e.g. carboplatin, vincristine, etoposide) or intra-arterial (ophthalmic artery) / intravitreal chemotherapy to shrink tumours and salvage the eye
  • Enucleation (removal of the eye) — for advanced/large tumours with no useful vision, or to prevent spread; a prosthesis is fitted
  • External-beam radiotherapy — reserved (avoided where possible in hereditary disease — it further raises the risk of second cancers/osteosarcoma in the radiation field)
Prognosis & Follow-up
  • Excellent — ~90% survive into adulthood in high-income countries
  • Worse with extraocular/optic nerve/central-nervous-system spread or metastasis
  • Hereditary survivors need lifelong surveillance for second malignancies — especially osteosarcoma (and soft-tissue sarcomas, melanoma), heightened by radiotherapy
  • “Trilateral retinoblastoma” — bilateral retinoblastoma + an intracranial (pineal) tumour — a rare, serious hereditary association
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest ocular malignancy of childhood; RB1 tumour-suppressor gene, chromosome 13q14; diagnosed ~18 months (nearly all <5 yr).
Hallmark
LEUKOCORIA (white pupil / absent red reflex) — often first seen in flash photos. New squint → exclude retinoblastoma.
Two-hit model
Both RB1 alleles must be inactivated. Hereditary (~40%, autosomal dominant germline) → bilateral/multifocal, early, + second-cancer risk; ALL bilateral cases are hereditary. Sporadic (~60%) → unilateral.
Diagnose
EUA + dilated fundoscopy + ocular ultrasound/MRI + RB1 genetic testing. NO biopsy (seeding risk).
Management
Life > eye > sight: local therapy (laser/cryo/brachytherapy) + chemotherapy (systemic/intra-arterial/intravitreal) + enucleation for advanced; avoid radiotherapy in hereditary disease.
Prognosis
~90% survival; hereditary → lifelong risk of second cancers (osteosarcoma).
Trilateral
Bilateral retinoblastoma + pineal tumour. Red-reflex screening (newborn/6-week check) catches it early.
PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasculitis:
Overview — paediatric vasculitis
The two childhood vasculitides — Kawasaki disease (medium-vessel) and Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA small-vessel).
The organising principle: Kawasaki = prolonged fever ≥5 days + mucocutaneous features → risk of coronary aneurysms; HSP = palpable purpura (buttocks/legs) + arthralgia + abdominal pain + nephritis, often post-URTI.
ConditionFeaturesManagement
Kawasaki diseasefever ≥5d + conjunctivitis, rash, cervical node, red cracked lips/strawberry tongue, extremity changesIVIG + aspirin; echo for coronary aneurysms
HSP / IgA vasculitispalpable purpura (extensor/buttocks), arthralgia, abdominal pain, IgA nephritisusually self-limiting; monitor BP + urine
Kawasaki disease → give IVIG within 10 days to reduce coronary-artery aneurysms (echo follow-up); one of the few paediatric indications for aspirin. In HSP, monitor blood pressure and urine for nephritis.
What & Why

Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood and — critically — the second most common childhood vasculitis after HSP, but the one that threatens the heart. It matters for one reason above all: it causes coronary artery aneurysms, and untreated it is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in the developed world. The whole clinical urgency is about recognising it and giving IVIG within 10 days to protect the coronaries.

The framing that matters: most childhood fevers with a rash are benign viral illnesses. Kawasaki is the one you cannot miss, because the intervention window is narrow and the consequence of missing it (a coronary aneurysm → thrombosis → MI → sudden death, in a toddler) is catastrophic.

Epidemiology: typically children <5 years (peak 6 months–4 years), more common in boys and in children of East Asian (Japanese) ancestry. Cause unknown — likely an abnormal immune response to an infectious trigger in a genetically susceptible child.

The Decisive Fork — Complete or Incomplete?

This determines how you diagnose — but both get the same urgent treatment:

Complete KawasakiIncomplete (atypical) Kawasaki
DiagnosisFever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5 principal featuresFever + fewer features + supportive labs/echo
WhoClassic presentationEspecially infants <1 year (present atypically, highest aneurysm risk)
Trap—Don’t wait for the full picture — infants with prolonged unexplained fever need an echo and a low threshold to treat
Clinical Features — Diagnostic Criteria
📷 Image placeholder — Kawasaki mucocutaneous signs — bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis (limbal sparing), cracked red lips with strawberry tongue, and swollen erythematous hands progressing to fingertip desquamation
Fever ≥5 days (high, persistent) PLUS ≥4 of 5 — mnemonic CRASH
  • C — Conjunctivitis: bilateral, non-purulent, limbal sparing
  • R — Rash: polymorphous (widespread, non-vesicular)
  • A — Adenopathy: cervical lymphadenopathy, often unilateral, ≥1.5 cm (the least common feature)
  • S — Strawberry tongue: + cracked red lips, oral mucositis
  • H — Hands/feet: erythema and oedema of palms/soles acutely → peeling (desquamation) of fingertips/toes in the convalescent phase
Two timing pearls: the desquamation of the extremities is a later (week 2+) sign — often after the acute illness. And there’s a classic association with redness/induration at the site of a previous BCG scar.

Fever duration is necessary but the criteria are increasingly applied flexibly — 2024 guidance emphasises comprehensive clinical assessment over rigidly waiting 5 days; treatment can start on day 4 if all features are present, and incomplete Kawasaki is treated promptly rather than observed.

Phases
  • Acute (1–2 weeks): fever, the principal features, irritability (very characteristic — a miserable child), myocarditis
  • Subacute (2–4 weeks): fever settles, desquamation, thrombocytosis (platelets rise strikingly), and the period of highest coronary aneurysm and thrombosis risk
  • Convalescent (weeks–months): clinical resolution, inflammatory markers normalise
Investigations

There is no single diagnostic test — it’s clinical, supported by:

  • Bloods: ↑↑ inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), neutrophilia, normocytic anaemia, ↑ ALT/bilirubin; thrombocytosis (platelets often >450, classically rising in the second week — an important supportive clue)
  • Echocardiogram: at diagnosis and repeated in follow-up — looks for coronary artery dilatation/aneurysm (a Z-score ≥2.5 defines abnormality), myocarditis, valve regurgitation, pericardial effusion. A normal early echo does NOT exclude Kawasaki and must not delay treatment
  • Investigations also serve to exclude mimics
Key Differentials (a mimic-heavy list)

Measles, scarlet fever, staphylococcal/streptococcal toxic shock, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, juvenile idiopathic arthritis (systemic), and — importantly since 2020 — MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, post-COVID), which overlaps clinically and is now an explicit differential.

Management
Guideline-verified — AHA 2024.
1. IVIG — the coronary-protecting treatment
  • 2 g/kg as a single infusion, given within 10 days of illness onset (as soon as possible after diagnosis)
  • Dramatically reduces the rate of coronary artery aneurysms
  • Still give it after day 10 if there is ongoing fever/inflammation or coronary abnormalities
2. Aspirin — the famous exception
  • High-dose aspirin acutely (anti-inflammatory) until afebrile, then low-dose aspirin (antiplatelet) for 6–8 weeks until a follow-up echo confirms no coronary changes
  • The key exception to the rule that aspirin is contraindicated in children (Reye’s syndrome risk) — one of the few paediatric indications
  • If coronary aneurysms develop → longer-term antiplatelet ± anticoagulation under cardiology
  • Adjuncts / IVIG resistance: corticosteroids for high-risk patients or IVIG resistance. IVIG resistance = fever recurring/persisting ≥36 hours after the first IVIG infusion → second IVIG dose, steroids, or infliximab
  • Follow-up: cardiology surveillance with serial echocardiography; avoid live vaccines for a period after IVIG (passive antibodies blunt the response — e.g. defer MMR/varicella ~11 months)
Complications
  • Coronary artery aneurysms — the defining complication → thrombosis, stenosis, MI, sudden death. Highest risk: infants <6–12 months, delayed/missed treatment, IVIG resistance
  • Myocarditis, pericarditis, arrhythmia, valve regurgitation in the acute phase
  • Kawasaki disease shock syndrome and macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) — rare, severe
Exam Pearls
What it is
Medium-vessel vasculitis, children <5, threatens the CORONARY ARTERIES.
Criteria
Fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5: CRASH — Conjunctivitis (non-purulent, limbal sparing), Rash, Adenopathy (cervical, unilateral, least common), Strawberry tongue/lip cracking, Hands & feet (erythema/oedema → later desquamation).
Timing
Desquamation of fingers/toes is a LATE (week 2+) sign. Look for BCG-scar redness. Platelets rise in the 2nd week (thrombocytosis).
Diagnosis
Clinical; echo looks for coronary aneurysm (Z-score ≥2.5); a normal early echo doesn’t exclude it and mustn’t delay treatment.
Treatment
IVIG 2 g/kg single dose within 10 days + aspirin.
Aspirin
Kawasaki is THE paediatric exception to the aspirin/Reye’s contraindication.
IVIG resistance
Fever ≥36 h after infusion → 2nd IVIG / steroids / infliximab.
Infants
<1 year present atypically (incomplete Kawasaki) and have the HIGHEST aneurysm risk — low threshold to treat. Avoid live vaccines after IVIG. Differentials: measles, scarlet fever, toxic shock, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, MIS-C.
What & Why

HSP — now formally called IgA vasculitis — is the commonest vasculitis of childhood, an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis driven by IgA immune-complex deposition in small vessels. It matters because it’s common, usually benign and self-limiting, but has one manifestation that dictates the whole follow-up plan: renal involvement (IgA vasculitis nephritis), the source of essentially all its long-term morbidity.

The framing that matters: the skin, joints, and gut settle on their own — you don’t chase those. The kidney is the reason for the follow-up schedule. A child can have a completely normal urinalysis at presentation and develop nephritis weeks later, which is why monitoring runs for months, not days.

Epidemiology: peak age 3–10 years (usually <10), slight male predominance, often 1–3 weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection (classically group A strep) — the URTI trigger is a favourite exam detail. More common in winter.

The Decisive Fork — Is the Kidney Involved?

Everything else is supportive; this is what changes prognosis and management:

No renal involvementIgA vasculitis nephritis
PresentationPurpura + joints + gut, normal urine/blood pressureHaematuria/proteinuria ± hypertension
CourseSelf-limiting, excellent prognosisThe source of long-term morbidity (rarely → chronic/end-stage kidney disease)
ActionSupportive + urine/blood-pressure surveillanceNephrology referral; treat; renal biopsy if severe
Normal early urinalysis does NOT exclude later nephritis — this is the reason HSP has a prolonged monitoring schedule.
Clinical Features — the Classic Tetrad
📷 Image placeholder — Symmetrical non-blanching palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor lower limbs — the required feature of HSP, with normal platelets
  • Palpable purpura (the required feature): symmetrical, non-blanching, over buttocks and extensor surfaces of the lower limbs. Not due to low platelets (platelets are normal/raised — key distinction from ITP)
  • Arthralgia/arthritis: large joints (knees, ankles), transient, non-destructive
  • Abdominal pain: colicky; from bowel-wall vasculitis. Can cause GI bleeding and — importantly — intussusception (classically ileoileal), the key acute abdominal complication
  • Renal involvement (IgA vasculitis nephritis): haematuria (micro/macroscopic) ± proteinuria; ranges from trivial to nephritic/nephrotic; rarely progresses to chronic kidney disease
  • Other: scrotal involvement (a differential for testicular torsion in boys)
Diagnosis
EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria — MANDATORY: palpable purpura (or petechiae) with lower-limb predominance, without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy — PLUS at least one of: (1) diffuse abdominal pain; (2) arthritis or arthralgia; (3) renal involvement (proteinuria or haematuria); (4) histopathology — leukocytoclastic vasculitis with predominant IgA deposition.

Diagnosis is essentially clinical. There is no diagnostic blood test — investigations exist to exclude mimics, map organ involvement, and monitor the kidney:

  • Urinalysis (haematuria/proteinuria) + urine protein:creatinine ratio + blood pressure — the core renal screen, repeated over follow-up
  • FBC & film — platelets normal/raised and no coagulopathy (this excludes ITP and other thrombocytopenic causes of purpura — the essential differential)
  • U&Es, albumin if renal involvement
  • Skin/renal biopsy only in atypical or severe cases → IgA deposition on immunofluorescence
Management
Guideline-verified — supportive is the mainstay (most cases self-limiting).
  • Rest, hydration, analgesia — simple analgesia/NSAIDs for joint pain (use NSAIDs cautiously/avoid if renal involvement). Most skin/joint symptoms resolve within ~4 weeks
  • Corticosteroids — NOT routine: they do not prevent nephritis and aren’t used for the rash. Considered for severe abdominal pain/GI involvement (may shorten it) and in significant nephritis under specialist care
  • Nephritis: refer to paediatric nephrology for significant proteinuria, hypertension, or impaired renal function; ACE inhibitors/ARBs for persistent proteinuria; immunosuppression for severe biopsy-proven nephritis (renal biopsy guides treatment)
Follow-up — the crucial part: regular urinalysis + blood-pressure monitoring for ~6–12 months after presentation, because nephritis can appear late even after a normal initial urine. The single most examinable management point.
HSP vs ITP — the Key Differential
HSP (IgA vasculitis)ITP
RashPalpable purpura (vasculitic)Non-palpable petechiae/purpura, bruising
PlateletsNormal / raisedLow (isolated thrombocytopenia)
MechanismIgA immune-complex small-vessel vasculitisAnti-platelet antibodies (anti-glycoprotein IIb/IIIa)
SystemicJoints, gut, kidneyUsually isolated bleeding/bruising
Both often post-infectious in children — but the palpable rash + normal platelets is the discriminator.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest childhood vasculitis; IgA-mediated small-vessel; often 1–3 weeks post-URTI.
Tetrad
Palpable Purpura (buttocks/legs) + Arthralgia + Abdominal pain + Renal (IgA nephritis).
Key distinction
Palpable purpura with NORMAL platelets — distinguishes it from ITP (low platelets, non-palpable).
Diagnosis
Clinical (EULAR/PRINTO/PRES: mandatory lower-limb purpura + ≥1 of abdo pain / arthritis / renal / IgA-histology).
GI complication
Intussusception (ileoileal). Scrotal involvement mimics torsion.
Steroids
Management supportive; steroids NOT routine (don’t prevent nephritis; reserve for severe GI or nephritis).
THE point
Monitor urinalysis + blood pressure for 6–12 months — nephritis can appear late despite a normal initial urine.
Prognosis
Excellent; long-term outcome is all about the kidney.
PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urinary Tract:
Overview — paediatric urinary tract
Common paediatric renal-tract problems — urinary tract infection, the reflux that predisposes to it (VUR), and nocturnal enuresis.
The organising principle: a childhood UTI needs a clean-catch sample and prompt treatment; atypical/recurrent UTI prompts imaging for underlying VUR (retrograde reflux → renal scarring). Enuresis is common and usually resolves.
