What & Why

A paediatric UTI is a bacterial infection of the urinary tract (lower = cystitis; upper = pyelonephritis) in a child. It matters because it’s common (~1 in 10 girls, ~1 in 30 boys by age 16), because in infants/young children the presentation is non-specific (a UTI can hide behind an “unexplained fever”), and because upper UTIs (pyelonephritis) can cause renal scarring → future hypertension and chronic kidney disease — which is why UTI is a flag for underlying structural/functional abnormalities (e.g. vesicoureteric reflux) that warrant investigation.

The core organism & mechanism: E. coli is the commonest cause (~80%) (ascending from the bowel/perineum); others include Klebsiella, Proteus (associated with stones), Enterococcus. Anything that impairs urine flow or drainage (reflux, obstruction, constipation, incomplete voiding) predisposes. A non-E. coli organism is a feature of “atypical” UTI (suggests an underlying abnormality).
Epidemiology
  • More common in BOYS until ~3 months (male neonates; often with structural anomalies) — thereafter much more common in girls (short urethra)
  • Uncircumcised infant boys have higher risk in early infancy
Clinical Features

Age-dependent, because young children can’t localise:

  • Infants: poor feeding, vomiting, irritability, fever, lethargy, poor weight gain, jaundice (neonate) — non-specific
  • Younger children: abdominal pain, fever, dysuria, vomiting, poor feeding
  • Older children: dysuria, frequency, urgency, haematuria, suprapubic pain, incontinence/enuresis, offensive/cloudy urine
  • Features suggesting UPPER UTI (pyelonephritis): temperature ≥38°C and/or loin pain/tenderness (± rigors, systemically unwell)
Investigations
When to test the urine
  • Symptoms/signs suggestive of UTI, OR
  • An unexplained fever ≥38°C, OR
  • An alternative site of infection but remains unwell
How to sample & test (NICE)
  • Clean-catch urine is the preferred method (non-invasive); if not possible → catheter sample or suprapubic aspiration (under ultrasound guidance)
  • Dipstick (leucocyte esterase + nitrites) in children ≥3 years; but in infants <3 months → send urine directly for urgent microscopy & culture (don’t rely on dipstick)
  • Urine microscopy, culture & sensitivity confirms the diagnosis and guides antibiotics. Refrigerate/boric acid if not cultured within 4 hours
Management
Guideline-verified — NICE NG224.
  • Infants <3 months → refer IMMEDIATELY to paediatrics (treat as per serious infection/sepsis pathway; IV antibiotics)
  • ≥3 months with UPPER UTI/pyelonephritis: consider hospital admission; if not admitted → oral antibiotics 7–10 days (e.g. cephalosporin or co-amoxiclav)
  • ≥3 months with LOWER UTI: oral antibiotics for 3 days (e.g. trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin, cephalosporin, or amoxicillin), per local sensitivities; review if not improving
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent UTIs (and treat underlying factors)
  • Address predisposing factors: constipation (a big one), incomplete/dysfunctional voiding, and adequate fluid intake/toileting
Imaging & Follow-up (NICE NG224)
📷 Image placeholder — Age-banded flowchart (<6 months / 6 months–3 years / ≥3 years × responds-well / atypical / recurrent) for when USS, DMSA and MCUG are indicated

Investigation depends on age, and whether the UTI is “atypical” or “recurrent”:

Atypical UTI
  • Seriously ill/septic, poor urine flow, abdominal/bladder mass, raised creatinine, non-E. coli organism, or failure to respond within 48h
Recurrent UTI
  • ≥2 upper UTIs, or 1 upper + ≥1 lower, or ≥3 lower UTIs
  • Ultrasound — structural abnormalities/obstruction; during the acute illness if atypical; within 6 weeks if <6 months (first UTI) or recurrent
  • DMSA scan — renal parenchymal defects/scarring; done 4–6 months after the infection (for atypical/recurrent, especially <3 years)
  • MCUG (micturating cystourethrogram) — detects vesicoureteric reflux and posterior urethral valves; considered in young infants with atypical/recurrent UTI (especially <6 months). Give prophylactic antibiotics around the procedure
NICE simplification: a child >6 months with a first, E. coli, treatment-responsive UTI needs NO routine imaging. Imaging is for the young (<6 months), atypical, or recurrent.
Exam Pearls
Organism
E. coli commonest (~80%); more common in boys <3 months, then girls.
Presentation
Non-specific in infants (poor feeding, vomiting, irritability, fever); older kids get dysuria/frequency/haematuria.
Think UTI
In ANY unexplained fever ≥38°C. Upper UTI clue: temp ≥38 + loin pain/tenderness.
Sample
Clean-catch (or catheter/suprapubic aspiration); dipstick ≥3 yrs; <3 months → urgent microscopy & culture.
Management
<3 months → immediate paeds referral (IV); ≥3 months upper → 7–10 days oral (cephalosporin/co-amoxiclav) ± admit; ≥3 months lower → 3 days oral (trimethoprim/nitrofurantoin/cephalosporin/amoxicillin).
Imaging
USS (structure) + DMSA (scarring, 4–6 mo) + MCUG (reflux) — for <6 months, ATYPICAL (non-E. coli, poor flow, no response in 48h), or RECURRENT. First simple E. coli UTI >6 months → no imaging.
Also
Treat constipation & voiding; prophylaxis for recurrent UTI.
What & Why

Vesicoureteric reflux is the abnormal backflow (retrograde flow) of urine from the bladder up the ureter towards the kidney. It matters because it’s the commonest urological abnormality found after a childhood UTI, because it predisposes to recurrent UTIs and — crucially — to pyelonephritis reaching the kidney, and because repeated infected reflux → renal scarring (“reflux nephropathy”) → hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

The core mechanism: normally the ureters enter the bladder at an oblique angle through the bladder wall, so that when the bladder contracts, the intramural ureter is compressed shut (a one-way flap valve) → no reflux. In VUR, the ureters are displaced laterally and enter the bladder more perpendicularly (a short/abnormal intramural tunnel) → the valve mechanism fails → urine refluxes back up during voiding.
Why VUR Is Harmful
  • Predisposes to UTI — refluxed urine that isn’t cleared is a reservoir for bacteria
  • Carries infection up to the kidney → pyelonephritis → renal scarring (reflux nephropathy)
  • Reflux nephropathy → hypertension, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease/renal failure (the long-term stakes)
  • Primary VUR = congenital abnormal vesicoureteric junction (the usual paediatric type); secondary VUR = from raised bladder pressure/obstruction (e.g. posterior urethral valves, neuropathic bladder)
Grading (International Reflux Study, I–V)
📷 Image placeholder — VUR grades I–V — from ureter-only reflux through to gross dilatation/tortuosity with lost calyceal impressions

Graded on MCUG by how far up urine refluxes and how dilated the system becomes:

GradeFindings
IReflux into the ureter only (no dilatation)
IIReflux up to the renal pelvis/calyces, no dilatation
IIIReflux with mild dilatation of ureter/pelvis/calyces
IVModerate dilatation + tortuous ureter, blunted calyces
VGross dilatation & tortuosity, ureteric kinking, loss of the calyceal/papillary impressions
Low-grade (I–II) usually resolves spontaneously (>80%) with growth; high-grade (IV–V) less likely to resolve and carries the highest scarring/chronic-kidney-disease risk.
Presentation
  • Most commonly detected during investigation of a childhood UTI (especially atypical or recurrent UTI — the NICE trigger)
  • Antenatally detected hydronephrosis on the 20-week/postnatal scan can be the first clue
  • Recurrent febrile UTIs / pyelonephritis; or found on family screening (there’s a familial tendency)
Investigations
  • Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) — the gold-standard diagnostic test AND how VUR is graded: contrast is instilled into the bladder via a catheter and X-rays taken during voiding to see reflux. (Give prophylactic antibiotics around the procedure)
  • DMSA scan — done afterwards to look for renal scarring/parenchymal defects (typically 4–6 months after an infection, so acute change isn’t mistaken for a scar)
  • Ultrasound — structural assessment (hydronephrosis, duplex systems); often the first-line imaging
  • Blood pressure, renal function, urinalysis (proteinuria) — monitor for reflux nephropathy
Management

The general principle is to protect the kidneys from infected reflux until the child grows out of it or it’s corrected:

  • Conservative / observation — especially low-grade VUR, which often resolves spontaneously as the child grows (the intramural ureter lengthens)
  • Treat/prevent UTIs: treat acute UTIs promptly; long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin) — considered especially in high-grade VUR, recurrent febrile UTIs, or existing scarring
  • Address bladder-bowel dysfunction — treat constipation and dysfunctional voiding (major contributors)
Surgical correction (high-grade/persistent VUR, breakthrough febrile UTIs on prophylaxis, or progressive scarring)
  • Endoscopic injection of a bulking agent (e.g. Deflux) beneath the ureteric orifice (the “STING” procedure) — minimally invasive
  • Open ureteric reimplantation (ureteroneocystostomy) — creates a longer oblique tunnel; highest success rate
  • Follow-up: monitor growth, blood pressure, renal function, and urine long-term (reflux nephropathy can present years later)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Retrograde backflow of urine from bladder → ureter/kidney; commonest urological abnormality found after childhood UTI.
Mechanism
Ureters insert too PERPENDICULARLY (laterally displaced, short intramural tunnel) → failed flap-valve → reflux.
Harm
Predisposes to UTI/pyelonephritis → renal SCARRING (reflux nephropathy) → HYPERTENSION + chronic kidney disease.
Diagnosis
Diagnosed & graded (I–V) on MCUG; DMSA detects scarring (4–6 months later).
Grading
Grade I = ureter only … Grade V = gross dilatation/tortuosity + lost calyceal impressions. Low-grade often resolves spontaneously; high-grade = worst prognosis.
Presentation
Via UTI investigation (atypical/recurrent) or antenatal hydronephrosis.
Management
Observation (low-grade) + treat UTIs/constipation ± antibiotic prophylaxis → surgery (endoscopic “STING” injection or ureteric reimplantation) for high-grade/breakthrough UTI/scarring.
Secondary VUR
Think posterior urethral valves / neuropathic bladder.
What & Why

Nocturnal enuresis is involuntary wetting during sleep (bedwetting) in a child aged ≥5 years — the age at which bladder control at night is normally expected. It matters because it’s very common (~15–20% of 5-year-olds, resolving spontaneously in ~15% per year), because it causes significant distress, embarrassment, and impact on self-esteem (so it must be handled sympathetically — it is NOT the child’s fault), and because it occasionally signals an underlying medical problem that must be excluded.

The core concept — the causes of primary bedwetting: the child’s bladder control matures late; contributory factors include (1) a “deep sleeper” who doesn’t wake to a full bladder (arousal problem), (2) nocturnal polyuria (reduced overnight antidiuretic hormone → too much urine at night), and (3) a small/overactive bladder (reduced functional capacity/detrusor overactivity) — often with a strong genetic/familial tendency.
Classification
  • Primary enuresis — the child has NEVER been reliably dry at night (>6 months) — the commonest; usually delayed maturation
  • Secondary enuresis — the child was previously dry for ≥6 months, then started wetting again — think of an acquired cause: UTI, constipation, diabetes, or a psychological/emotional stressor (bullying, family upheaval, abuse)
  • Monosymptomatic (bedwetting only) vs non-monosymptomatic (bedwetting + daytime symptoms — urgency, frequency, daytime wetting → points to bladder dysfunction)
Assessment — Look for Underlying Causes
  • First reassure and give advice if the child is <5 — bedwetting is normal at that age, no treatment
  • Look for underlying causes/triggers: constipation, diabetes mellitus, and UTI — plus daytime symptoms (bladder dysfunction), sleep-disordered breathing (obstructive sleep apnoea), and psychosocial stressors (especially secondary enuresis)
  • History: pattern (primary/secondary, monosymptomatic or not), fluid/caffeine intake, toileting, bowels, family history, and impact
  • Urinalysis — NOT routine; only if recent-onset (?diabetes/UTI), daytime symptoms, unwell, or signs of ill health
Management
1. General advice & modifiable factors (first for everyone)
  • Reassure — bedwetting is common and NOT the child’s fault (avoid punishment/blame)
  • Fluids — adequate daytime intake but reduce fluids (and avoid caffeine/fizzy drinks) in the evening/before bed
  • Toileting patterns — empty the bladder regularly during the day and just before sleep
  • Treat constipation and any UTI first — these may resolve the enuresis alone
  • Reward systems — e.g. star charts rewarding agreed behaviours (drinking well, toileting before bed, helping change sheets) — NOT rewarding “dry nights” (which the child can’t fully control)
2. Enuresis alarm — FIRST-LINE active treatment
  • A sensor pad/alarm that detects wetness and wakes the child → conditions them to wake to a full bladder / hold on
  • First-line for most children — best long-term/sustained success, but takes weeks and needs commitment from child and family
3. Desmopressin — for short-term/rapid control
  • A synthetic antidiuretic hormone analogue → reduces overnight urine production
  • Used for short-term/rapid results — e.g. sleepovers/school trips/camp, or when an alarm is unsuitable/declined or has failed
  • Fluid caution: avoid excessive fluid around dosing (risk of hyponatraemia/water intoxication). Can be combined with an alarm for partial responders
  • 4. If refractory: refer to specialist; options include anticholinergics (e.g. oxybutynin) for overactive bladder, and rarely tricyclics (imipramine — specialist only, cardiac risk)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Involuntary bedwetting in a child ≥5 years; common (~15% of 5-year-olds), resolves ~15%/year; NOT the child’s fault.
Under 5
<5 years → reassure, no treatment.
Primary vs secondary
Primary (never dry) vs Secondary (dry ≥6 months then relapsed → hunt for a cause: UTI, constipation, DIABETES, psychosocial stress).
Subtypes
Monosymptomatic (bedwetting only) vs non-monosymptomatic (+ daytime symptoms → bladder dysfunction).
Exclude
Constipation, UTI, diabetes; urinalysis only if recent-onset/daytime symptoms/unwell.
Ladder
General advice (evening fluids, toileting, treat constipation, reward systems — reward behaviour not dry nights) → ENURESIS ALARM (1st-line, best long-term) → DESMOPRESSIN (short-term/rapid, e.g. sleepovers).
Desmopressin
Synthetic antidiuretic hormone; watch fluids (hyponatraemia risk).
Refractory
Anticholinergics (oxybutynin) ± specialist referral.

The organising principle: age is the key discriminator for the painful/limping hip. DDH (neonatal screen); Perthes (4–8yr, avascular necrosis); SUFE (adolescent, often overweight); Osgood-Schlatter (adolescent knee, overuse).

Adolescent with hip or referred knee pain + externally rotated leg → think SUFE (urgent fixation; avoid weight-bearing). Always examine the hip in a child presenting with knee pain.
What & Why

Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a spectrum of abnormal development of the hip joint — from a shallow/dysplastic acetabulum, through a subluxatable/dislocatable hip, to a frankly dislocated hip. It matters because it’s common (~1–3% of newborns have some instability), because early detection and simple treatment (a harness) give excellent outcomes, whereas late diagnosis means surgery and lifelong consequences (limp, pain, early osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis) — which is why it’s a core component of UK newborn screening (NIPE).

The core concept: the hip is a ball-and-socket joint that must develop congruently — a well-seated femoral head stimulates the acetabulum to deepen. If the head sits abnormally, the acetabulum stays shallow, worsening the problem — a vicious cycle. This is why early reduction and holding the hip flexed/abducted (Pavlik harness) allows normal development, and why delay makes it progressively harder to correct.
Risk Factors
  • Breech presentation (the strongest — especially breech at/after 36 weeks, or breech at delivery)
  • Female sex (~6:1 — female hips are more sensitive to maternal ligament-laxity hormones)
  • Family history (first-degree relative with DDH)
  • Firstborn (tighter uterus/less room); oligohydramnios, macrosomia, multiple pregnancy (packaging/crowding)
  • Left hip most commonly affected (fetal positioning against the maternal spine)
  • Associated “packaging” disorders: talipes (club foot), congenital torticollis, plagiocephaly; genetic syndromes with laxity (Down, Ehlers-Danlos)
Screening & Clinical Features
UK screening — NIPE (high-yield)
  • Screened in the Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE): a newborn hip exam (<72 h) and a repeat at the 6–8-week check
  • Ultrasound at ~4–6 weeks (even if exam normal) for: breech (at/after 36 weeks or at delivery), first-degree family history, or an abnormal/uncertain clinical exam
Examination manoeuvres (the two you must know)
  • Ortolani test — relocates a dislocated hip: with hips/knees flexed, abduct and lift the femur → a palpable “clunk” as the head reduces into the acetabulum (“Ortolani = Open out, back In”)
  • Barlow test — dislocates a dislocatable hip: adduct the flexed hip and apply gentle posterior pressure → the head slips out posteriorly (“Barlow = pushes Back”)
  • A “clunk” (not a benign click) is significant
Other / later signs
  • Limited/asymmetrical hip abduction (a key sign, especially after the neonatal period)
  • Asymmetrical skin/thigh/gluteal creases
  • Leg-length discrepancy — Galeazzi sign (knees at different heights when hips/knees flexed, feet flat)
  • Later (walking age): painless limp, waddling/Trendelenburg gait (if bilateral), toe-walking
Investigations
  • Ultrasound — the investigation of choice under ~4.5–6 months (the femoral head is not yet ossified, so X-ray is unreliable). Assesses acetabular morphology and head position; Graf classification grades severity
  • X-ray (pelvis) — used from ~4.5–6 months onward (once the femoral head ossifies)
  • Timing pitfall: ultrasound too early (first few weeks) over-detects transient laxity — hence screening ultrasound at ~4–6 weeks
Management
  • Many mild cases / neonatal instability resolve spontaneously in the first few weeks — hence delayed screening ultrasound rather than immediate treatment
  • Pavlik harness — first-line for infants <6 months with persistent dysplasia/instability/dislocation: a dynamic splint holding the hips flexed and abducted → allows normal acetabular development. Worn continuously for several weeks (~6–12), with regular ultrasound monitoring. Avoid forced/full abduction — risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head
  • Older infants (>6 months) or failed harness → surgery: closed reduction (± adductor tenotomy) and hip spica cast, or open reduction ± acetabular/femoral osteotomy for late/severe cases
  • Follow-up to ensure normal development
Complications
  • Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (both from untreated DDH and from over-aggressive splinting)
  • Persistent dysplasia/subluxation, leg-length discrepancy, gait abnormality
  • Early (premature) osteoarthritis of the hip — the major long-term consequence of missed/late DDH
  • Redislocation, need for repeat surgery
Exam Pearls
What it is
Spectrum from acetabular dysplasia → subluxation → dislocation; early treatment = excellent outcome, late = surgery + early osteoarthritis.
Risk factors
BREECH, Female, Family history, Firstborn, oligohydramnios; LEFT hip commonest; associated talipes/torticollis.
Screening
UK = NIPE (newborn + 6–8 wk exam); ultrasound at ~6 wk for breech / family history / abnormal exam.
Exam
Ortolani (relocates — clunk IN on abduction) & Barlow (dislocates — OUT on adduction + posterior pressure). Also: limited abduction, asymmetric creases, Galeazzi sign.
Imaging
Ultrasound <6 months (femoral head not ossified); X-ray >4.5–6 months.
Management
Pavlik harness <6 months (flexion/abduction); surgery (closed/open reduction + spica) if >6 months or harness fails.
Complication
Avascular necrosis of femoral head (untreated OR over-abduction in harness) + early osteoarthritis.
Clunk vs click
A “clunk” is significant; a “click” is usually benign.
What & Why

Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head in a child — the blood supply to the developing femoral epiphysis is temporarily disrupted, the bone dies, collapses, and then slowly revascularises and remodels. It matters because it’s a key cause of the limping child, because it’s the classic “painless limp in a young school-age boy”, and because — although self-limiting/self-healing — the shape the femoral head heals into determines lifelong hip function (a flattened, deformed head → early osteoarthritis).

The core mechanism: the femoral head’s blood supply in this age group is precarious (largely via the lateral epiphyseal vessels, little collateral). An interruption → osteonecrosis of the epiphysis. The dead bone is structurally weak → it collapses/fragments under weight-bearing, then the body resorbs and replaces it (revascularisation/remodelling) over months–years. The goal of treatment is to keep the softened head well-seated (“contained”) in the acetabulum during healing, so it remodels round rather than flattened.
Epidemiology & Associations
  • Age 4–8 years (range ~2–12); the classic exam age
  • Boys ~4–5:1
  • Usually unilateral; bilateral ~10–15% (bilateral → investigate for multiple epiphyseal dysplasia / hypothyroidism / sickle cell — it shouldn’t be symmetrical Perthes)
  • Associations: low birth weight / small for age / delayed bone age, more physically active children, passive smoking, low socioeconomic status, ADHD
  • A diagnosis of exclusion — rule out other causes of femoral head osteonecrosis (sickle cell, leukaemia, steroids, Gaucher’s)
The Decisive Fork — Perthes vs SUFE vs Transient Synovitis

The paediatric-hip differential is examinable gold — age is the biggest discriminator:

Age4–8 yr10–15 yr3–10 yr

Any limping child who is unwell/febrile → exclude SEPTIC ARTHRITIS first (Kocher criteria) — that’s the emergency, not Perthes.
Clinical Features
  • Painless or mildly painful limp — often insidious over weeks–months (the classic)
  • Hip, groin, thigh, or referred KNEE pain (always examine the hip in a child with knee pain)
  • Worse with activity, better with rest; no systemic upset (afebrile, well)
  • On examination: restricted hip movement — especially abduction and internal rotation; antalgic gait; later Trendelenburg gait, and thigh/gluteal muscle wasting from disuse
Investigations
  • X-ray of both hips (AP + frog-leg lateral) — first-line. Findings evolve: early widened joint space → ↑density/sclerosis and a smaller epiphysis → subchondral fracture/“crescent sign” → fragmentation → flattening/collapse → remodelling (Waldenström stages)
  • MRI — more sensitive for early disease (before X-ray changes) and to assess the extent of necrosis
  • Bloods (FBC, CRP/ESR) — normal in Perthes; used to exclude septic arthritis/infection/malignancy
  • Technetium bone scan — reduced uptake early (less used now)
Management
  • Refer to paediatric orthopaedics. The principle is “containment” — keep the femoral head deep in the acetabulum so it remodels spherically
  • Younger children (<6 years) with limited involvement → conservative: observation, activity restriction, physiotherapy (maintain range of movement, especially abduction), analgesia, and monitoring — most remodel well (years of growth left)
  • Restricted weight-bearing / abduction bracing/casting in selected cases (containment)
  • Older children (>6–8 years) or severe involvement → surgery — femoral or pelvic (Salter) osteotomy to re-contain and re-orient the head
  • Long-term follow-up; total hip replacement may eventually be needed if the head heals poorly
Prognosis
  • Younger age at onset = better prognosis (more remodelling potential; children <6 often do very well)
  • Worse prognosis: older age (>8), female sex, more of the head involved (lateral pillar/Herring classification), and greater deformity/incongruence at healing
  • Main long-term risk: premature osteoarthritis of the hip (from a non-spherical “coxa magna/plana” head)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Idiopathic AVASCULAR NECROSIS of the femoral head; boy aged 4–8; PAINLESS limp; well child.
Referred pain
Pain may refer to the KNEE — always examine the hip.
Signs
Restricted ABDUCTION + INTERNAL ROTATION; antalgic/Trendelenburg gait; muscle wasting.
X-ray
AP + frog-leg: sclerosis → subchondral crescent → fragmentation → flattening/collapse → remodelling. MRI for early disease. CRP/ESR normal (check to exclude septic arthritis).
Bilateral
Bilateral Perthes → investigate (multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, hypothyroid, sickle cell). It’s a diagnosis of exclusion.
Management
CONTAINMENT: young/mild → conservative (rest, physio, monitor); older/severe → osteotomy surgery.
Prognosis
Younger = better prognosis; main long-term risk = early osteoarthritis.
Contrast
Perthes (4–8, painless, avascular necrosis) vs SUFE (10–15, overweight, external rotation) vs transient synovitis (post-viral, self-limiting) vs septic arthritis (unwell/febrile — the emergency).
What & Why

Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (also slipped capital femoral epiphysis, SCFE) is a displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis relative to the metaphysis through the growth plate (physis) — the femoral neck slips anteriorly and rotates externally, while the femoral head stays seated in the acetabulum. It matters because it’s the commonest hip disorder of adolescence, because it’s frequently missed (up to ~50% at first presentation) — classically because it presents with knee pain, not hip pain — and because delayed diagnosis dramatically raises the risk of avascular necrosis and lifelong hip disability.

The core mechanism: during the adolescent growth spurt, the physis is at its weakest and under high shear. Excess load (obesity) and/or hormonal factors overwhelm it → the epiphysis “slips.” Think of it as a Salter-Harris type I fracture through the growth plate occurring atraumatically (or after trivial trauma). This is why it clusters at puberty, in overweight children, and why endocrine disease is a red flag.
Epidemiology & Risk Factors
  • Age 10–15 years (adolescent; boys ~13, girls ~12 — around the growth spurt)
  • Boys ~2–3:1
  • Obesity — the strongest modifiable risk factor (the classic “overweight adolescent male”)
  • Rapid growth spurt (can also affect tall/thin children who’ve grown fast)
  • Endocrine associations — hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency/treatment, panhypopituitarism; also renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency. Screen for endocrine disease if the child is young (<10), underweight, or has bilateral slips
  • Bilateral in ~20–40% (often sequential)

  • Hip, groin, thigh, or — classically — KNEE pain (referred; ~25–50% present with knee/thigh pain, and hip pain may be absent in up to half)
  • Limp (antalgic), reduced weight-bearing; may be a painless limp

Investigations
  • X-ray of BOTH hips — AP AND frog-leg lateral views (the frog-leg lateral is the most sensitive — a subtle slip may be invisible on AP)
  • Trethowan’s sign / Klein’s line: a line along the superior border of the femoral neck should normally intersect part of the epiphysis; in SUFE it doesn’t (epiphysis slips below it) — the “melting ice-cream cone/scoop” appearance
  • Southwick slip angle — grades severity; MRI for a suspected pre-slip or equivocal X-ray
  • Bloods normal (helps exclude septic arthritis); endocrine work-up (TFTs etc.) if atypical/young/bilateral
Classification
Stable (can weight-bear, ± crutches) vs Unstable (cannot weight-bear even with crutches) — unstable slips carry a much higher risk of avascular necrosis (the key prognostic split). Also graded by chronicity (acute/chronic/acute-on-chronic) and magnitude.
Management
  • Make the child NON-WEIGHT-BEARING and refer to orthopaedics urgently (further slipping worsens outcome)
  • Surgical fixation — the mainstay: “pinning in situ” with a single cannulated screw across the physis to stabilise the epiphysis and prevent further slip
  • Severe/unstable slips → open reduction/realignment osteotomy in specialist hands (higher avascular necrosis risk with manipulation)
  • Prophylactic pinning of the contralateral (unaffected) hip — considered, especially with an underlying endocrine disorder or young age (high bilateral risk)
Complications
  • Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (the major complication — much higher with unstable slips and with forced reduction)
  • Chondrolysis (cartilage loss → stiffness)
  • Leg-length discrepancy, deformity, altered gait
  • Premature osteoarthritis of the hip (long-term)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Femoral neck slips anteriorly/externally through the physis; femoral head stays in the acetabulum. Commonest adolescent hip disorder.
Classic
OVERWEIGHT adolescent BOY (10–15), around the growth spurt, ± minor trauma.
Presentation
Hip OR KNEE/thigh pain + limp — always examine the hip in knee pain (up to 50% missed).
Signs
Leg held in EXTERNAL rotation + loss of internal rotation; Drehmann’s sign (obligate external rotation on hip flexion).
X-ray
AP + FROG-LEG lateral; Trethowan’s sign / Klein’s line (epiphysis slips below the line) — “melting ice-cream cone.”
Endocrine
Young/underweight/bilateral → screen for ENDOCRINE cause (hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth hormone issues).
Management
NON-weight-bearing + urgent ortho referral → in-situ pinning (cannulated screw); consider prophylactic contralateral pinning.
Complication
AVASCULAR NECROSIS (worse with unstable slips/forced reduction) → early osteoarthritis. Stable (can weight-bear) vs unstable (cannot) — unstable = high avascular necrosis risk.
What & Why

Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity — inflammation and micro-injury at the growth-plate/apophysis where the patellar tendon inserts into the top of the shin — one of the commonest causes of anterior knee pain in adolescents, especially active/sporty boys. It matters because it’s a benign, self-limiting overuse condition with a clinical diagnosis and conservative management, and recognising it avoids unnecessary imaging and lets you reassure confidently.

The core mechanism: the patellar (quadriceps) tendon inserts into the tibial tuberosity, which in adolescence is still a growth plate (apophysis) — the weak link. During a growth spurt, repetitive, forceful pull of the quadriceps (running, jumping, kicking) causes repeated micro-avulsions → inflammation and new bone growth → a visible/palpable lump. Initially tender (inflamed); as it heals, the lump becomes hard, non-tender, and permanent.
Epidemiology
  • Adolescents during the growth spurt — girls ~8–12, boys ~10–15 (slightly younger in girls)
  • More common in boys and in physically active children — jumping/sprinting sports (basketball, football, volleyball, gymnastics, running)
  • Usually unilateral, but can be bilateral (~20–30%)
Clinical Features
  • Gradual (insidious, atraumatic) onset
  • A visible/palpable, tender, hard lump over the tibial tuberosity (the classic sign)
  • Anterior knee pain
  • Pain exacerbated by physical activity, kneeling, and knee extension (especially resisted extension / squatting / stairs / running/jumping)
  • Relieved by rest; no systemic symptoms, no true joint effusion, knee otherwise normal (full range of movement)
  • Tenderness localised to the tibial tuberosity (not the joint line — helps distinguish from intra-articular pathology)
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — the history and localised tuberosity tenderness are usually sufficient; no imaging needed in a typical case
  • X-ray (lateral knee) — only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude other pathology; may show fragmentation/irregularity or a separate ossicle at the tuberosity (changes overlap with normal, so confirmatory not required)
  • Consider alternatives if atypical (night pain, rest pain, systemic symptoms, effusion, non-tuberosity pain) → exclude infection, malignancy (osteosarcoma around the knee), juvenile idiopathic arthritis, patellar tendinopathy
Management
Reassurance — it is self-limiting and settles as the growth plate fuses (skeletal maturity). The key message.
Initial (reduce pain/inflammation)
  • Reduction/modification of physical activity (relative rest from aggravating sports — not complete inactivity)
  • Ice after activity
  • NSAIDs / simple analgesia
Once symptoms settle
  • Stretching and physiotherapy — quadriceps/hamstring stretching and strengthening to offload the tuberosity
  • Protective knee pads for kneeling; occasionally a short period of reduced loading
  • Outcome: symptoms fully resolve over time (months–up to ~2 years), typically leaving a painless hard bony lump at the tuberosity
  • Rarely → complete avulsion fracture (the tuberosity separates from the tibia) → needs surgery; and rarely a persistent painful ossicle in skeletally mature patients may warrant excision
Exam Pearls
What it is
Traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity (patellar tendon insertion); commonest cause of anterior knee pain in active adolescents, especially boys.
Mechanism
Repetitive quadriceps pull → micro-avulsions at the tuberosity apophysis → inflammation + bony lump.
Features
Gradual anterior knee pain + TENDER BONY LUMP over the tibial tuberosity; worse with activity/kneeling/knee extension; relieved by rest.
Diagnosis
Clinical — no imaging usually needed (X-ray only if atypical, to exclude other causes).
Management
REASSURE (self-limiting) + activity modification + ice + NSAIDs → stretching/physio; pain resolves leaving a painless hard bump.
Red flags
Night/rest pain, systemic symptoms, effusion → exclude infection/malignancy (osteosarcoma)/juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Rare
Complete tibial tuberosity avulsion → surgery.
PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Disorders:
Overview — chromosomal disorders
Aneuploidies — abnormal chromosome number — with characteristic phenotypes and associated anomalies. (See also the Genetic Syndromes topic.)
The organising principle: recognise the pattern, then screen for the associated conditions. Trisomy 21 (Down) is commonest; Turner (45,X) affects girls.
DisorderKaryotypeFeatures & associations
Down syndrome & trisomiesTrisomy 21hypotonia, characteristic facies, single palmar crease; AVSD, duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, leukaemia; also Edwards (18)/Patau (13)
Turner syndrome45,Xshort stature, webbed neck; coarctation/bicuspid valve, ovarian failure; growth hormone, oestrogen
Each aneuploidy carries specific associations to actively screen for (e.g. cardiac defects and hypothyroidism in Down syndrome; coarctation and gonadal failure in Turner).
What & Why

Chromosomal trisomies — an extra copy of a whole chromosome — are the commonest survivable autosomal aneuploidies. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most important: the commonest chromosomal cause of learning disability, compatible with long survival, and the target of the national antenatal screening programme. Edwards (trisomy 18) and Patau (trisomy 13) are rarer and usually fatal in infancy. All three are screened for together antenatally.

The core genetic point: all three arise most often from meiotic non-disjunction (a chromosome fails to separate → the gamete gets two copies → the zygote has three). The single biggest risk factor is advancing maternal age (older eggs → more non-disjunction).
The Three Trisomies at a Glance
Down (T21)Edwards (T18)Patau (T13)
Chromosome211813
FrequencyCommonest (~1/700)~1/5000~1/10,000
SurvivalOften into adulthoodMost die <1 yearMost die <1 year
HallmarksFlat face, epicanthic folds, single palmar crease, hypotoniaMicrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, overlapping fingersMicrocephaly/small eyes, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, scalp defects
Down Syndrome — Genetics
  • Non-disjunction (~94%) — sporadic meiotic error; risk ↑ with maternal age. Standard trisomy 21 (47,XX/XY +21)
  • Robertsonian translocation (~4%) — an extra chromosome 21 fused to another (often 14). Can be inherited from a balanced-carrier parent → recurrence risk; parental karyotyping needed
  • Mosaicism (~2%) — some cells trisomic, some normal → often a milder phenotype
Down Syndrome — Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Neonatal Down syndrome facies — flat face, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, protruding tongue; with a single palmar (simian) crease and sandal gap
👶 Craniofacial
  • Round/flat face, flat occiput (brachycephaly)
  • Small, low-set ears
  • Epicanthic folds + upslanting palpebral fissures
  • Brushfield spots (speckled iris); protruding tongue (relative macroglossia), small mouth
✋ Limbs / other
  • Single palmar (simian) crease
  • Hypotonia (floppy baby — often the first sign)
  • Sandal gap (wide 1st–2nd toe gap), clinodactyly (incurved 5th finger), short stature
Down Syndrome — Associated Conditions
  • Congenital heart disease (~50%) — atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) is the classic/most characteristic; also VSD, ASD, tetralogy of Fallot → all need echocardiography
  • Learning disability (variable; the commonest genetic cause)
  • GI: duodenal atresia (“double bubble”), Hirschsprung’s disease, imperforate anus, coeliac disease, oesophageal atresia
  • Conductive hearing loss (recurrent glue ear) + sensorineural; vision: cataracts, refractive errors, squint
  • Haematological: ↑ leukaemia (ALL and AML); transient abnormal myelopoiesis in neonates
  • Endocrine: hypothyroidism (screen), diabetes; atlantoaxial instability (caution: contact sports/anaesthesia)
  • Early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (amyloid precursor protein gene is on chromosome 21); recurrent infections, obstructive sleep apnoea, subfertility, epilepsy, depression
Antenatal Screening & Diagnosis
📷 Image placeholder — Screening pathway — combined test (11⁺²–14⁺¹) or quadruple test (14⁺²–20⁺⁰) → higher chance ≥1 in 150 → NIPT (cffDNA) → diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis karyotype

All pregnant women are offered screening for T21, T18 and T13 together (NHS Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme). Screening gives a chance/risk, not a diagnosis.

🩸 Combined test (first-line, 11⁺²–14⁺¹ wks)
  • Nuchal translucency (NT) — increased in Down’s
  • β-hCG — increased
  • PAPP-A — decreased
  • (+ maternal age)
🩸 Quadruple test (14⁺²–20⁺⁰ wks)
  • If the combined-test window is missed / NT not obtainable:
  • AFP ↓, uE3 (oestriol) ↓, hCG ↑, inhibin-A ↑
  • “Higher chance” = risk ≥1 in 150 → offered further testing
  • NIPT (non-invasive prenatal test) — cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood; very high detection (~99% for T21) but still a screening test (positive needs diagnostic confirmation)
  • Diagnostic (definitive) — karyotype: chorionic villus sampling (CVS, 11–14 wks) or amniocentesis (>15 wks) — both carry a ~0.1–0.2% procedure-related miscarriage risk (RCOG)
  • Postnatal diagnosis: clinical suspicion → karyotyping confirms
Management
  • No cure — MDT support to optimise development + health surveillance for the complications
  • Health surveillance: echocardiography (CHD screen at birth), regular thyroid function, hearing + vision checks, growth monitoring, developmental support, coeliac screening
  • MDT: paediatrician, cardiology, SALT, physio/OT, education, audiology, ophthalmology; family support (Down’s Syndrome Association). Life expectancy now ~60 years
Edwards (T18) & Patau (T13)

Both are severe, usually lethal in infancy, picked up on the same screening (with low hCG + low PAPP-A patterns, unlike Down’s).

🔴 Edwards (T18)
  • Micrognathia (small jaw), low-set ears
  • Rocker-bottom feet, overlapping/clenched fingers (index over middle)
  • Prominent occiput, cardiac + renal malformations, severe learning disability
  • Most die within the first year
🔴 Patau (T13)
  • Microcephaly, small/abnormal eyes (microphthalmia)
  • Cleft lip/palate; polydactyly; scalp defects (cutis aplasia)
  • Holoprosencephaly, cardiac/renal defects, severe learning disability
  • Most die within days – the first year
Memory anchors: Edwards = 18 = “E for Extremities” (overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia). Patau = 13 = “P for Polydactyly, cleft Palate, holoProsencephaly”.
Exam Pearls
Trisomies
From non-disjunction (↑ maternal age); Down (21) > Edwards (18) > Patau (13).
Down features
Flat face/occiput, epicanthic folds, upslanting fissures, Brushfield spots, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, HYPOTONIA.
Down complications
AVSD (classic CHD, ~50% have CHD), duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung’s, hypothyroidism, leukaemia (ALL/AML), glue ear, atlantoaxial instability, early Alzheimer’s.
Genetics
~94% non-disjunction, ~4% Robertsonian translocation (inheritable → parental karyotype), ~2% mosaic (milder).
Screening
Combined (11⁺²–14⁺¹): ↑NT, ↑β-hCG, ↓PAPP-A. Quadruple (14⁺²–20⁺⁰): ↓AFP, ↓uE3, ↑hCG, ↑inhibin-A.
Higher chance
≥1 in 150 → NIPT (cffDNA, ~99% but still screening) → diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis (karyotype, ~0.1–0.2% miscarriage risk).
Edwards (18)
Micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, overlapping fingers — die <1 yr.
Patau (13)
Microcephaly, small eyes, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, scalp defects — die <1 yr.
What & Why

Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder of females caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome (45,X), producing short stature, gonadal dysgenesis (ovarian failure), and somatic features — most importantly cardiac and renal anomalies. It’s the commonest sex-chromosome abnormality in females (~1 in 2500), usually presents with short stature and delayed/absent puberty, and its cardiovascular complications — aortic dissection — are the leading cause of premature death.

The core genetics: loss of all or part of one X chromosome — monosomy 45,X (~50%), mosaicism (45,X/46,XX), or a structural X abnormality (deletion of Xp, isochromosome, ring X). Unlike the trisomies, Turner’s is NOT associated with advancing maternal age.
The Core Endocrine Mechanism
📷 Image placeholder — Turner hypergonadotropic hypogonadism — streak ovaries → ↓oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → ↑FSH/LH → primary amenorrhoea
  • “Streak ovaries” — the ovaries are dysgenetic (fibrous streaks) → gonadal dysgenesis / primary ovarian failure
  • Low oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → ↑ GnRH → HIGH FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism)
  • Consequence: primary amenorrhoea, absent/incomplete puberty, and infertility
This is why Turner’s is a classic cause of primary amenorrhoea with a HIGH FSH (high FSH = ovarian/gonadal cause).
Clinical Features
📏 Growth / skeletal
  • Short stature (most consistent feature — SHOX gene haploinsufficiency)
  • Shield chest with widely-spaced nipples
  • Short 4th metacarpal; cubitus valgus (↑ carrying angle), scoliosis, high-arched palate
🧣 Neck / lymphatics
  • Webbed neck (from a resolved cystic hygroma), low posterior hairline
  • Cystic hygroma (antenatal — a fetal clue)
  • Lymphoedema of the hands and feet in the neonate (a classic newborn presentation)
❤️ Cardiac
  • Bicuspid aortic valve (~15%) — the commonest cardiac defect
  • Coarctation of the aorta (~5–10%) — ejection systolic murmur
  • Risk of aortic dilatation and dissection (the key life-threatening complication)
🫘 Renal / other
  • Horseshoe kidney — the commonest renal abnormality
  • Primary amenorrhoea, delayed/absent puberty, infertility
  • Multiple pigmented naevi; recurrent otitis media / conductive hearing loss
  • Autoimmune: hypothyroidism (Hashimoto’s), coeliac disease, type 1 diabetes
  • Normal intelligence (mean IQ ~90) but difficulties with non-verbal/spatial skills and social cognition (verbal skills preserved)
Investigations
  • Karyotype — the definitive diagnostic test (45,X or a variant)
  • Gonadotrophins (FSH/LH) elevated; low oestradiol
  • Echocardiography (± cardiac MRI) — for bicuspid valve, coarctation, and aortic root diameter (baseline + surveillance)
  • Renal ultrasound (horseshoe kidney); screen for autoimmune disease (TFTs, coeliac); audiometry; growth/bone age; blood pressure
  • May be picked up antenatally (cystic hygroma/hydrops/lymphoedema on scan, or abnormal NIPT/screening) → karyotype confirmation
Management

MDT, lifelong. Two hormonal pillars:

💉 Hormonal
  • Growth hormone — to improve final adult height (started in childhood once growth faltering is evident)
  • Oestrogen replacement — to induce + maintain puberty, secondary sexual characteristics, and protect bone; started around normal puberty age, then combined (oestrogen + progestogen) HRT to ~51
🔍 Surveillance / complications
  • Lifelong cardiac surveillance — echo/cardiac MRI for aortic dilatation; aortic dissection is the leading cause of death — BP control
  • Treat coarctation/valve disease, hypertension; thyroid/coeliac screening; hearing + renal monitoring
Fertility: usually infertile (streak ovaries) → assisted reproduction with donor eggs is possible; pregnancy carries a high risk of aortic dissection and needs specialist cardiac/obstetric care. Plus psychological/educational support.
Key Differential — Noonan Syndrome
Turner syndromeNoonan syndrome
Genetics45,X (chromosomal)Autosomal dominant (PTPN11 etc.)
SexFemales onlyBoth sexes
CardiacLeft-sided: bicuspid AV, coarctationRight-sided: pulmonary stenosis, HCM
KaryotypeAbnormal (45,X)Normal
FertilityInfertile (streak ovaries)Usually normal
Noonan is sometimes called “male Turner’s” but affects both sexes with a normal karyotype and pulmonary stenosis.
Exam Pearls
What it is
45,X (or variant); FEMALES only; commonest sex-chromosome disorder in females. NOT linked to maternal age.
Endocrine
Streak ovaries → low oestrogen → HIGH FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) → primary amenorrhoea + infertility.
Features
SHORT STATURE, webbed neck, shield chest with widely-spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpal, high-arched palate, multiple naevi.
Neonate
Lymphoedema of hands/feet; antenatal cystic hygroma.
Cardiac
Bicuspid aortic valve (commonest) + coarctation → risk of aortic DILATATION/DISSECTION (leading cause of death — lifelong echo/MRI surveillance).
Renal
Horseshoe kidney = commonest renal anomaly.
Associations
Recurrent otitis media, hypothyroidism, coeliac; normal IQ but poor non-verbal/spatial skills.
Diagnosis + Rx
KARYOTYPE (45,X); FSH/LH high. Treatment: growth hormone (height) + oestrogen replacement; donor-egg IVF; pregnancy = high aortic-dissection risk.
Differential
Noonan (autosomal dominant, both sexes, normal karyotype, PULMONARY stenosis).
PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmental & Behavi:
Overview — neurodevelopmental & behavioural
Disorders of development and behaviour — global developmental delay and the neurodevelopmental conditions ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.
The organising principle: distinguish global delay (multiple domains — needs investigation) from specific patterns. ASD = social-communication + restricted/repetitive behaviours; ADHD = inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings. Assess against developmental milestones.
ConditionFeaturesManagement
Developmental delaydelay across gross/fine motor, speech, socialscreen for cause (hearing, vision, genetic, metabolic); MDT
ADHDinattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity in ≥2 settings, impairingbehavioural strategies; methylphenidate
Autism spectrum disorderpersistent social-communication difficulty + restricted/repetitive behavioursMDT diagnosis and support
Watch for developmental red flags (loss of skills/regression, no social smile by 8 weeks, not walking by 18 months) → prompt referral. Always check hearing and vision.
What & Why

Developmental delay is when a child fails to reach expected developmental milestones at the expected age. It matters because development is the paediatric equivalent of a vital sign — deviation flags underlying pathology (genetic, neurological, sensory, metabolic, or environmental) — and because early identification → early intervention materially improves outcomes. The single most useful concept is the limit age — the age by which a skill should have appeared; failure to reach it (not the average age) is what triggers action.

The core framework — four domains: development is assessed in four streams, and the pattern of which are affected points to the cause: (1) Gross motor; (2) Fine motor & vision; (3) Speech, language & hearing; (4) Social, emotional & behavioural.
Key Definitions
  • Developmental delay — delay in one or more domains
  • Isolated (specific) delay — one domain affected (e.g. isolated speech delay) — often has a specific, sometimes reversible cause (e.g. hearing loss → speech delay)
  • Global developmental delay (GDD) — delay in ≥2 domains in a child <5 years (formally, ≥2 standard deviations below the mean). Suggests a broader/underlying cause
  • Developmental regression — LOSS of previously acquired skills — a serious red flag always warranting investigation (suggests a neurodegenerative/metabolic condition, e.g. a leukodystrophy, or Rett syndrome)
  • Correct for prematurity: subtract the weeks of prematurity from chronological age when assessing (until ~2 years) — “milestone age = age − weeks born early”
Developmental Milestones — Gross Motor
AgeMilestone
3 monthsLittle/no head lag when pulled to sit; good head control prone; lumbar curve when held sitting
6 monthsLifts on extended arms (prone); grasps feet (supine); pulls to sitting; sits with back straight (held); rolls front→back
7–8 monthsSits without support (refer at 12 months)
9 monthsPulls to standing; crawls
12 monthsCruises; walks with one hand held
13–15 monthsWalks unsupported (refer at 18 months)
18 monthsSquats to pick up a toy
2 yearsRuns; walks up/down stairs holding rail
3 yearsRides a tricycle (pedals); walks upstairs without rail
4 yearsHops on one leg
Memory hooks: “6, 9, 12” — 6 = sits with support, 9 = sits with no support, 12 = refer if can’t sit unsupported. “3, 6, 9, 12 — heads, shoulders, knees and toes” — 3 mo head control, 6 mo sitting (supported), 9 mo crawling, 12 mo walking.
Developmental Milestones — Other Domains
Fine motor & vision
  • 3 mo: reaches for objects; holds rattle briefly; visually alert (especially faces); fixes and follows to 180°
  • 6 mo: palmar grasp; passes objects hand to hand; “visually insatiable”
  • 9 mo: points with finger; early pincer — 12 mo: good pincer grip; bangs toys together
  • Bricks: tower of 2 (15 mo), 3 (18 mo), 6 (2 yr), 9 (3 yr)
  • Drawing: circular scribble (18 mo) → vertical line (2 yr) → circle (3 yr) → cross (4 yr) → square & triangle (5 yr)
  • Book: pats page (15 mo) → turns several pages (18 mo) → one page at a time (2 yr)
  • Hand preference before 12 months is ABNORMAL — may indicate a contralateral hemiplegia/cerebral palsy
Speech, language & hearing
  • 3 mo: quietens to parent’s voice; turns to sound; squeals
  • 6 mo: double syllables (“adah”, “erleh”) — 9 mo: says “mama”/“dada”; understands “no”
  • 12 mo: knows and responds to own name — 12–15 mo: 2–6 words (refer at 18 months); understands simple commands
  • 2 yr: combines 2 words; points to body parts — 2½ yr: ~200-word vocabulary
  • 3 yr: short sentences (3–5 words); asks what/who; names colours; counts to 10 — 4 yr: asks why/when/how
Social, behaviour & play
  • Smiles at 6 weeks (refer at 10 weeks); laughs at 3 mo
  • Not shy at 6 mo → shy/stranger awareness at 9 mo
  • Play: peek-a-boo (9 mo) → waves bye/pat-a-cake (12 mo) → plays alone contentedly (18 mo) → parallel play — near, not with (2 yr) → plays with other children (4 yr)
  • Feeding: hand on bottle (6 mo) → cup + spoon (12–15 mo) → spoon & fork (3 yr) → knife & fork (5 yr)
  • Dressing: helps (12–15 mo) → takes off shoes (18 mo) → puts on hat/shoes (2 yr) → dresses independently, not laces/buttons (4 yr)
Red Flags
Any of these → refer for paediatric assessment.
  • Loss of any previously acquired skill (regression) — the most serious
  • No smile by 8–10 weeks; no eye contact by ~3 months
  • No reaching for objects by 6 months
  • No sitting by 9–12 months; no walking by 18 months
  • No words by 18 months; no 2-word phrases by 2 years
  • Hand preference before 12 months
Causes
  • Genetic/chromosomal: Down syndrome, Fragile X, other syndromes
  • Antenatal: congenital infection (TORCH), fetal alcohol syndrome, teratogens
  • Perinatal: prematurity, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, kernicterus
  • Postnatal: meningitis/encephalitis, head injury, non-accidental injury, hypothyroidism (screened on newborn blood spot), metabolic disorders
  • Neurological: cerebral palsy, neuromuscular disease (e.g. Duchenne), neural tube defects
  • Sensory: hearing impairment (→ speech delay), visual impairment
  • Environmental/social: neglect, understimulation, safeguarding concerns
  • Often idiopathic — and much isolated delay is time-limited with a good prognosis
Assessment & Management
  • Detailed history (pregnancy/birth, milestones, family history, hearing/vision, social) + examination (growth, head circumference, neuro, dysmorphism) + development assessment
  • Always check hearing and vision — reversible sensory causes
  • Investigations (guided by findings): genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, Fragile X), TFTs, creatine kinase (if motor delay — Duchenne), metabolic screen, ± MRI/EEG
  • Management is MDT — community paediatrics, and SALT (speech), physiotherapy (gross motor), occupational therapy (fine motor), audiology, orthoptics, portage, health visitor, and educational support. Treat any reversible cause; safeguarding referral if neglect suspected
Exam Pearls
Four domains
Gross motor, fine motor/vision, speech-language/hearing, social/behavioural.
GDD
Delay in ≥2 domains in a child <5 years (implies underlying cause).
Regression
LOSS of acquired skills = always a red flag (neurodegenerative/metabolic).
Prematurity
Correct for prematurity until age 2.
Key limit ages
Sit unsupported by 12 mo, walk by 18 mo, first words by 18 mo, 2-word phrases by 2 yr; smile by 10 weeks.
Classic sign
Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal (?hemiplegic cerebral palsy).
Always check
HEARING and VISION (reversible causes); isolated speech delay → think hearing loss first.
Management
MDT (community paeds, SALT, physio, OT, audiology) + treat reversible cause + safeguard if neglect.
What & Why

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that is developmentally inappropriate and impairs functioning across multiple settings (home and school/work). It matters because it’s common (~5% of children), because untreated it causes academic underachievement, low self-esteem, and secondary problems (conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, substance misuse), and because it’s very treatable.

The core concept: ADHD sits on a spectrum with normal behaviour — what makes it a disorder is that symptoms are persistent (≥6 months), present before age 12, occur in ≥2 settings, and cause real impairment. This is why diagnosis requires observation across settings (school reports, not just clinic) and cannot be made on a rating scale alone.
The Decisive Fork — Which Presentation?

Two symptom dimensions give three presentations:

PresentationPredominant features
Predominantly inattentiveInattention (the “daydreamer”; easily missed, commoner in girls)
Predominantly hyperactive-impulsiveHyperactivity/impulsivity
CombinedBoth (the commonest)
Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5)
Symptoms must be persistent, present for ≥6 months, onset before age 12, occur in ≥2 settings, and cause ≥moderate impairment. Number of symptoms needed: children/young people (<17 years) ≥6 features from a domain; adults (≥17 years) ≥5 features (the threshold drops for adults).
InattentionHyperactivity / Impulsivity
Doesn’t follow through on instructionsUnable to play quietly
Reluctant to engage in mentally-intense tasksTalks excessively
Easily distractedDoesn’t wait their turn easily
Difficulty sustaining attention on tasksLeaves seat when expected to sit
Difficulty organising tasks/activitiesOften “on the go”
Often forgetful in daily activitiesOften interrupts/intrudes on others
Often loses things needed for tasksAnswers prematurely (before question finished)
Doesn’t seem to listen when spoken toRuns/climbs in inappropriate situations
Associations & Comorbidities
  • ADHD + epilepsy may co-occur
  • Autism spectrum disorder, oppositional defiant/conduct disorder, tic disorders/Tourette’s, learning disability/specific learning difficulties (dyslexia), anxiety and depression, attachment/sleep problems
  • Consider safeguarding, attachment disorder, and hearing/vision as mimics/contributors
Assessment
  • Diagnosis by a specialist (psychiatrist, paediatrician, or appropriately trained clinician) after a full clinical and psychosocial assessment, developmental and psychiatric history, and observer reports from ≥2 settings (e.g. school)
  • Do NOT diagnose on rating scales or observation alone — but Conners’ rating scales and the Strengths & Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) are useful adjuncts, and QbTest may aid diagnosis in 6–17s
  • Exclude/identify: mood/anxiety disorders, autism spectrum disorder, hearing/vision problems, sleep disorders, safeguarding, substance misuse
Management

The NICE NG87 ladder — guideline-verified:

1. General / first-line (before medication)
  • Watchful waiting (up to 10 weeks) for mild symptoms; do NOT offer medication first-line for pre-school children — offer a group parent-training/education programme
  • Education about ADHD, environmental modifications (seating, structure, “I need a break” cards, written instructions, teaching-assistant support), sleep/diet/exercise advice
  • ADHD-focused group parent-training (children) and CBT (older children/adults with persistent impairment despite medication)
2. Pharmacological (if persistent significant impairment)
  • First-line: methylphenidate (a stimulant; short- or long-acting) for children ≥5 and young people
  • Second-line: lisdexamfetamine (or dexamfetamine) if a 6-week trial of methylphenidate gives insufficient benefit
  • Non-stimulants: atomoxetine (SNRI) or guanfacine — if stimulants ineffective/not tolerated/contraindicated (or where diversion/misuse is a concern)
  • Adults: first-line methylphenidate OR lisdexamfetamine
3. Baseline checks & monitoring (stimulants) — high-yield
  • Before starting: measure height, weight, baseline BP and HR, and take a cardiac history (ECG if cardiac history/signs — stimulants raise HR/BP)
  • Monitor height and weight (stimulants can suppress growth/appetite — plot on centile charts) and BP/HR (every dose change and ~6-monthly). Growth-monitoring is a classic exam point
  • Watch for: reduced appetite, insomnia, tics, mood changes; atomoxetine — monitor for suicidal ideation and hepatic toxicity
Note: SSRIs (for repetitive behaviours/anxiety/aggression) and antipsychotics (for aggression) describe autism/challenging-behaviour management, NOT core ADHD — for ADHD itself the drug is a stimulant (methylphenidate).
Exam Pearls
What it is
Persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, onset <12 yrs, ≥2 settings, causing impairment.
DSM-5 counts
≥6 symptoms (under 17) / ≥5 (17 and over) from a domain, for ≥6 months.
Presentations
Inattentive (often girls/missed), hyperactive-impulsive, combined (commonest).
Diagnosis
Specialist, multi-setting; rating scales (Conners’, SDQ) are adjuncts, not sufficient alone.
Management
Parent-training/behavioural + environmental support FIRST; medication if persistent impairment.
Drugs
First-line METHYLPHENIDATE (stimulant); 2nd-line lisdexamfetamine; non-stimulants atomoxetine/guanfacine.
Monitoring
Monitor HEIGHT & WEIGHT (growth suppression) + BP/HR; baseline cardiac assessment before stimulants.
Comorbidities
Autism, conduct/oppositional defiant disorder, tics/Tourette’s, dyslexia, anxiety/depression, epilepsy.
Key point
ADHD itself is NOT treated with SSRIs/antipsychotics (those are for autism-related behaviours).
What & Why

Autism spectrum disorder is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition defined by two core domains: (1) persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and (2) restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities. It matters because it’s common (~1–2%), because early recognition and support markedly improve function and quality of life, and because it’s frequently missed or misattributed — especially in girls and in those with normal/high intelligence.

The core concept — “spectrum”: ASD spans a huge range from profound impairment with intellectual disability and no speech, to highly able individuals with subtle social difficulties (what used to be called Asperger’s — now subsumed into ASD in DSM-5). This is why presentation is so variable and why management is individualised.
The Decisive Fork — the Two-Domain “Dyad” (DSM-5)

Diagnosis requires deficits in BOTH domains, present from early childhood, causing functional impairment:

A. Social communication & interaction deficitsB. Restricted, repetitive behaviours (RRBs)
Poor social-emotional reciprocity (back-and-forth conversation, sharing interests/emotions)Stereotyped/repetitive movements or speech (hand-flapping, lining up toys, echolalia)
Impaired non-verbal communication (reduced eye contact, gestures, facial expression)Insistence on sameness, inflexible routines, distress at change
Difficulty developing/maintaining relationships; lack of interest in peers; absent imaginative/shared playHighly restricted, fixated interests of abnormal intensity
 Hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input (sounds, textures, pain, lights)
Early Features / Red Flags
Prompt referral if any of these (recognition — NICE CG128).
  • No babble/pointing/gesture by ~12 months
  • No single words by 16 months; no 2-word phrases by 24 months
  • Reduced/absent eye contact; not responding to their name
  • Lack of pointing to share interest (protodeclarative pointing); lack of joint attention
  • Not showing objects to others; limited pretend play
  • Loss of language or social skills at any age (regression) — always investigate
  • Repetitive behaviours, unusual sensory responses, preference for being alone
Causes / Associations
  • Strongly genetic/heritable; polygenic, with many associated syndromes
  • Associated conditions: Fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, Rett syndrome, Down syndrome, fetal valproate/alcohol exposure, prematurity/small-for-gestational-age
  • NOT caused by the MMR vaccine — the alleged link is comprehensively discredited/fraudulent; reassuring this is a high-yield public-health point
Comorbidities
  • ADHD (very common overlap)
  • Intellectual disability / learning disability, and specific learning difficulties
  • Epilepsy (increased incidence)
  • Anxiety and depression, OCD
  • Sleep disorders, feeding problems; tics/Tourette’s, motor coordination difficulties (dyspraxia)
Assessment & Diagnosis
  • Diagnosis is clinical and MULTIDISCIPLINARY (a specialist “autism team”) — based on a detailed developmental history + observation across settings (home + school), against DSM-5 criteria. There is no single diagnostic blood test or scan
  • Structured tools support (but don’t replace clinical judgement): ADOS (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule), ADI-R (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised)
  • Assess for comorbidities, and check hearing and vision (exclude sensory causes)
  • Consider genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, Fragile X) where indicated
Management
There is NO cure — management is support-based, individualised, and MDT-led, aimed at maximising function and quality of life (guideline-verified — NICE CG170).
1. Core / first-line (non-pharmacological)
  • Psychosocial/behavioural interventions are the foundation — a play-based intervention with parents/carers/teachers to increase joint attention, engagement, and reciprocal communication
  • Speech & language therapy, occupational therapy (incl. sensory strategies), educational support/EHCP, structured/predictable environments
  • Parent/carer training and support; support for the whole family
2. Pharmacological (COMORBIDITIES / challenging behaviour ONLY)
  • No medication treats the core social-communication/RRB features (a key exam point)
  • Antipsychotics (e.g. risperidone/aripiprazole) — specialist, for behaviour that challenges (aggression, self-injury); review at 3–4 weeks, stop by 6 weeks if no benefit
  • SSRIs — for comorbid anxiety, depression, or OCD/repetitive behaviours (specialist, cautiously)
  • Methylphenidate — for comorbid ADHD; treat epilepsy, sleep disorders (e.g. melatonin)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Lifelong neurodevelopmental condition; DYAD of (1) social communication/interaction deficits + (2) restricted/repetitive behaviours, from early childhood.
Social domain
Poor reciprocity, reduced eye contact/gestures, difficulty with relationships/peer play.
RRBs
Stereotypies, insistence on sameness, fixated interests, sensory hyper/hypo-reactivity.
Red flags
No pointing/joint attention, no words by 16 mo / 2-word phrases by 24 mo, no response to name, REGRESSION.
Diagnosis
Clinical + MDT (autism team), history + multi-setting observation (ADOS/ADI-R); no blood test.
Myth
NOT caused by MMR (discredited).
Comorbidities / associations
ADHD, learning disability, epilepsy, anxiety/depression, OCD, sleep problems; Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis, Rett, fetal valproate.
Management
NO cure — support-based (psychosocial/play-based, SALT, OT, education). Medication only for COMORBIDITIES: antipsychotics (risperidone) for aggression, SSRIs for anxiety/OCD, methylphenidate for ADHD — NOT the core features.
PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding & Child Protec:
Overview — safeguarding & child protection
Recognising and acting on child maltreatment, and the legal/ethical frameworks underpinning children's care.
The organising principle: maintain a professional suspicion — injuries inconsistent with the history or developmental stage, delayed presentation, or inconsistent accounts. Know the frameworks for consent and protection.
TopicKey points
Non-accidental injury (NAI)injuries inconsistent with history/development (e.g. bruising in a non-mobile infant, certain fractures), delayed presentation; document + escalate
SUDIsudden unexpected death in infancy; risk reduction (back to sleep, smoke-free); multi-agency investigation
Safeguarding frameworksGillick competence (capacity to consent), Fraser guidelines (contraception), Children Act (welfare paramount)
Bruising or a fracture in a non-mobile infant, or injuries inconsistent with the mechanism given, mandates a safeguarding assessment and escalation. The child's welfare is paramount.
What & Why

Non-accidental injury is physical harm to a child inflicted or knowingly not prevented by a carer — one form of child maltreatment (alongside neglect, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, and fabricated/induced illness). It matters more than almost any paediatric topic because missing it can be fatal, because every doctor has a statutory safeguarding duty, and because the presentation is deliberately obscured — recognition depends on a pattern of red flags, not any single injury. The mindset: “could this injury, in this child, with this explanation, be non-accidental?”

The framing that matters: you are not there to prove abuse or confront the family — you are there to recognise the possibility, keep the child safe, document meticulously, and refer. The safeguarding system (social care, police, named/designated professionals) does the investigating. A child’s safety overrides confidentiality.

NICE CG89 language you must know: the guideline splits features into “consider” maltreatment (one possible explanation) and “suspect” maltreatment (a serious level of concern → must act/refer).

The Decisive Question — Does the Injury Fit the Story?
Red flagWhy it raises concern
Injury inconsistent with the explanationMechanism given can’t produce that injury
Injury inconsistent with developmental stage“Those who don’t cruise rarely bruise” — bruising in a non-mobile infant is the single most important red flag
Changing / vague / absent historyStory shifts between accounts or professionals
Delay in presentationUnexplained delay seeking help
Inappropriate carer–child interaction / affectDetachment, hostility, or lack of concern
Multiple injuries of different agesRepeated episodes
Repeated attendancesPattern across visits (check records)
Bruising in a non-independently-mobile infant (can’t crawl, cruise, bottom-shuffle, or even roll) — accidental bruising is rare (0–1.3%) and this is a sentinel injury that mandates safeguarding action. The highest-yield single fact.
Suggestive Injury Patterns
Bruising
  • Non-mobile infant — any bruise
  • Sites unusual for accidents: ears, neck, cheeks, trunk, buttocks, genitalia, inner thighs (accidental bruises are over bony prominences — shins, forehead, knees)
  • Patterned bruises: hand/slap marks, grip marks, ligature marks, implement outlines, bite marks
  • You cannot accurately age a bruise by its colour with the naked eye (a common exam misconception)
Fractures
  • Any fracture in a non-mobile infant without a clear major-trauma explanation
  • Multiple fractures, especially of different ages (different healing stages)
  • Posterior rib fractures in infants (from squeezing/compression) — highly specific
  • Metaphyseal corner (“bucket-handle”) fractures — from shaking/pulling/twisting; highly specific for NAI
Head injury — abusive head trauma (Shaken Baby)
  • The triad: encephalopathy + subdural haemorrhage(s) + retinal haemorrhages, in a child 0–5 years, from intentional shaking
  • NICE: suspect maltreatment with multiple subdural haemorrhages ± subarachnoid/hypoxic-ischaemic damage, or retinal haemorrhages, without major confirmed accidental trauma or medical cause
  • Head-injury immediate-CT triggers include suspicion of non-accidental head injury and <1 yr with bruise/swelling/laceration >5 cm on the head — these are safeguarding triggers
Burns/scalds & other
  • Glove-and-stocking / immersion scalds with sharp margins, cigarette burns (well-demarcated circular), burns to unusual sites, patterns matching an implement
  • Intracranial, intra-abdominal, or intrathoracic injury without confirmed major accidental trauma (may have no external marks)
  • Oral injuries (torn frenulum in a non-mobile infant); anogenital signs
Types of Maltreatment (know the five)

Physical abuse (NAI), neglect (commonest form overall), emotional abuse, sexual abuse (including child sexual exploitation), and fabricated or induced illness (FII). Also on the safeguarding radar: FGM, trafficking, and criminal/child sexual exploitation.

Assessment
  • Full history — mechanism, timeline, who was present; take carefully and non-judgementally; document verbatim where possible
  • Full examination — growth/plotting, whole skin (body map every mark with size/site/description), developmental assessment, demeanour and interaction
  • Skeletal survey (a defined radiographic series) ± repeat at ~2 weeks for occult/healing fractures, in infants/young children
  • CT/MRI head for suspected abusive head trauma; ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages
  • Coagulation screen/FBC and consider bone profile — to exclude bleeding disorders (ITP, haemophilia, leukaemia) and osteogenesis imperfecta / rickets as mimics
  • Consider the differential honestly: meningococcal septicaemia, coagulopathy, Mongolian blue spots, osteogenesis imperfecta, birth-related retinal haemorrhage — exclude these before concluding NAI
Management — What a Doctor Actually Does
The steps (Working Together / GMC)
  • Ensure the child is safe now — admit if necessary (a legitimate protective measure)
  • Escalate immediately — inform the senior paediatrician / named or designated safeguarding lead; don’t manage alone
  • Refer to children’s social care (and police if a crime is suspected) — a duty; refer on reasonable suspicion, you don’t need proof
  • Document meticulously and contemporaneously — body maps, verbatim quotes, times, who was present (records may become evidence)
  • Consider siblings — other children in the household may also be at risk
  • Communicate with the family honestly about referrals where it doesn’t increase risk to the child; explain, don’t accuse
Child safety overrides confidentiality — you may share information without consent if a child is at risk of significant harm (GMC). If unsure → discuss with a senior/named safeguarding professional; the threshold to seek advice is low. It is not your job to investigate or prove abuse — it is to recognise, protect, document, and refer.
Exam Pearls
Core question
Does the injury fit the explanation and the child’s developmental stage?
Biggest red flag
Bruising in a non-mobile infant (“if you don’t cruise, you don’t bruise”) → suspect maltreatment. You cannot age a bruise by colour.
Specific fractures
POSTERIOR RIB fractures and METAPHYSEAL (bucket-handle) corner fractures; multiple fractures of different ages.
Abusive head trauma
Triad = encephalopathy + subdural haemorrhage + retinal haemorrhages, age 0–5 (Shaken Baby).
NICE CG89
“Consider” vs “suspect” maltreatment — suspect means act/refer.
Investigations
Skeletal survey (± repeat), CT head, ophthalmology, coagulation/FBC — document injuries AND exclude mimics (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta, meningococcaemia).
Management
Make child safe → escalate to senior/named safeguarding lead → refer to social care (± police) → document verbatim + body maps → consider siblings. Child safety overrides confidentiality; refer on suspicion, not proof.
Five types
Physical, NEGLECT (commonest), emotional, sexual, fabricated/induced illness.
What & Why

SUDI is the sudden, unexpected death of an infant (or child) where the cause is not immediately obvious at presentation. It matters because it is the leading category of postneonatal infant death in the UK (~200 deaths/year in England and Wales), because much of it is preventable through safe-sleep advice, and because every such death triggers a statutory multi-agency investigation with a safeguarding dimension. The two things that matter: the modifiable risk factors you can counsel on, and that SUDI is a presentation, not a diagnosis.

The terminology that trips people up: SUDI = the umbrella term used at the point of presentation (sudden, unexpected, before investigation). SIDS (“cot death”) = the diagnosis of exclusion used only after a full investigation (including post-mortem) finds no cause. SUDC = the equivalent term when the child is >12 months.
The Decisive Fork — Explained or Unexplained?

SUDI is a starting point; every case is worked up to sort into one of these:

Explained SUDIUnexplained → SIDS
Found on investigationInfection (sepsis, myocarditis), inborn error of metabolism, congenital cardiac/arrhythmia, trauma (accidental or inflicted)No cause after full work-up + post-mortem
ImplicationDirected management/counselling; possible safeguarding or genetic implicationsRisk-reduction counselling; bereavement support
A proportion of SUDI is inflicted injury/neglect — which is why every SUDI is investigated jointly with a safeguarding lens (not an accusation, a duty).
Epidemiology & the “Triple-Risk” Model
  • Peak age 1–2 months; ~87% occur before 6 months. Rare after 6 months
  • Strong socioeconomic gradient — highest rates in young parents and deprivation (up to ~4× the general rate)
Triple-risk model: SIDS occurs when three things coincide — a vulnerable infant (e.g. prematurity, low birth weight), a critical developmental period (the first months, immature cardiorespiratory/arousal control), and an exogenous stressor (e.g. prone sleeping, overheating, smoke exposure).
Risk Factors
Infant (non-modifiable)
  • Prematurity, low birth weight (<2.5 kg), male sex, multiple birth
Modifiable / environmental (counsel on these)
  • Smoking — the single most strongly linked modifiable factor (in pregnancy + household exposure)
  • Prone or side sleeping — prone increases risk up to ~6-fold
  • Hazardous co-sleeping — especially sofa/armchair (never safe), or bed-sharing when a parent smokes/drinks alcohol/takes drugs, or the baby was premature/low birth weight
  • Overheating / head covering; soft/cluttered sleep surface (pillows, duvets, bumpers, soft toys, sleep pods)
  • Maternal: young age, high parity, late/no antenatal care, drug/alcohol use
Protective: breastfeeding, room-sharing (without bed-sharing) for the first 6 months, immunisation, and dummy/pacifier use (once breastfeeding established).
Prevention — Safe Sleep Advice (Lullaby Trust)
  • Back to sleep — supine for every sleep, day and night (the “Back to Sleep” campaign cut UK SIDS by >80%)
  • Clear, flat cot — firm flat mattress; no pillows, duvets, bumpers, soft toys, or sleep positioners
  • “Feet to foot” — baby’s feet at the foot of the cot so they can’t wriggle under bedding
  • Room-share, don’t bed-share — own sleep space in the parents’ room for the first 6 months
  • Smoke-free pregnancy and household; never sleep with baby on a sofa or armchair
  • Avoid overheating — room 16–20°C, no hat indoors, appropriate layers
  • Breastfeed where possible; keep immunisations up to date
What Happens After a SUDI — the Process
  • Full resuscitation attempted unless clearly inappropriate; the infant is usually taken to the emergency department
  • Joint Agency Response (JAR) is triggered — a coordinated multi-agency investigation (paediatrics, police, coroner, social care)
  • Detailed history and examination, body map, and a structured set of investigations to find a cause and exclude inflicted injury/metabolic disease: bloods, cultures/septic screen, metabolic samples, toxicology, imaging/skeletal survey, and (via the coroner) a post-mortem
  • Coroner referral is mandatory (sudden unexplained death); a home visit / death-scene assessment documents the sleep environment; Child Death Review processes follow
  • Bereavement support for the family throughout — non-negotiable; investigation is explained as routine, not accusatory
Exam Pearls
Terminology
SUDI = presentation (before work-up); SIDS = diagnosis of exclusion after full investigation + post-mortem finds no cause; SUDC if >12 months.
Epidemiology
Peak 1–2 months; ~87% before 6 months.
Triple-risk
Vulnerable infant + critical developmental window + exogenous stressor.
Biggest modifiable
Smoking (pregnancy + household) and prone sleeping (prone ~6× risk).
Co-sleeping
Hazardous on sofa/armchair (never safe), or bed-sharing with smoking/alcohol/drugs/prematurity.
Safe sleep
Back to sleep, clear flat cot, feet-to-foot, room-share not bed-share for 6 months, smoke-free, 16–20°C.
Protective
Breastfeeding, room-sharing, immunisation, dummy.
Process
Every SUDI → Joint Agency Response, coroner referral + post-mortem, safeguarding lens, bereavement support. Always exclude inflicted injury and metabolic disease.
What & Why

This is the legal and ethical scaffolding behind everything you do with children — who can consent, who holds responsibility, and when the state can intervene. Paediatric practice constantly involves people who are legally not yet fully autonomous: a 14-year-old asking for contraception, a parent refusing a life-saving transfusion for their child, a toddler with unexplained bruising. The whole area balances respecting a child’s growing autonomy against the overriding duty to act in the child’s best interests.
