The three things that get confused — separate them cleanly: Gillick competence = can this under-16 consent to this treatment? (capacity). Fraser guidelines = the specific criteria for giving contraception/sexual-health advice to an under-16 without parental knowledge (a specific situation). Children Acts 1989/2004 = the statutory framework for welfare, parental responsibility, and state intervention (the safeguarding system).
The Decisive Fork — How Old Is the Patient?
AgeConsent status
16–17Presumed to have capacity to consent to treatment, like an adult (Family Law Reform Act 1969). But their refusal can be overridden by a person with parental responsibility or a court if refusal risks death/serious harm
Under 16No automatic right; may consent IF Gillick competent for that specific decision
Under 13Cannot legally consent to any sexual activity — any disclosure of sexual activity is an automatic safeguarding referral, regardless of competence
The asymmetry to remember: a competent minor can consent to beneficial treatment, but their refusal of life-saving treatment can be overridden (by a parental-responsibility holder or the court). This is not true for a competent adult. Justified only where refusal would likely lead to death or grave, irreversible harm.
Gillick Competence

Gillick v West Norfolk & Wisbech, House of Lords 1985:

  • A child under 16 can consent to their own medical treatment if they have “sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully understand what is proposed” — its purpose, nature, benefits, risks, alternatives, and consequences
  • Origin: Victoria Gillick challenged guidance letting doctors give contraceptive advice to under-16s without parental knowledge; the Lords ruled that parental rights are not absolute and diminish as the child matures (Lord Scarman’s test = “Gillick competence”)
  • It is decision-specific — a child may be competent for a simple decision but not a complex one; assess each time
  • Consent must be voluntary — not coerced by a partner, parent, or anyone else. Now used broadly across medical, social-care, and safeguarding practice (not just contraception)
Fraser Guidelines
Contraceptive/sexual-health advice to an under-16 without parental consent — ALL five must be satisfied
  • The young person understands the advice
  • They cannot be persuaded to inform their parents (or to let the professional inform them)
  • They are likely to begin or continue having sexual intercourse with or without contraception
  • Without treatment their physical or mental health is likely to suffer
  • Their best interests require the advice/treatment without parental consent
Gillick vs Fraser — the exam distinction: Gillick = the general test of a child’s capacity to consent (Lord Scarman). Fraser = the specific checklist for contraception/sexual health (Lord Fraser). Not interchangeable. Always encourage the young person to involve a parent — but their refusal doesn’t block treatment if the criteria are met.
Parental Responsibility

Children Act 1989:

  • Parental responsibility = the legal rights, duties, and authority a parent has for a child; consent from one holder is usually sufficient
  • Who has it: the mother automatically; the father if married to the mother or named on the birth certificate (from Dec 2003); others via court orders/agreements (step-parents, guardians, local authority under a care order)
  • Exercised for the child’s benefit and yields to the child’s own competent decisions as they mature
The Children Acts — the Safeguarding Statute
Children Act 1989 — the foundation
  • “The child’s welfare is the paramount consideration” (the welfare/paramountcy principle) — the single most quotable line
  • Section 17 — duty on the local authority to safeguard and promote the welfare of “children in need”
  • Section 47 — duty to investigate where there is reasonable cause to suspect a child is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm
  • Defines parental responsibility, care/supervision orders, emergency protection orders, and the “no order” principle
Children Act 2004 & Working Together (2023)
  • Children Act 2004: strengthened multi-agency working after the Victoria Climbié inquiry; created the Children’s Commissioner; embedded “Every Child Matters”
  • Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023): “Safeguarding is everyone’s responsibility” — the multi-agency duty across health, education, police, and social care; replaced the old structure with multi-agency safeguarding partnerships (local authority, integrated care board, police)
Confidentiality & Information Sharing
  • Young people are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults
  • But confidentiality is NOT absolute — it is overridden where a child is at risk of significant harm. You may share information without consent when necessary to protect a child
  • Under-13 disclosing sexual activity → always refer (cannot consent in law)
  • Consider the Sexual Offences Act 2003 context: assess for exploitation, grooming, or a significant age gap even when an under-16 appears “competent”
  • Tell the young person what you’re sharing and why, unless doing so would increase risk
Putting It Together — Worked Logic
A 14-year-old requests the pill and won’t tell her parents → assess Gillick competence (does she understand?) → apply the Fraser criteria (can’t persuade her to tell parents, likely to have sex anyway, health will suffer, best interests) → also screen for safeguarding: age of partner, coercion, exploitation, and check she’s ≥13. If all satisfied → you can prescribe; document each criterion.
Exam Pearls
Age bands
16–17: presumed capacity to consent; under 16: need Gillick competence; under 13: cannot consent to sexual activity → automatic referral.
The asymmetry
A competent minor can CONSENT to treatment, but their REFUSAL of life-saving treatment can be overridden by a parental-responsibility holder or court (unlike a competent adult).
Gillick vs Fraser
Gillick = general capacity to consent (Lord Scarman). Fraser = specific criteria for contraception/sexual health (Lord Fraser). Not interchangeable.
Fraser (all 5)
Understands advice; can’t be persuaded to tell parents; likely to have sex anyway; health will suffer without; best interests require it.
Parental responsibility
Mother automatically; father if married or on birth certificate (post-2003); one holder’s consent usually suffices.
Children Act 1989
Welfare is paramount; s17 “children in need”; s47 “significant harm” investigation.
Children Act 2004 / 2023
2004: post-Climbié, multi-agency cooperation. Working Together (2023): “safeguarding is everyone’s responsibility”; multi-agency partnerships.
Confidentiality
Overridden when a child is at risk of significant harm.
PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seizures:
Overview — paediatric seizures
Seizure disorders specific to childhood — infantile spasms (a serious epileptic encephalopathy) and febrile convulsions (common, usually benign).
The organising principle: age + context. Infantile spasms (~4–8 mo; clusters of flexion spasms, developmental regression, hypsarrhythmia on EEG) is serious; febrile convulsion (6mo–5yr; brief generalised seizure with fever, normal neurology) is common and benign.
ConditionClueManagement
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)clusters of flexion “salaam” spasms, regression; hypsarrhythmiavigabatrin / ACTH; poor prognosis
Febrile convulsion6mo–5yr with fever; simple (brief, generalised) vs complexreassure, antipyretics; small ↑ epilepsy risk if complex
Infantile spasms need urgent EEG and treatment (outcome depends on early control). A febrile convulsion that is focal, prolonged (>15 min) or recurrent within 24h is “complex” → further assessment; always exclude meningitis/encephalitis if unwell.
What & Why

Infantile spasms (West syndrome, now also called infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, IESS) is a severe, age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy. It matters because it’s a paediatric neurological emergency in disguise — the spasms are easily mistaken for colic, reflux, or startle, yet delayed treatment worsens the already-serious developmental outcome — and because it’s defined by a classic examinable triad.

The core concept — the triad (the definition): (1) Epileptic (infantile) spasms — the “salaam attacks”; (2) Hypsarrhythmia on EEG — chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern; (3) Developmental stagnation or regression — loss/plateau of skills.
Epidemiology & Causes
  • Onset typically 4–8 months (peak 3–7 months; almost always <1–2 years); slight male predominance
  • ~70–75% have an identifiable underlying cause (“symptomatic”) — the brain insult matters for prognosis
  • Tuberous sclerosis complex (a classic — and it changes treatment: vigabatrin is especially effective here)
  • Structural/malformations (cortical dysplasia, lissencephaly), hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, congenital infection, Down syndrome, metabolic disorders, genetic (ARX, CDKL5)
  • “Cryptogenic/idiopathic” (no cause found) — better prognosis
Clinical Features
  • “Salaam attacks” — a sudden flexion of the head, trunk, and arms, then extension of the arms (like the “salaam” greeting; also called “jack-knife” spasms)
  • Each spasm is brief (1–2 seconds) but occurs in CLUSTERS — repeated up to ~50 times
  • Typically on waking / drifting off to sleep (a classic timing clue)
  • Developmental regression / loss of skills — the infant stops smiling, loses head control, becomes less interactive (completes the triad)
Key differential — infantile colic: in colic, the baby is distressed DURING the episodes; in infantile spasms, the baby is often distressed/unsettled BETWEEN the spasms (and may cry after a cluster). If in doubt, do an EEG.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Hypsarrhythmia on EEG — chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised slow waves with multifocal spikes (the key test in infantile spasms — obtain an urgent/sleep EEG)
  • EEG — the key test: shows HYPSARRHYTHMIA (chaotic, high-voltage, disorganised slow waves and multifocal spikes). An urgent/sleep EEG is needed
  • MRI brain — to identify a structural cause (malformation, tuberous sclerosis tubers, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy)
  • Investigate the underlying cause: examine skin for tuberous sclerosis signs (ash-leaf macules under Wood’s lamp, shagreen patch), metabolic/genetic work-up, TORCH screen
Management
Refer urgently to paediatric neurology and treat promptly — early control improves developmental outcome.
  • First-line: vigabatrin — a GABAergic anticonvulsant; the drug of choice especially in tuberous sclerosis. Caveat: risk of irreversible peripheral visual field loss (retinal toxicity) — needs monitoring
  • Corticosteroids — high-dose oral prednisolone (or ACTH): used first-line either alone or combined with vigabatrin (UK practice often uses combination hormonal therapy + vigabatrin, e.g. the ICISS trial approach). Hormonal therapy gives faster short-term spasm control; long-term outcomes similar
  • Avoid steroids as first-line in tuberous sclerosis (use vigabatrin) — a classic distinction
  • Refractory: other anticonvulsants, ketogenic diet, or epilepsy surgery (for a focal structural cause)
Prognosis
  • Generally poor — most children have long-term intellectual disability and ongoing epilepsy (may evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome)
  • Depends on the cause: cryptogenic/idiopathic + prompt treatment = better; symptomatic (structural/tuberous sclerosis) = worse
  • Early recognition and treatment improve outcomes — hence the urgency
Exam Pearls
Triad
(1) epileptic spasms + (2) hypsarrhythmia on EEG + (3) developmental regression. Onset ~3–8 months.
Salaam attacks
Sudden flexion of head/trunk/arms then extension, lasting 1–2s, in CLUSTERS (up to ~50), often on waking.
Colic differential
Colic = distressed DURING episodes; infantile spasms = distressed BETWEEN spasms → do an EEG.
Investigations
EEG = HYPSARRHYTHMIA; MRI for structural cause; look for TUBEROUS SCLEROSIS.
Management
URGENT neurology referral → vigabatrin (1st-line, especially tuberous sclerosis) ± high-dose prednisolone/ACTH (hormonal therapy).
Vigabatrin
Irreversible visual field loss (monitor).
Prognosis
Poor: intellectual disability + ongoing epilepsy (may evolve to Lennox-Gastaut); better if cryptogenic + treated early.
What & Why

A febrile convulsion is a seizure triggered by a fever in a young child, WITHOUT any central-nervous-system infection or other identifiable neurological cause. It matters because it’s the commonest seizure disorder of childhood (~3% of children), because it’s usually benign and self-limiting (so the core skill is reassurance and safety-netting), but also because the fever means you must exclude a serious cause — especially meningitis/encephalitis — before attributing the seizure to a simple febrile convulsion.

The core concept: the immature brain has a low seizure threshold, and a rapidly rising temperature (during an intercurrent viral illness) tips it over → a seizure. It requires the fever to be from outside the central nervous system (e.g. viral URTI, tonsillitis, otitis media) — a seizure with fever from meningitis is NOT a febrile convulsion.
Definition & Epidemiology
  • A seizure provoked by fever in an otherwise normal/neurologically healthy child
  • Age 6 months – 5 years (some say up to 6; peak ~18 months)
  • No central-nervous-system infection, no metabolic cause, no history of afebrile seizures (part of the definition)
The Decisive Fork — Simple vs Complex
📷 Image placeholder — Simple (<15 min, generalised, full recovery, no 24h recurrence) vs complex (>15 min, focal, or recurs within 24h) vs febrile status (>30 min)

This classification drives risk and management:

SimpleComplexFebrile status epilepticus
Duration<15 min15–30 min>30 min
TypeGeneralised (tonic-clonic)Focal featuresProlonged/continuous
Recurrence in 24h / same illnessNoMay recur within 24h—
RecoveryComplete, <1 hourSlower/incomplete—
“Complex” = any one of: >15 min, focal features, or recurring within 24h/the same febrile illness.
Clinical Features
  • Occur early in a viral illness, as the temperature rapidly rises
  • Usually brief — last <5 minutes
  • Mostly generalised tonic-clonic
  • A post-ictal period of drowsiness, then complete recovery (in simple febrile convulsion)
  • Often a family history of febrile convulsions
Assessment — Exclude a Serious Cause
  • The priority is to find the source of the fever and EXCLUDE serious infection — especially meningitis/encephalitis (and pneumonia, UTI, etc.)
  • Use the NICE “traffic-light” (green/amber/red) system to risk-stratify the febrile child
  • Have a low threshold for lumbar puncture in the very young (<18 months, especially <12 months) — meningeal signs are hard to elicit, and a febrile seizure can be the presenting feature of meningitis
  • No routine investigations for a typical simple febrile convulsion in a well child with an obvious infection source; investigate as directed by the illness
Management
  • The seizure is usually over by the time of assessment — supportive care, recovery position, and identify/treat the underlying infection
Admit / refer to paediatrics if
  • First febrile convulsion
  • Complex features (>15 min, focal, or recurrent in the same illness)
  • Child <18 months, diagnostic uncertainty, suspected serious infection (e.g. meningitis), or the child appears unwell / incomplete recovery
  • Prolonged seizure (>5 minutes) → rescue benzodiazepine: buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam (as per APLS/status epilepticus pathway)
  • Rescue benzodiazepines at home — only initiated by a specialist, for children with prolonged seizures/high recurrence risk/poor access to care
  • Antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) are for comfort — they do NOT prevent febrile convulsions
  • No routine prophylactic anti-epileptic drugs (benign condition; adverse effects outweigh benefit)
Parental Advice / Prognosis
  • Recurrence: ~1 in 3 (30%) will have another febrile convulsion
  • Very low risk of progressing to epilepsy — after a simple febrile convulsion the risk is only slightly above the general population (~1–2% baseline → ~2–7%); higher after complex febrile convulsion (and with family history of epilepsy, neurodevelopmental abnormality, or complex features)
  • Teach parents seizure first aid: protect from injury, recovery position, time the seizure, don’t restrain or put anything in the mouth, and call an ambulance if the seizure lasts >5 minutes, or there are repeated seizures, breathing difficulty, or the child doesn’t recover
  • Recurrence risk factors: younger age at onset (<18 months), lower fever/shorter fever before seizure, family history
Exam Pearls
What it is
Seizure with fever in a child 6 months–5/6 years, WITHOUT central-nervous-system infection/metabolic cause/prior afebrile seizures. Commonest childhood seizure.
Simple vs complex
Simple (<15 min, generalised, no recurrence in 24h, full recovery) vs Complex (>15 min, OR focal, OR recurs within 24h) vs febrile status (>30 min).
Timing
Occurs early in a viral illness as temperature rises rapidly; usually <5 min, generalised tonic-clonic.
Exclude
Serious infection — especially MENINGITIS; low threshold for lumbar puncture if <18 months.
Admit
First seizure, complex features, <18 months, unwell, or diagnostic uncertainty.
Prolonged
>5 min → buccal midazolam / rectal diazepam. No routine prophylactic anti-epileptic drugs.
Antipyretics
Do NOT prevent febrile convulsions (comfort only).
Advice
~30% recurrence; LOW epilepsy risk (higher after complex febrile convulsion); seizure first aid + call ambulance if >5 min.
PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy:
What & Why

Cerebral palsy is a permanent disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain. It’s the commonest cause of physical disability in childhood (~2–2.5 per 1000 births). The crucial concept: the brain lesion is static but its clinical manifestations evolve as the child grows — so it presents as delayed/abnormal motor milestones, not regression. Good care = early recognition + lifelong MDT support of both the motor disorder and its many comorbidities.

CP is non-progressive — the underlying brain injury doesn’t worsen. If a child shows regression / loss of previously acquired skills, it is NOT cerebral palsy → think a neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder instead.
Definition
  • A disorder of movement and posture due to a non-progressive lesion of the motor pathways in the developing brain
  • Often accompanied by disturbances of sensation, cognition, communication, perception, behaviour, and by epilepsy (the comorbidities)
Aetiology — by Timing
TimingProportionCauses
Antenatal (~80%)CommonestCerebral malformations, congenital infection (TORCH — CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis), vascular events, genetic
Perinatal (~10%)Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) (birth asphyxia), prematurity (→ periventricular leukomalacia, IVH), kernicterus
Postnatal (~10%)Meningitis/encephalitis, head injury (incl. NAI), intracranial haemorrhage, hypoglycaemia
Prematurity is a major risk factor — periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) (white-matter damage) is the classic lesion behind spastic diplegia. Timing shapes the lesion: 1st-trimester insults → malformations; 2nd/3rd-trimester + perinatal → white-matter (PVL) or basal-ganglia injury.
The Decisive Fork — Classification by Motor Type
📷 Image placeholder — GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System) levels I–V — grading functional severity from independent walking (I) to fully dependent/wheelchair (V)

The type reflects where the brain is damaged.

Type~%Lesion siteFeatures
Spastic~70%UMN / motor cortex & pyramidal tractsIncreased tone (velocity-dependent), hyperreflexia, clonus
Dyskinetic~10%Basal ganglia / substantia nigraAthetosis (slow writhing), chorea, dystonia, oro-motor problems (drooling, dysarthria); often kernicterus/HIE
Ataxic~5%CerebellumCerebellar signs — incoordination, intention tremor, ataxic gait, hypotonia
MixedMultipleCombination
🦵 Spastic subtypes
  • Hemiplegia — one side (arm often > leg); may present as early hand preference (<12 months)
  • Diplegia — all four limbs but LEGS >> arms (classic of prematurity/PVL); scissoring gait, tiptoe walking
  • Quadriplegia — all four limbs severely + trunk; most severe, highest rate of seizures, cognitive impairment, feeding problems
🧠 Where & why
  • Spastic = UMN (cortex/pyramidal) → tone up, brisk reflexes
  • Dyskinetic = basal ganglia (kernicterus)
  • Ataxic = cerebellum
Presentation
  • Abnormal motor development — delayed milestones (not sitting by 8 months, not walking by 18 months, no hand function by 1 year)
  • Abnormal tone — hypotonia (floppiness) early, later spasticity/dystonia
  • Abnormal movements/posture — fidgety or paucity of movement, asymmetry
  • Persistence of primitive reflexes (e.g. Moro) beyond normal age; early hand preference (<12 months)
  • Feeding difficulties, faltering growth, delayed speech; gait abnormalities — tiptoe/scissoring (spastic diplegia)
NICE motor red flags: not sitting by 8 months (corrected), not walking by 18 months, hand preference before 1 year, persistent toe-walking.
Associated Comorbidities
CP is never “just” a motor disorder — the comorbidities are heavily tested.
🧩 Neuro / sensory
  • Learning disability (~half); epilepsy (~a third)
  • Visual impairment (squint, cortical visual impairment) + hearing impairment
  • Speech & language / communication difficulties
  • Behavioural/emotional problems, sleep disturbance, chronic pain
🍽️ Systemic / orthopaedic
  • Feeding difficulties, GORD, aspiration, faltering growth (→ may need gastrostomy)
  • Drooling, constipation
  • Orthopaedic: hip subluxation/dislocation, scoliosis, contractures (secondary to spasticity)
Investigations
  • Largely a clinical diagnosis (history + neurological/developmental exam, often confirmed over time as the picture evolves)
  • MRI brain — to investigate the aetiology (PVL, malformation, HIE); recommended if the cause isn’t clear. It won’t accurately date a hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and subtle changes may not appear until ~2 years
  • Assess for comorbidities — vision, hearing, cognition, speech, feeding, growth
  • Consider genetic/metabolic testing if atypical or regression (to exclude a progressive disorder)
Management
MDT approach — no cure; the goal is to maximise function, participation, and quality of life, and manage comorbidities. Team: paediatrician, physiotherapist, OT, SALT, dietitian, orthotist, orthopaedics, neurology, social care, education.
💪 Spasticity management
  • Physiotherapy + occupational therapy (mainstay — maintain range of movement, prevent contractures)
  • Oral diazepam; oral or intrathecal baclofen (muscle relaxant)
  • Botulinum toxin type A injections — for focal spasticity
  • Orthopaedic surgery (tendon release, hip/scoliosis surgery); selective dorsal rhizotomy for selected spastic diplegia
🩺 Other
  • Anticonvulsants for epilepsy; analgesia for pain
  • Manage comorbidities: feeding (SALT, gastrostomy for unsafe swallow), GORD, drooling (anticholinergics), constipation, hip surveillance, vision/hearing support, communication aids
  • Support for family/carers, education, social care
Exam Pearls
What it is
Non-progressive lesion of the developing brain → permanent movement/posture disorder. Static lesion, evolving picture — REGRESSION means it’s NOT CP.
Aetiology
Mostly ANTENATAL (~80%) — malformations, congenital infection (CMV/rubella/toxo); perinatal = HIE/prematurity (PVL → spastic diplegia); postnatal = meningitis/head injury.
Classification
Spastic (~70%, UMN — hemi/di/quadriplegia), dyskinetic (basal ganglia — athetosis, kernicterus), ataxic (cerebellum), mixed.
Spastic diplegia
Legs >> arms (prematurity/PVL), scissoring/tiptoe gait.
Red flags
Delayed motor milestones, abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, HAND PREFERENCE <12 months.
Comorbidities
Learning disability, epilepsy, visual/hearing impairment, speech/feeding difficulties, hip dislocation, scoliosis.
Imaging
MRI to find the cause (won’t date the injury).
Management
MDT; spasticity: physio/OT → baclofen/diazepam → botulinum toxin (focal) → orthopaedic surgery / selective dorsal rhizotomy; + anticonvulsants, analgesia, feeding support.
PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular Disorders:
Overview — Inherited Neuromuscular Disorders

Inherited neuromuscular disorders impair movement by affecting the muscle itself (the muscular dystrophies) or the motor neuron/lower motor unit (spinal muscular atrophy). This topic covers the four you need for finals: the two dystrophinopathies (DMD, Becker), myotonic dystrophy, and spinal muscular atrophy.

ConditionGeneticsHallmark
Duchenne (DMD)X-linked recessive; no dystrophin (Xp21)Boy ~2–5 yrs, proximal weakness, Gower’s sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, huge CK
Becker (BMD)X-linked recessive; partial dystrophin (in-frame)Same picture but milder + later; prominent cardiomyopathy
Myotonic dystrophy (DM1)Autosomal dominant; CTG repeat (DMPK); anticipationMyotonia (can’t release grip) + distal weakness, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction block
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)Autosomal recessive; SMN1 deletion (a motor-neuron disease, NOT a dystrophy)Floppy baby, areflexia, tongue fasciculations, preserved intellect
The key framing: dystrophies are primary muscle diseases (proximal weakness, high CK) — except myotonic dystrophy, which is distal + multisystem. SMA is a lower-motor-neuron disease (anterior horn cell) → floppy, areflexic, with fasciculations.
What & Why

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe, progressive, X-linked recessive muscle-wasting disease caused by a near-total absence of dystrophin — a structural protein anchoring the muscle-cell membrane to the internal cytoskeleton. It’s the commonest and most severe inherited muscular dystrophy of childhood (~1 in 3500–5000 male births), following a relentless, predictable course (walking → wheelchair by ~teens → death from cardiorespiratory failure in the 20s–30s). Early recognition (a boy with proximal weakness + a hugely raised CK) enables surveillance + steroid treatment that meaningfully alter the course.

The core mechanism: the dystrophin gene (Xp21) — the largest human gene. DMD = a frameshift/nonsense mutation → NO functional dystrophin → muscle-membrane fragility → repeated damage → necrosis → replacement by fat and fibrous tissue. Becker’s = an in-frame mutation → some partial dystrophin → milder, later disease. The amount of residual dystrophin determines severity.
The Decisive Fork — Duchenne vs Becker
Duchenne (DMD)Becker (BMD)
MutationFrameshift → NO dystrophinIn-frame → reduced/partial dystrophin
SeveritySevereMilder
Onset~2–5 yearsLater (teens–adulthood)
Wheelchair~by early teensMuch later / may not
Survival20s–30sNear-normal / later
CKVery highHigh
Inheritance
  • X-linked recessive → affects boys; mothers are usually carriers (may have raised CK / mild cardiomyopathy)
  • ~1/3 are new (de novo) mutations (no family history)
  • Genetic counselling for the family; carrier testing
Clinical Features
  • Progressive PROXIMAL muscle weakness from ~2–5 years — delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty climbing stairs/running, waddling gait, difficulty getting up off the floor
  • Gower’s sign — the child “walks his hands up his legs” to stand from squatting/the floor (proximal hip/thigh weakness)
  • Calf pseudohypertrophy — enlarged calves from fat/fibrous replacement of muscle (looks bulky but is weak)
  • ~30% have intellectual impairment / learning difficulty
  • Later: loss of ambulation, contractures, scoliosis, respiratory muscle weakness
Complications
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy — the leading cardiac problem → heart failure, arrhythmias (the most common association)
  • Respiratory failure — progressive respiratory-muscle weakness → nocturnal hypoventilation, recurrent chest infections → the commonest cause of death (with cardiomyopathy)
  • Scoliosis, contractures, osteoporosis (worsened by steroids/immobility); learning/behavioural difficulties (ADHD, autism spectrum)
Investigations
  • Markedly RAISED creatine kinase (CK) — often 10–100× normal; a key screening clue in a boy with weakness
  • Definitive: genetic testing (dystrophin gene deletion/duplication/point mutation — MLPA + sequencing) — the diagnostic standard, replacing muscle biopsy in most cases
  • Muscle biopsy (if genetics inconclusive) — absent dystrophin on immunostaining (DMD) vs reduced (Becker’s)
  • Baseline/surveillance: echocardiography/cardiac MRI + ECG (cardiomyopathy) and lung function/spirometry
Management
No cure — supportive, MDT care; the goal is to preserve function, prevent complications, and prolong survival.
💊 Disease-modifying
  • Corticosteroids (prednisolone / deflazacort) — slow the decline + prolong ambulation (the mainstay; monitor weight gain, osteoporosis, growth suppression). Vamorolone is a newer steroid with a better side-effect profile
  • Mutation-specific: exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides (eteplirsen — exon-51-skippable mutations), ataluren (nonsense mutations), and gene therapy (micro-dystrophin, e.g. delandistrogene moxeparvovec) — evolving, availability varies
🫀 Organ protection & support
  • Cardiac: ACE inhibitors ± beta-blockers for the dilated cardiomyopathy (started early/prophylactically)
  • Respiratory: monitoring, non-invasive ventilation (NIV), cough assist, chest physio, vaccinations
  • MDT: physiotherapy (prevent contractures), OT, orthotics, scoliosis surgery, bone health (vit D/bisphosphonates), nutrition, psychology, education
Exam Pearls
What it is
X-linked recessive; NO dystrophin (Xp21, largest gene); affects BOYS; ~1/3 de novo.
Presentation
~2–5 years: progressive PROXIMAL weakness, delayed walking, falls, waddling gait.
Classic signs
Gower’s sign + calf PSEUDOhypertrophy (fat/fibrosis). ~30% intellectual impairment.
Investigations
CK VERY high (10–100×); definitive = genetic testing (biopsy = absent dystrophin).
The killers
Dilated cardiomyopathy + respiratory failure (death 20s–30s) → surveillance echo + lung function.
Management
Supportive MDT + CORTICOSTEROIDS + ACEi/β-blocker (cardiomyopathy) + NIV (respiratory).
Becker’s
In-frame mutation → partial dystrophin → milder, later onset.
Newer
Exon-skipping (eteplirsen), ataluren (nonsense mutations), gene therapy — mutation-specific.
What & Why

Becker muscular dystrophy is a milder, later-onset X-linked muscle-wasting disease caused by a partial deficiency of dystrophin — the same protein and gene as Duchenne, but with some partially-functional dystrophin preserved. It’s the allelic (same-gene) counterpart of DMD — the two sit on a severity spectrum set by how much functional dystrophin remains. The exam point is the contrast with DMD: same features, but later, slower, milder — with survival often into normal adult life, and cardiomyopathy that can dominate.

The core mechanism: an IN-FRAME mutation in the dystrophin gene (Xp21) → a shortened but partially FUNCTIONAL dystrophin (contrast: DMD = frameshift/out-of-frame → NO functional dystrophin). This is the “reading-frame rule”: mutations that keep the reading frame → milder Becker; those that disrupt it → severe Duchenne. Residual dystrophin sets the severity.
The Decisive Fork — Becker vs Duchenne

Both are X-linked recessive dystrophinopathies in boys with proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, high CK, and cardiomyopathy — the differences are all degree + timing.

Becker (BMD)Duchenne (DMD)
MutationIn-frame → PARTIAL dystrophinFrameshift → NO dystrophin
Dystrophin on biopsyReduced (present but abnormal)Absent
OnsetLater (~5–15 yrs, up to adulthood)~2–5 yrs
ProgressionSlowerRapid
AmbulationOften walking into 40s+Wheelchair by ~early teens
CognitionUsually normal~30% impaired
SurvivalNear-normal / later adulthood20s–30s
CKHighVery high
Rule of thumb: a boy still walking after age 16 = Becker; wheelchair-bound before 13 = Duchenne. Between those, genetic testing settles it.
Clinical Features
  • Progressive PROXIMAL weakness, legs/pelvic girdle first (like DMD but later + milder) — difficulty running, climbing stairs, getting up; later trunk/upper limbs
  • Calf pseudohypertrophy (as in DMD); Gower’s sign may be present; muscle cramps on exertion are relatively characteristic
  • Cardiac involvement can be the FIRST/presenting sign — dilated cardiomyopathy may appear (and be severe) even when skeletal weakness is mild
  • Cognition usually normal (unlike the ~30% impairment in DMD)
Complications
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy — a frequent, important complication, and often the leading cause of death in BMD (skeletal disease being milder, the heart becomes the limiting problem); arrhythmias/conduction defects
  • Respiratory muscle weakness (later/milder than DMD); scoliosis, contractures (later)
  • Female carriers can develop dilated cardiomyopathy (and mildly raised CK) — worth cardiac screening
Investigations & Management
  • Raised CK — high, though generally less extreme than DMD; definitive = genetic testing (identifies the in-frame mutation); biopsy shows reduced/patchy dystrophin (vs absent in DMD)
  • Cardiac surveillance: echocardiography/cardiac MRI + ECG — important + ongoing (cardiomyopathy may outpace skeletal disease)
  • No cure — supportive MDT (physiotherapy, prevent contractures; OT, orthotics, exercise advice)
  • Cardiac protection: ACE inhibitors ± beta-blockers — central to BMD care given the cardiac burden; heart-failure/arrhythmia management
  • Corticosteroids — role less established than in DMD (used more selectively); respiratory monitoring; genetic counselling + cardiac screening of female carriers; dystrophin-restoration therapies being explored
Exam Pearls
What it is
Milder, later allelic partner of Duchenne; SAME gene (dystrophin, Xp21), X-linked recessive, boys.
Genetics
IN-FRAME mutation → PARTIAL (reduced) dystrophin (vs DMD frameshift → NONE) — the “reading-frame rule”; severity ∝ residual dystrophin.
Features
Proximal weakness (legs first) + calf pseudohypertrophy, but LATER onset (~5–15 yrs), SLOWER, MILDER.
Clinical rule
Still walking after 16 → Becker; wheelchair before 13 → Duchenne. Cognition usually normal; near-normal survival.
Cardiac
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a key complication + can be the PRESENTING feature / leading cause of death — surveillance + ACEi/β-blockers. Female carriers → screen the heart.
Investigations
CK high (less than DMD); genetic testing; biopsy = REDUCED dystrophin (vs absent in DMD).
Management
Supportive MDT + cardiac protection; steroids less established than in DMD.
What & Why

Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the commonest adult-onset muscular dystrophy, an autosomal dominant, multisystem disorder caused by a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the DMPK gene. It stands apart in three exam-defining ways: it’s autosomal dominant (not X-linked), it causes myotonia (delayed relaxation) with DISTAL rather than proximal weakness, and it’s multisystem — so the cardiac and respiratory complications (not the weakness) are what kill. It’s the classic example of genetic anticipation.

The core mechanism: an unstable CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the 3′-untranslated region of DMPK (chromosome 19). The expanded repeat produces a toxic RNA that disrupts RNA splicing across many tissues → the multisystem picture. The repeat expands in successive generations → earlier onset + more severe disease = genetic anticipation (normal <~34 repeats; disease >~50; congenital >~1000–2000).
The Decisive Fork — DM1 vs the Other Dystrophies
Myotonic dystrophy (DM1)DMD / BMD
InheritanceAutosomal dominant (CTG repeat, anticipation)X-linked recessive
SexBothBoys
OnsetAdulthood (usually 20s–40s)Childhood
WeaknessDISTAL (hands, foot drop), face, neckProximal
Signature signMYOTONIA (can’t release grip)Gower’s/pseudohypertrophy
SystemicMultisystem (heart, eyes, endocrine, CNS)Mainly muscle + heart
Clinical Features
Myotonia = the hallmark: delayed muscle relaxation after contraction — e.g. can’t quickly let go of a handshake/grip (“grip myotonia”), or a percussion dimple slow to relax; warms up (improves) with repeated use.
💪 Muscle (distal pattern)
  • Distal weakness first (hand grip, foot drop)
  • Facial weakness → long, thin “hatchet”/myopathic face, ptosis, wasted temples/masseters, weak neck flexors
  • Dysphagia, dysarthria (bulbar involvement)
🌐 Multisystem (“not just muscle”)
  • Cataracts (early, posterior subcapsular — a classic clue)
  • Cardiac conduction defects & arrhythmias — heart block, AF; risk of sudden cardiac death
  • Frontal balding (esp. men); insulin resistance/diabetes, testicular atrophy/hypogonadism
  • Excessive daytime sleepiness, mild cognitive impairment; respiratory-muscle weakness; constipation
Congenital DM1
Almost always inherited from an affected MOTHER (very large repeat expansions). Presents at birth with severe hypotonia (“floppy infant”), facial diplegia, feeding/respiratory difficulty, talipes, and later intellectual disability; high neonatal mortality — a key example of anticipation in action.
Investigations
  • Genetic testing — the definitive diagnosis: detects the DMPK CTG-repeat expansion (length roughly correlates with severity/onset)
  • CK — normal or mildly raised (unlike the very high CK of DMD/BMD — a useful distinguishing point)
  • EMG — characteristic “dive-bomber”/myotonic discharges (waxing-waning)
  • ECG (essential — conduction defects; regular surveillance), echocardiography; slit-lamp (cataracts), glucose/HbA1c, sleep/respiratory assessment
Management
  • No cure — supportive, MDT care; the priority is surveillance and treating the systemic complications, especially cardiac
  • Cardiac surveillance is central: annual ECG (± Holter/echo); pacemaker/ICD for significant conduction disease/arrhythmia (reduces sudden death) — the most important intervention
  • Anaesthetic caution — DM1 patients are highly sensitive to anaesthetic agents + opioids (respiratory depression, prolonged apnoea, arrhythmia) → specialist anaesthetic care
  • Myotonia if troublesome → mexiletine (sodium-channel blocker); physiotherapy/OT, orthotics (foot drop); modafinil for hypersomnia; treat diabetes; cataract surgery; respiratory support (NIV); dysphagia/aspiration management
  • Genetic counselling — autosomal dominant, anticipation, congenital-form risk (maternal transmission)
Note: DM2 is a milder, purely adult, proximal variant — CCTG repeat in CNBP/ZNF9 (chromosome 3); no congenital form, no clear anticipation.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest ADULT-onset MD; AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT; CTG repeat in DMPK (chr 19); classic ANTICIPATION.
Hallmark
MYOTONIA (can’t release grip — delayed relaxation); DISTAL weakness + facial (ptosis, hatchet face).
Diagnosis
CK normal/mildly raised (vs very high in DMD/BMD); EMG myotonic “dive-bomber” discharges; genetic (DMPK CTG).
Multisystem
Cataracts, CARDIAC conduction defects/arrhythmias (sudden death), frontal balding, diabetes/insulin resistance, testicular atrophy, hypersomnia.
The killers
Cardiac + respiratory failure → annual ECG surveillance ± pacemaker/ICD.
Congenital DM1
Maternal transmission, floppy infant, facial diplegia, intellectual disability.
Anaesthesia
Sensitivity to opioids/anaesthetics → respiratory depression — flag before surgery.
Management
Supportive MDT + cardiac surveillance; mexiletine for myotonia; genetic counselling.
What & Why

Spinal muscular atrophy is an autosomal recessive motor neuron disease in which the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord degenerate → progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and wasting. Despite being grouped with the dystrophies in revision, it is NOT a muscular dystrophy — the lesion is in the NERVE (anterior horn cell), not the muscle. Until 2016 it was the leading genetic cause of infant death; disease-modifying therapies (nusinersen, gene therapy, risdiplam) + newborn screening have transformed its outlook.

The core mechanism: homozygous loss of the SMN1 gene (survival motor neuron 1, chromosome 5) → deficient SMN protein → degeneration of anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) → the muscle loses its nerve supply → denervation atrophy. A near-identical back-up gene, SMN2, makes ~10–15% functional protein — so MORE SMN2 copies → MILDER disease (explains the type 0–4 spectrum + is the target of every modern therapy).
The Decisive Fork — SMA (nerve) vs Muscular Dystrophy (muscle)
SMAMuscular dystrophy (DMD/BMD)
LesionAnterior horn cell (motor NEURON)The muscle fibre
TypeNeurogenic — NOT a dystrophyMyopathic (dystrophy)
InheritanceAutosomal recessive (SMN1)X-linked recessive (dystrophin)
ReflexesAbsent (areflexia)Reduced late
FasciculationsYes (tongue)No
CKNormal / mildly raisedVery high (DMD)
PseudohypertrophyNoYes (calves)
CognitionNormal~30% impaired (DMD)
Clinical Features — the “Floppy Infant”
  • Symmetrical, PROXIMAL muscle weakness + hypotonia (legs > arms)
  • Areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes — a key sign of the lower motor neuron lesion)
  • Tongue fasciculations (a hallmark of anterior horn cell disease)
  • Weak cry, poor feeding/swallow; “bell-shaped chest” with paradoxical (abdominal) breathing (intercostals weak, diaphragm spared) in severe forms
  • NORMAL cognition + a bright, alert, expressive face — the child is mentally normal, “trapped” in a weak body
  • No pseudohypertrophy; sensation and sphincters intact
The Subtypes (by onset / maximum motor function)
TypeEponymOnsetMax function / course
0—PrenatalNever sits; very severe, death in days–weeks
1Werdnig-Hoffmann<6 monthsNEVER SITS; commonest; historically death <2 yrs (respiratory)
2(intermediate)6–18 monthsSITS but never walks; survival into adulthood
3Kugelberg-Welander>18 monthsWALKS (may lose it); near-normal lifespan

Memory: Type 1 never Sits, Type 2 Sits, Type 3 Stands/walks, Type 4 adult. More SMN2 copies → higher type number → milder.
Investigations
  • Genetic testing — the definitive diagnosis: homozygous SMN1 deletion/mutation; SMN2 copy number (prognostic — guides severity/treatment)
  • CK — normal or mildly raised (helps distinguish from the very high CK of DMD)
  • EMG / nerve conduction — neurogenic pattern (denervation, fibrillations) — largely replaced by genetics
  • Newborn screening — increasingly detects SMA presymptomatically → early treatment (dramatically better outcomes); muscle biopsy (grouped denervation atrophy) rarely needed now
Management
🧬 Disease-modifying (all raise SMN protein)
  • Nusinersen (Spinraza) — intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide modifying SMN2 splicing → more functional SMN
  • Onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) — a one-off IV gene therapy delivering a working SMN1 gene (AAV9 vector); infants
  • Risdiplam — an oral SMN2-splicing modifier
  • Earlier treatment = better outcome (before motor neurons are lost) → the rationale for newborn screening
🩺 Supportive / MDT (still essential)
  • Respiratory (the main threat): NIV, cough assist, chest physio, secretion management, vaccination (respiratory failure = leading cause of death in severe types)
  • Nutrition: feeding support/gastrostomy for bulbar weakness; aspiration prevention
  • Physiotherapy/OT, orthotics, wheelchairs; scoliosis surgery; contracture prevention
  • Genetic counselling (autosomal recessive — carrier testing; 1-in-4 recurrence risk)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Degeneration of ANTERIOR HORN CELLS (motor neuron disease) — NOT a dystrophy. Autosomal recessive SMN1 loss (chr 5); SMN2 copies determine severity (more = milder).
Classic
FLOPPY infant, symmetrical PROXIMAL weakness, AREFLEXIA, TONGUE FASCICULATIONS, but NORMAL cognition + bright alert face.
Distinguishers
CK normal/mildly raised; no pseudohypertrophy (vs DMD).
Types
1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann, <6 mo, never sits, most severe) → 2 (sits) → 3 (Kugelberg-Welander, walks) → 4 (adult).
Diagnosis
Genetic (SMN1 deletion + SMN2 copy number); newborn screening increasingly used.
Death
Respiratory failure = leading cause of death in severe types.
Now treatable
Nusinersen (intrathecal), onasemnogene abeparvovec/Zolgensma (gene therapy), risdiplam (oral) — earlier = better.
PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome:
What & Why

Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a thrombotic microangiopathy defined by a triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. It’s the commonest cause of acute kidney injury in children, classically follows an E. coli O157 gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhoea, and contains two crucial management points: it is largely supportive and you must AVOID antibiotics and anti-motility agents (they increase the risk).

The core mechanism: Shiga toxin (from STEC) → damages vascular endothelium (especially the renal microvasculature) → platelet activation + microthrombi in small vessels (thrombotic microangiopathy). This explains the whole triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (red cells sheared through the clogged microvasculature → fragmented cells / schistocytes); thrombocytopenia (platelets consumed in microthrombi); AKI (microthrombi occlude the glomerular microvasculature).
The Decisive Fork — Typical (STEC) vs Atypical HUS
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film in HUS — schistocytes (fragmented red cells) of microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia; a negative Coombs test (except the Coombs-positive pneumococcal-associated exception)
Typical HUS (STEC-HUS / “D+HUS”)Atypical HUS (aHUS)
Frequency~90%~10%
TriggerShiga toxin — E. coli O157:H7 (or Shigella); preceding bloody diarrhoeaComplement dysregulation (alternative-pathway defects); often no diarrhoea
AgeYoung childrenAny age; often recurrent/familial
TreatmentSupportiveEculizumab (anti-C5)
PrognosisUsually recoversWorse; relapsing
A further form: Streptococcus pneumoniae-associated HUS (~5–15%, e.g. after invasive pneumococcal disease/pneumonia).
Clinical Features
  • Prodrome (STEC-HUS): a diarrhoeal illness — classically BLOODY diarrhoea (haemorrhagic colitis), abdominal pain, vomiting — from contaminated food (undercooked beef, unpasteurised milk), petting farms, person-to-person
  • HUS typically develops ~5–14 days after the diarrhoea starts (in ~10–15% of infected children)
  • Then the triad appears: anaemia (pallor, lethargy, jaundice), thrombocytopenia (bruising, petechiae, bleeding), and AKI — reduced urine output (oliguria/anuria), oedema, hypertension, rising creatinine
  • Extra-renal (severe, ~20%): CNS involvement (irritability, seizures, encephalopathy — worse prognosis), cardiac, pancreatic (glucose)
Investigations
  • FBC + blood film: anaemia with schistocytes (fragmented RBCs), thrombocytopenia; reticulocytosis
  • Haemolysis screen: ↑ LDH, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin, NEGATIVE Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test (non-immune haemolysis)
  • U&E/creatinine (AKI), urinalysis (haematuria/proteinuria); stool culture / PCR for STEC / E. coli O157 + Shiga toxin
  • Coagulation screen NORMAL — the key distinction from DIC (where it is deranged); complement studies / ADAMTS13 if atypical HUS or TTP suspected
The Key Differentials
📷 Image placeholder — HUS vs TTP — HUS renal-dominant, child, follows bloody diarrhoea, ADAMTS13 normal; TTP neuro-dominant, adult, ADAMTS13 <10% → urgent plasma exchange, never platelet transfusion
🩸 TTP
  • The “pentad” (MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI + neurological signs + fever)
  • Caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency; more neuro / less renal than HUS, adults > children
  • Treated with plasma exchange
🧬 DIC
  • HUS has a NORMAL coagulation screen
  • DIC is deranged: ↑PT/APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer — the key discriminator
Management
Mainly SUPPORTIVE — there’s no specific treatment for STEC-HUS; most children recover with supportive care.
  • Careful fluid + electrolyte management (AKI — fluid balance, treat hyperkalaemia/acidosis), BP control, nutrition
  • Blood transfusion for symptomatic anaemia; platelets generally avoided unless active bleeding/surgery (can fuel microthrombi)
  • Dialysis / renal replacement therapy — needed in ~50% (AKI, hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, uraemia)
  • AVOID antibiotics and anti-motility/antidiarrhoeal agents in suspected STEC — they increase Shiga toxin release/absorption and the risk of HUS
  • Atypical (complement-mediated) HUS → eculizumab (anti-C5 monoclonal antibody) — transformed its outcome (also used in severe STEC-HUS with CNS involvement in some centres)
  • Public health: notify (STEC/E. coli O157 is notifiable); source tracing
Prognosis
  • STEC-HUS: acute mortality now <5%; most recover, but ~1/3 have long-term renal sequelae (chronic kidney disease, hypertension, proteinuria) → long-term renal follow-up. CNS involvement worsens outcome
Exam Pearls
Triad
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (a thrombotic microangiopathy).
Cause
Commonest cause of AKI in children; ~90% = STEC (E. coli O157:H7) → Shiga toxin, ~5–14 days after (often BLOODY) diarrhoea.
Bloods
Blood film: SCHISTOCYTES; Coombs NEGATIVE; coagulation screen NORMAL (distinguishes from DIC).
Management
SUPPORTIVE (fluids/electrolytes, transfusion, ~50% need DIALYSIS); AVOID ANTIBIOTICS + anti-motility agents in STEC (↑ HUS risk).
Atypical HUS
Complement dysregulation → ECULIZUMAB.
Differentials
TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency, more neuro, pentad + fever, plasma exchange); DIC (deranged clotting).
Prognosis
Mostly recovers (mortality <5%) but ~1/3 have long-term renal sequelae → follow-up. Notifiable.
PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thrombocytopenic Pur:
What & Why

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder in which antibodies destroy platelets, causing isolated thrombocytopenia with bruising and a petechial/purpuric rash. It’s the commonest cause of acute-onset thrombocytopenia in an otherwise-well child, has a characteristic benign, usually self-limiting course (unlike the sinister mimics — leukaemia, aplastic anaemia), and its management is a key teaching point: most children need only “watchful waiting”, NOT treatment — the decision to treat is driven by BLEEDING, not the platelet number.

The core mechanism: an immune-mediated reduction in platelet count — antibodies against the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex → a type II hypersensitivity reaction → antibody-coated platelets are destroyed by the spleen (± impaired production). In children it’s typically acute and post-viral — often 1–2 weeks after a viral infection (or, less often, vaccination) — a transient immune response, which is why it usually resolves.
The Decisive Fork — Benign ITP or a Sinister Cause?

ITP is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion — the whole assessment is confirming isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child and excluding marrow failure/malignancy.

FeatureReassuring (ITP)Red flag (leukaemia/aplastic anaemia)
Other cell linesNormal Hb & WCC (isolated ↓platelets)Anaemia / abnormal WCC (pancytopenia)
Systemic featuresWellFever, weight loss, bone pain, malaise
ExamNo hepatosplenomegaly / lymphadenopathyLymphadenopathy / hepatosplenomegaly
Blood filmNormal (just few platelets)Blasts / abnormal cells
CourseResponds/resolvesFails to respond
If any red flag is present → bone marrow examination to exclude leukaemia BEFORE giving steroids (steroids could partially treat/mask leukaemia).
Clinical Features
  • Age: classically 2–7 years; often 1–2 weeks after a viral illness
  • Bruising (ecchymoses)
  • Petechial or purpuric rash — non-blanching, often on the legs
  • Bleeding is less common — typically epistaxis or gingival (gum) bleeding; mucosal (“wet purpura” — a marker of higher bleeding risk)
  • The child is otherwise WELL — no systemic upset, no organomegaly (the key contrast with malignancy)
  • Serious bleeding is RARE — intracranial haemorrhage in <0.5% (the feared but uncommon complication)
Investigations
  • FBC → isolated thrombocytopenia — normal haemoglobin and white cell count (this “isolated” pattern is central)
  • Blood film — confirms low platelets (often large/young platelets), excludes blasts, fragments (HUS/TTP), and pseudothrombocytopenia (clumping)
  • Bone marrow examination ONLY if atypical features: lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, failure to respond to treatment, abnormal other cell lines, or before starting steroids if leukaemia is a concern
  • (ITP is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion — no confirmatory test; anti-platelet antibody testing is not routine)
Classification (by duration)
  • Newly diagnosed: <3 months
  • Persistent: 3–12 months
  • Chronic: >12 months (~20–30% of children — more likely in older children/adolescents, insidious onset, girls)
Management
The guiding principle: treat the BLEEDING, not the platelet count. Most children recover spontaneously.
👀 Watchful waiting (first-line for most)
  • For no or only minor bleeding (bruising/petechiae only) — regardless of how low the count is
  • ~80% resolve spontaneously within ~6 months
  • Advice: avoid contact sports and trauma; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin and IM injections; written safety-net; return if significant bleeding
💊 Treat only for significant/mucosal bleeding
  • First-line: oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) — reduce platelet destruction (short course; the mainstay)
  • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) — when a faster rise is needed (active bleeding, before a procedure), or if steroids unsuitable
  • IV anti-D immunoglobulin — an alternative in Rh-positive, non-splenectomised children
  • Platelet transfusion — only for life-threatening bleeding (transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed too — used with IVIG/steroids as rescue, not routinely)
  • Life-threatening bleeding (e.g. intracranial haemorrhage): combination rescue — platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG (± tranexamic acid; emergency splenectomy as last resort)
  • Chronic/refractory ITP (2nd-line): thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim); rituximab; splenectomy (generally deferred/avoided in children given the high spontaneous-resolution rate + infection risk — reserved for chronic, refractory disease, usually age >5)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Autoimmune platelet destruction; antibodies vs glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (type II hypersensitivity); spleen destroys antibody-coated platelets.
In children
Acute, ~1–2 weeks POST-VIRAL (or post-vaccination), age 2–7, usually SELF-LIMITING (~80% resolve within 6 months).
Presentation
Well child + bruising/petechiae/purpura; bleeding (epistaxis/gum) less common; intracranial haemorrhage rare (<0.5%).
Bloods
ISOLATED thrombocytopenia (normal Hb & WCC); blood film normal (excludes blasts/HUS/clumping).
Bone marrow
Only if atypical: lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, other cell lines abnormal, failure to respond, or before steroids if leukaemia possible.
Management
WATCHFUL WAITING for most (treat the bleeding, not the count); avoid contact sports/NSAIDs.
Treat bleeding
1st-line prednisolone or IVIG (IVIG faster); platelets ONLY for life-threatening bleeding (+ steroids + IVIG).
Chronic/refractory
Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag/romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy (avoided in kids).
Key differential
Acute leukaemia (red flags: unwell, other cytopenias, organomegaly, bone pain).
PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndrome (paediat:
What & Why

Nephrotic syndrome is a triad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and oedema, caused by increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier to protein. It matters because it’s the commonest glomerular disorder of childhood, because — crucially, unlike in adults — it’s overwhelmingly minimal change disease (~90%), which is steroid-responsive, so children are treated empirically with steroids WITHOUT a biopsy, and because its complications (infection, thrombosis) can be life-threatening.

The core mechanism: the glomerular filtration barrier — specifically the podocytes and their foot processes — becomes leaky to protein. In minimal change disease, podocyte foot-process effacement (visible only on electron microscopy — the glomeruli look “normal” on light microscopy, hence “minimal change”) → massive protein (mainly albumin) leaks into the urine → proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts into tissues → oedema.
The Triad (+ a common fourth feature)
📷 Image placeholder — Periorbital oedema — the classic first sign of nephrotic syndrome, often mistaken for allergy
FeatureDetail
Heavy proteinuriaNephrotic-range (>3.5 g/day adult; in children >40 mg/m²/hour or a very high urine protein:creatinine ratio); “frothy urine”
Hypoalbuminaemiaserum albumin <25 g/L (albumin lost in urine)
OedemaPeriorbital (classically — puffy eyes in the morning), then peripheral, ascites, scrotal/labial, ± anasarca
(Hyperlipidaemia)Often a fourth feature (liver ↑ lipoprotein synthesis in response to low albumin)
Causes

The paediatric distribution is the key exam point:

  • Minimal change disease (~90% in children) — the dominant cause, steroid-responsive (contrast adults, where membranous is common). Often follows a viral URTI
  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) — more often steroid-resistant; commoner in older children/certain ethnicities
  • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; membranous (rare in kids)
  • Secondary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura, SLE (lupus nephritis), infection (HIV, hepatitis), diabetes — consider if atypical
  • Congenital nephrotic syndrome (<3 months, e.g. NPHS1/nephrin mutations — severe, not steroid-responsive)
Clinical Features
  • Age: classically 2–5 years (minimal change); boys > girls
  • Oedema — periorbital puffiness (often the first sign, mistaken for allergy), then generalised (ascites, peripheral, scrotal); frothy urine
  • Weight gain, reduced urine output; usually normotensive with normal renal function in minimal change (features that suggest otherwise → atypical → biopsy)
  • Atypical features (suggest NOT minimal change → biopsy): hypertension, haematuria, impaired renal function, age <1 or >12 years, or steroid resistance
Investigations
  • Urine dipstick + urine protein:creatinine ratio (uPCR) — heavy proteinuria (3+/4+; nephrotic-range uPCR)
  • Serum albumin (low <25), U&E/creatinine, FBC, lipids
  • Look for a cause/complications: complement (C3/C4), ASO/anti-DNase (post-strep), ANA/anti-dsDNA (lupus), hepatitis/HIV, ± varicella immunity (before steroids)
  • Renal biopsy — NOT routine in typical childhood cases; reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance (the empirical steroid trial IS the “test” in typical minimal change)
Management
Guideline-verified.
  • Corticosteroids (oral prednisolone) — first-line, WITHOUT a biopsy in typical cases: a course of high-dose prednisolone (e.g. ~60 mg/m²/day) then tapering. ~80–90% of minimal change disease responds (“steroid-sensitive”)
  • Supportive: salt and fluid restriction, diuretics (careful — intravascular depletion) for severe oedema, IV albumin for severe symptomatic oedema/hypovolaemia, penicillin prophylaxis (see complications), and treat/prevent complications
  • Steroid-resistant/frequent-relapsing/steroid-dependent → biopsy + second-line agents: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/ciclosporin), levamisole, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab; ACE inhibitors (reduce proteinuria)
Response Terminology
📷 Image placeholder — Steroid-sensitive (~90%, minimal change) vs steroid-resistant (no remission at ~4 weeks → biopsy, often FSGS) vs relapsing/frequently-relapsing/steroid-dependent

Paediatric nephrotic syndrome is classified by steroid response, not biopsy — high-yield:

Steroid-SENSITIVE
  • Remission with steroids (~90% — usually minimal change)
Steroid-RESISTANT
  • No remission after ~4 weeks of steroids → biopsy (often FSGS)
Relapsing / frequently-relapsing / steroid-dependent: relapses on tapering/stopping.
Complications

Driven by urinary protein loss — high-yield:

  • Infection — loss of immunoglobulins + complement (and immunosuppression) → risk of SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS and pneumococcal/encapsulated-organism infection → penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal vaccination; careful with live vaccines on steroids (the “why do nephrotics get infections” point)
  • Thromboembolism (hypercoagulable state) — loss of antithrombin III in urine + haemoconcentration → VTE, renal vein thrombosis, and rarely cerebral sinus thrombosis
  • Hypovolaemia (fluid in tissues not vessels → shock; care with diuretics)
  • Hyperlipidaemia, acute kidney injury, growth impairment/steroid side effects
Exam Pearls
What it is
Heavy PROTEINURIA + HYPOALBUMINAEMIA (<25) + OEDEMA (± hyperlipidaemia). Leaky glomerular barrier (podocyte foot-process effacement).
In children
~90% = MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (steroid-responsive) → treat with STEROIDS WITHOUT a biopsy.
Presentation
Age 2–5, boys > girls; PERIORBITAL oedema first, frothy urine; usually normotensive/normal renal function.
Atypical (→ biopsy)
Hypertension, haematuria, impaired renal function, age <1 or >12, steroid resistance (think FSGS).
Management
Oral PREDNISOLONE (1st-line, no biopsy) + salt/fluid restriction ± diuretics/IV albumin; steroid-resistant/relapsing → biopsy + calcineurin inhibitors/rituximab/ACE inhibitor.
Response classes
Steroid-sensitive (~90%) / steroid-resistant / relapsing/dependent.
Complications
INFECTION (lost immunoglobulins/complement → spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, pneumococcus → penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal vaccine), THROMBOSIS (lost antithrombin III → VTE/renal vein), hypovolaemia, hyperlipidaemia.
Contrast
NEPHRITIC syndrome: haematuria + hypertension + mild proteinuria + acute kidney injury (inflammatory).
PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric):
What & Why

SVT is a narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia originating at or above the atrioventricular node — the commonest significant arrhythmia in children, and the commonest cause of a pathological tachycardia in infancy. It matters because in an infant it can be hard to spot (they can’t report palpitations — they present with poor feeding, irritability, or, if prolonged, heart failure and shock), and because the acute management is a clean, algorithmic, high-yield emergency: vagal → adenosine → shock, gated by whether the child is stable or unstable.

The framing that matters: the whole topic is one flowchart — is the child stable or unstable? Everything downstream (vagal manoeuvres and adenosine vs. immediate synchronised DC cardioversion) hangs on that single assessment. And the first diagnostic step is distinguishing SVT from sinus tachycardia, because they look superficially similar but mean completely different things.
The Decisive Fork — Stable or Unstable?
Stable SVTUnstable SVT (shock/decompensation)
SignsAlert, perfusing, no heart failureHypotension, poor perfusion, altered consciousness, heart failure/shock
Step 1Vagal manoeuvresImmediate synchronised DC cardioversion
Step 2IV adenosineAdenosine only if it doesn’t delay cardioversion / while preparing
PrincipleTry to convert non-invasivelyElectricity first — don’t waste time
SVT vs Sinus Tachycardia — the Essential First Distinction
FeatureSVTSinus tachycardia
RateVery fast: infants often >220, children >180Usually <220 infant / <180 child
Onset/offsetAbrupt (“switch on/off”)Gradual, varies with activity
Rate variabilityFixed, monotonous — doesn’t vary with stimulationBeat-to-beat variability, settles with fluids/rest
P wavesAbsent/abnormal, hidden in QRS/TNormal P waves, normal axis
HistoryNo cause, or known SVTA reason (fever, dehydration, pain, sepsis, blood loss)
QRSNarrow (usually)Narrow
If there’s an obvious cause and the rate varies → treat the cause (it’s sinus tachy), don’t give adenosine.
Mechanism

Most paediatric SVT is atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) using an accessory pathway — the classic being Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) (delta wave + short PR on the resting/post-conversion ECG). AVNRT (re-entry within the atrioventricular node) is more common in older children/adolescents. Both are atrioventricular-node-dependent, which is why node-blocking manoeuvres (vagal, adenosine) work.

Clinical Features
  • Infants: non-specific — poor feeding, irritability, pallor, tachypnoea, sweating, and if prolonged (hours) → heart failure/cardiogenic shock (SVT can be present a long time before it’s noticed)
  • Older children: palpitations, chest discomfort, dizziness, “racing heart”, sometimes syncope
  • ECG: narrow-complex tachycardia, fixed rate, absent/abnormal P waves
Investigations
  • 12-lead ECG — confirm SVT, distinguish from sinus tachy, look for WPW
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring throughout treatment (and record a rhythm strip during adenosine — it’s diagnostic as the rhythm transiently blocks)
  • Assess for the effect (heart failure, perfusion) and reversible contributors (electrolytes, fever, drugs)
  • Echocardiography — assess ventricular function and exclude structural disease (especially if recurrent or in heart failure)
Management — Acute (APLS Algorithm)
Guideline-verified — APLS / Resuscitation Council UK / ERC. Always: ABC, high-flow oxygen, cardiac monitoring, IV/intraosseous access.
If STABLE
  • Vagal manoeuvres first: infants — the “diving reflex” (a bag of iced water / ice pack applied briefly to the face); older children — Valsalva (blow through a syringe / modified Valsalva with leg-raise)
  • If vagal fails → IV/intraosseous adenosine (rapid bolus into a large proximal vein + immediate saline flush): first dose 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg) → 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg) → a further 0.3 mg/kg (max 12 mg) per APLS
  • Warn: brief flushing/chest tightness/“sense of doom”; very short half-life (<10 s)
  • If adenosine fails/recurs: senior + paediatric cardiology; consider amiodarone
If UNSTABLE (shock, hypotension, reduced consciousness, heart failure)
  • Synchronised DC cardioversion without delay: 1 J/kg → 2 J/kg, with sedation/analgesia if time allows
  • Adenosine only if it does not delay cardioversion (e.g. while the defibrillator is charging and IV access is in)
  • Consider amiodarone before a third shock; involve seniors/cardiology/PICU
Long-Term Management
  • Many infants grow out of it; recurrent episodes may need prophylaxis (e.g. beta-blockers, or other antiarrhythmics — avoid atrioventricular-node blockers in known WPW/pre-excitation, where they can be hazardous)
  • Radiofrequency catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is curative — used for recurrent/refractory SVT in older children
  • Teach parents/patient age-appropriate vagal manoeuvres and when to seek help
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest significant arrhythmia in children; narrow-complex, very fast (infants often >220), fixed rate, abrupt onset.
SVT vs sinus tachy
SVT = no cause, fixed rate, abnormal/absent P waves, abrupt; sinus tachy = has a cause, variable rate, normal P waves.
Mechanism
Usually AVRT via accessory pathway (WPW — delta wave, short PR).
Infant presentation
Poor feeding/irritability/pallor → heart failure if prolonged.
Stable
Vagal manoeuvres → adenosine 0.1 → 0.2 (→0.3) mg/kg rapid IV push + flush.
Vagal manoeuvres
Infant = ice/cold water to the face (diving reflex); older child = Valsalva.
Unstable
Shock → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion 1 → 2 J/kg — don’t let adenosine delay it.
Pearls
Record a rhythm strip during adenosine (diagnostic). Definitive cure = catheter ablation; avoid atrioventricular-node blockers in WPW.
PAEDIATRICS__Rickets:
What & Why

Rickets is defective mineralisation of growing bone at the epiphyseal growth plates, producing soft, weak, deformable bones in children. It matters because it is largely preventable and treatable, it is a marker of underlying vitamin D or calcium deficiency (with public-health and safeguarding dimensions), and it is a favourite exam topic for its classic deformities and biochemical fingerprint. The adult equivalent — after the growth plates fuse — is osteomalacia (same process, no bowing deformities).

The framing that matters: rickets is almost always calcium-pathway (calcipenic) — usually vitamin D deficiency — and the biochemistry follows one logic: low vitamin D → low calcium → secondary hyperparathyroidism → PTH drags calcium back toward normal but wastes phosphate in the urine. So the hallmark is low phosphate + high ALP with calcium often near-normal. The rarer, high-yield exception is phosphate-wasting (X-linked hypophosphataemic) rickets, which flips the mechanism.
The Decisive Fork — Calcipenic or Phosphopenic?

This is the organising principle — it is what the biochemistry is for:

Calcipenic (calcium / vitamin D)Phosphopenic (phosphate-wasting)
CauseVitamin D deficiency (commonest), dietary calcium deficiencyX-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (commonest inherited); Fanconi, renal disease
Mechanism↓ vit D → ↓ Ca → ↑ PTH (2° hyperparathyroidism) → phosphate wastingRenal phosphate wasting via ↑ FGF-23
CalciumLow / low-normalNormal
PTHHighNormal (or slightly ↑)
PhosphateLowLow
ALPHighHigh
Causes & Risk Factors
Nutritional (the usual story)
  • Vitamin D deficiency — the usual cause; dietary calcium deficiency
  • Prolonged/exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, unsupplemented formula/cow’s milk
  • Lack of sunlight — darker skin, covering clothing, northern latitudes, institutionalised children
Secondary & inherited causes
  • Malabsorption (coeliac, CF, cholestatic liver disease)
  • Chronic kidney disease (renal rickets — failure of 1-α-hydroxylation)
  • Anticonvulsants (induce vitamin D catabolism)
  • X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets — commonest inherited form; PHEX mutation → ↑ FGF-23 → renal phosphate wasting (normal Ca/PTH, low phosphate)
  • Vitamin D-dependent rickets — type 1 (1-α-hydroxylase defect) / type 2 (receptor defect)
Clinical Features
  • Aching bones and joints; general misery, delayed motor milestones, hypotonia
  • Lower-limb deformity (weight-bearing): genu varum (bow legs) in toddlers → genu valgum (knock knees) in older children — the age-dependent switch is a classic exam point
  • Rachitic rosary — expansion of the costochondral junctions → beading along the chest
  • Craniotabes — soft skull with delayed suture/fontanelle closure and frontal bossing
  • Harrison’s sulcus — horizontal groove along the lower ribcage (diaphragmatic pull on soft ribs)
  • Kyphoscoliosis; wide/swollen wrists and ankles (metaphyseal flaring)
  • Delayed dentition with enamel hypoplasia
  • If calcium falls far enough → hypocalcaemic features: tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures, and (in infants) stridor — occasionally the presenting problem
Investigations
Bloods — the biochemical fingerprint of nutritional rickets
  • ↓ 25-hydroxyvitamin D — the storage form measured to assess status
  • ↓ / low-normal calcium — PTH defends it
  • ↓ phosphate — a key positive finding
  • ↑↑ ALP — raised in all forms of rickets; a sensitive marker of osteoblast activity/healing
  • ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) — the linking mechanism
  • If phosphate is low with normal calcium and normal PTH → think X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets
Imaging — X-ray (classically the wrist): cupping, fraying and splaying of the metaphyses, widened growth plate, osteopenia — the radiological hallmark.
Management
Guideline-verified — NHS/SACN vitamin D guidance; burosumab per NICE (guidance revised April 2025).
  • Nutritional rickets → oral vitamin D (colecalciferol) with adequate dietary calcium. Healing doses are high for weeks-to-months, then a maintenance dose — the mainstay
  • Correct the underlying cause (treat malabsorption, adjust diet, sunlight advice)
  • Monitor ALP and biochemistry to confirm healing
  • Renal rickets / vitamin D-dependent rickets → activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol), because the failing step is 1-α-hydroxylation — plain colecalciferol will not work
  • X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets — historically oral phosphate + activated vitamin D (calcitriol), but this risks nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism. Burosumab (an anti-FGF-23 monoclonal antibody) is now recommended (NICE) for children ≥1 year with radiographic bone disease and outperforms conventional therapy for skeletal outcomes
Prevention — the high-yield UK public-health point
  • UK advice: all breastfed infants and at-risk groups receive vitamin D supplementation (~400 IU / 10 µg daily)
  • Pregnant and breastfeeding women should supplement too (10 µg daily) — consistent with antenatal-care guidance
Exam Pearls
Definition
Defective mineralisation of GROWING bone; osteomalacia is the adult (post-growth-plate) form.
Commonest cause
Vitamin D deficiency — breastfeeding without supplements, dark skin, low sunlight.
Biochemistry (nutritional)
↓ vit D, ↓/low-normal Ca, ↓ phosphate, ↑↑ ALP, ↑ PTH (2° hyperparathyroidism is the linking mechanism).
Deformities
Genu varum (toddlers) → genu valgum (older kids); rachitic rosary, craniotabes/frontal bossing, Harrison’s sulcus.
X-ray wrist
Metaphyseal cupping, fraying, splaying.
Treatment
Oral colecalciferol + calcium; treat the cause. UK prevention = vitamin D supplements for infants.
The flipped exception
Phosphate LOW, Calcium & PTH NORMAL → X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (↑ FGF-23) → now treatable with burosumab.
Activated vitamin D
Renal / vitamin D-dependent rickets → give activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol), NOT plain colecalciferol.
Watch
Severe hypocalcaemia → seizures/tetany/stridor may be the presentation.
PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndromes:
What & Why

Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited (single-gene) cause of learning disability and the commonest known monogenic cause of autism, caused by a CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. It has a recognisable phenotype (long face, large ears, macro-orchidism + a behavioural picture), is a trinucleotide-repeat disorder showing anticipation, and has important carrier (premutation) consequences in the wider family.

The core mechanism: an unstable CGG repeat expansion in the 5′-UTR of FMR1 (Xq27.3). A full mutation (>200 repeats) → hypermethylation → the gene is silenced → loss of FMRP (needed for synaptic development) → intellectual disability. The repeat expands across generations (anticipation), and — a key quirk — a premutation only expands to a full mutation when transmitted through the MOTHER.
The Repeat-Size Spectrum

CGG repeatsCategoryEffect
~5–44Normal—
45–54Intermediate (“grey zone”)Usually asymptomatic
55–200Premutation (carrier)Usually normal intellect, but risk of FXTAS (males) + FXPOI (females); can expand to full mutation via the mother

Inheritance
  • X-linked (FMR1 on the X) — often described as X-linked dominant with reduced penetrance/variable expressivity (unusual because of X-inactivation + anticipation)
  • Males more severely affected (one X → no back-up); females variably/more mildly affected (a normal second X partially compensates — ~50% have some learning disability)
  • Anticipation: the repeat expands each generation → earlier/more severe disease. Full-mutation expansion occurs only through maternal transmission
Clinical Features
🧠 Cognitive / behavioural (the core)
  • Intellectual disability / developmental delay (moderate–severe in males, milder in females) — often language delay first
  • Autism spectrum features (commonest monogenic cause of autism); social anxiety, poor eye contact, hand-flapping/biting
  • ADHD, hyperactivity, impulsivity, sensory hypersensitivity, anxiety; hypotonia in infancy
🧬 Physical (clearer with age)
  • Long, narrow face with a prominent forehead + jaw (prognathism)
  • Large, protruding ears
  • Macro-orchidism (large testes) — after puberty (a specific male hallmark)
  • High-arched palate, joint hypermobility/hyperextensible fingers, flat feet, mitral valve prolapse (MVP), macrocephaly
Premutation Carrier Disorders
Carriers aren’t “unaffected”: FXTAS (Fragile X-associated Tremor/Ataxia Syndrome) — older male premutation carriers (>50 yrs) → intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, cognitive decline/parkinsonism (often misdiagnosed as Parkinson’s/essential tremor). FXPOI (Fragile X-associated Primary Ovarian Insufficiency) — ~20% of female premutation carriers → premature ovarian failure/early menopause (test FMR1 in unexplained POI).
Investigations & Management
  • Genetic testing — definitive: FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis (PCR + Southern blot for methylation) — repeat number + methylation status. Test in unexplained developmental delay/intellectual disability, autism, or a suggestive phenotype/family history
  • No cure — MDT supportive care: special educational support, speech and language therapy, OT, behavioural/psychological support
  • Treat comorbidities: ADHD (stimulants), anxiety (SSRIs), aggression/irritability, sleep problems, seizures (epilepsy ~10–20%); manage vision/hearing, connective-tissue (MVP, joints), recurrent otitis media
  • Genetic counselling + cascade testing — inheritance, anticipation, carrier/premutation implications (FXTAS/FXPOI), reproductive options
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest INHERITED cause of learning disability + commonest monogenic cause of AUTISM.
Genetics
CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 (Xq27.3); >200 = full mutation → methylation silences FMR1 → loss of FMRP. Trinucleotide-repeat disorder with ANTICIPATION.
Inheritance
X-linked; MALES more severely affected; females variable/milder. Full-mutation expansion only via MATERNAL transmission.
Phenotype
Learning disability + autism/ADHD/anxiety + LONG FACE, large protruding EARS, prominent jaw, MACRO-ORCHIDISM (post-puberty); joint hypermobility.
Premutation
55–200 repeats: FXTAS (older males — tremor/ataxia) + FXPOI (females — premature ovarian insufficiency).
Diagnosis/Rx
FMR1 CGG-repeat genetic testing; MDT supportive + genetic counselling.
What & Why

Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by loss of function of PATERNALLY-inherited genes on chromosome 15q11–q13, producing an evolving phenotype of neonatal hypotonia → later insatiable hyperphagia and obesity, with hypogonadism, short stature, learning disability, and behavioural problems. It’s the classic teaching example of genomic imprinting (the same region causes Angelman syndrome depending on parent of origin), and the hyperphagia-driven obesity is the main cause of morbidity/mortality.

Genomic imprinting: some genes are expressed only from the paternal copy (the maternal copy switched off by methylation). At 15q11–q13, PWS results when the paternally-expressed genes are absent/silenced → no expression from either copy. Most of the picture (hyperphagia, temperature instability, high pain threshold, hormone deficiencies) reflects hypothalamic dysfunction.
Genetics — the Three Mechanisms
  • Paternal deletion of 15q11–q13 (~65–75%) — the paternal region is deleted → no paternal expression (the commonest)
  • Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) (~20–30%) — both copies of chromosome 15 come from the mother → no paternal expression
  • Imprinting defect (~1–3%) — the imprinting centre fails to activate the paternal genes
  • Diagnosis: DNA methylation analysis — detects all three mechanisms + distinguishes PWS from Angelman
The Imprinting Contrast — Prader-Willi vs Angelman
