Memory: “Prader-Willi = Paternal problem”; Angelman = “hAppy” child, mAternal (UBE3A).
Clinical Features — Evolving with Age
👶 Infancy (Phase 1)
  • Severe central hypotonia (“floppy infant”) with a weak cry
  • Poor suck/feeding difficulty → FAILURE TO THRIVE (counterintuitively — they can’t feed well early)
  • Reduced fetal movements, lethargy
🍔 Later childhood (Phase 2)
  • HYPERPHAGIA — insatiable appetite / lack of satiety → food-seeking → OBESITY (the central problem + main cause of morbidity/mortality: type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea, cardiorespiratory disease)
  • Short stature (GH deficiency), small hands/feet; hypogonadism/hypogenitalism (cryptorchidism, delayed puberty, infertility)
  • Mild–moderate learning disability; behavioural problems (tantrums, OCD traits, skin-picking, stubbornness)

Characteristic facies: narrow bifrontal diameter, almond-shaped eyes, thin upper lip, down-turned mouth. Also hypopigmentation (deletion cases), scoliosis, sleep disturbance, high pain threshold, temperature instability.

Investigations & Management
  • DNA methylation analysis of 15q11–q13 — first-line/definitive (detects >99% across all mechanisms + separates PWS from Angelman); FISH/microarray (deletion), UPD studies define the mechanism (recurrence-risk); assess endocrine axis, growth, sleep study (OSA)
  • Strict dietary control / supervised eating environment — the cornerstone: control access to food, structured low-calorie diet, exercise — to prevent life-threatening obesity
  • Growth hormone therapy — improves height, body composition, motor function (started early childhood); sex hormone replacement (puberty, bone); treat hypothyroidism/adrenal insufficiency
  • MDT: dietitian, endocrinology, physiotherapy, SALT, psychology/behavioural support, education; treat OSA, scoliosis. Genetic counselling (recurrence varies by mechanism)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Loss of PATERNALLY-expressed genes at 15q11–q13 (paternal deletion ~70%, maternal UPD ~25%, imprinting defect). Classic genomic IMPRINTING disorder.
Two phases
Infancy = HYPOTONIA + poor feeding/FAILURE TO THRIVE → childhood = HYPERPHAGIA/insatiable appetite → OBESITY.
Plus
Short stature, hypogonadism/genital hypoplasia, learning disability, behavioural problems (tantrums, skin-picking), characteristic facies.
Mortality
Obesity + complications (type 2 diabetes, OSA) = main cause of morbidity/mortality.
Angelman contrast
Same locus, opposite parent = ANGELMAN (maternal UBE3A loss → severe LD, ataxic gait, seizures, happy/laughing). “Prader = Paternal; Angelman = hAppy/mAternal.”
Diagnosis/Rx
DNA methylation analysis (distinguishes from Angelman). Strict dietary control (cornerstone) + growth hormone + sex hormones + MDT.
What & Why

Noonan syndrome is a common autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused by overactivation of the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway (a “RASopathy”), producing short stature, characteristic facial features, congenital heart disease (classically pulmonary stenosis), a webbed neck, and a bleeding tendency. It’s often taught as “the male version of Turner syndrome” — yet is a completely different disorder: autosomal dominant, both sexes, NORMAL karyotype, and RIGHT-sided (pulmonary) heart disease.

The core mechanism: germline mutations activating the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway (controls cell growth/differentiation). Commonest gene is PTPN11 (~50%); others include SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS. Because it’s a developmental signalling pathway, effects are multisystem.
The Decisive Fork — Noonan vs Turner

One-liner: same “webbed neck + short stature” look, but Noonan = autosomal dominant, both sexes, NORMAL karyotype, PULMONARY stenosis; Turner = 45,X, females, coarctation/bicuspid valve.
Clinical Features
👦 Craniofacial / skeletal
  • Broad forehead, hypertelorism (wide-spaced eyes), down-slanting palpebral fissures, ptosis, low-set posteriorly-rotated ears, high-arched palate, short/webbed neck
  • Short stature; pectus excavatum (lower)/carinatum (upper), cubitus valgus, scoliosis; cryptorchidism (males); lymphoedema (fetal cystic hygroma)
❤️ Cardiac + haematological
  • Pulmonary (valve) stenosis — commonest/classic (~50%; may be dysplastic)
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM); also ASD (secundum), VSD, PDA
  • Bleeding tendency / coagulation defects (factor deficiencies, platelet dysfunction) — check clotting before surgery
  • Increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (JMML) (RASopathy → oncogenic pathway)

Variable/usually mild learning difficulties; feeding problems in infancy; hearing loss, lymphatic problems.

Investigations & Management
  • Clinical diagnosis (recognisable phenotype), confirmed by genetic testing (RASopathy gene panel — PTPN11, SOS1, RAF1); karyotype is NORMAL (distinguishes from Turner)
  • Echocardiography + ECG (pulmonary stenosis, HCM) — essential; coagulation screen (bleeding diathesis), FBC; growth/hearing/vision/developmental assessment
  • MDT supportive care — manage pulmonary stenosis (balloon valvuloplasty/surgery) + HCM; growth hormone for short stature; correct cryptorchidism; developmental/educational support
  • Bleeding precautions — coagulation assessment before any surgery/dental work; genetic counselling (autosomal dominant — 50% transmission; many de novo)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Autosomal dominant RASopathy (RAS-MAPK; PTPN11 ~50%); NORMAL karyotype; BOTH sexes.
Turner contrast
“Male version of Turner’s” — but AD, both sexes, normal karyotype, and PULMONARY (right-sided) heart disease (vs Turner’s 45,X, females, coarctation/bicuspid = left-sided).
Features
Short stature, webbed neck, pectus deformity, hypertelorism/ptosis/down-slanting fissures, low-set ears.
Cardiac
PULMONARY STENOSIS (commonest) + hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Bleeding
Bleeding tendency → check clotting before surgery. Cryptorchidism (males); usually normal/mild LD; ↑ risk of JMML.
Diagnosis/Rx
Clinical + genetic (RASopathy panel); normal karyotype; echo essential. MDT + growth hormone + cardiac management + bleeding precautions + genetic counselling.
What & Why

Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23 (including the elastin gene, ELN), producing cardiovascular disease (classically supravalvular aortic stenosis), a characteristic “elfin” face, infantile hypercalcaemia, mild learning disability, and an unusually friendly, over-social (“cocktail party”) personality. The cardiovascular lesions (elastin-arteriopathy) are progressive and can be life-threatening, needing lifelong surveillance.

The core mechanism: a contiguous-gene microdeletion at 7q11.23 removes one copy of ~26–28 genes. Haploinsufficiency of the elastin gene (ELN) → deficient elastin → weak, narrowed elastic arteries → the arteriopathy (supravalvular aortic stenosis, arterial stenoses, hypertension). Neighbouring genes (e.g. GTF2I) account for the neurocognitive profile. Usually de novo (sporadic).
Clinical Features
❤️ Cardiovascular (elastin arteriopathy)
  • Supravalvular aortic stenosis (SVAS) — classic/commonest (~75%)
  • Peripheral/branch pulmonary artery stenosis, renal artery stenosis (→ hypertension), other arterial stenoses
  • Systemic hypertension; the arteriopathy is PROGRESSIVE → lifelong cardiac surveillance
  • Risk of sudden death (coronary ostial stenosis, especially with anaesthesia)
🧝 Facies + metabolic + behaviour
  • “Elfin facies”: broad forehead, periorbital fullness, stellate (star-like) iris, short upturned nose, long philtrum, full lips/wide mouth
  • Transient infantile hypercalcaemia (irritability, feeding difficulty, constipation, failure to thrive); hypothyroidism; later glucose intolerance
  • Mild–moderate learning disability — strong verbal/social but weak VISUOSPATIAL skills; overly friendly “cocktail-party personality”; hyperacusis

Also: connective-tissue laxity (joints, soft skin, hernias), constipation, renal/urinary anomalies, dental anomalies.

Investigations & Management
  • Genetic testing — confirmatory: FISH or chromosomal microarray showing the 7q11.23 (ELN) deletion
  • Echocardiography (± cardiac imaging) for SVAS/arterial stenoses — regular cardiovascular surveillance (progressive); serum calcium (hypercalcaemia, esp. infancy), thyroid function, glucose; BP monitoring, renal ultrasound
  • MDT supportive care — manage SVAS/arterial stenoses (surgery if severe), treat hypertension; cautious anaesthesia (arrhythmia/sudden-death risk); lifelong cardiology follow-up
  • Hypercalcaemia: avoid vitamin D and calcium supplementation; low-calcium diet if needed; educational/behavioural support, SALT, psychology; treat hypothyroidism; genetic counselling (usually de novo; autosomal dominant if inherited)
Exam Pearls
What it is
7q11.23 microdeletion including the ELASTIN (ELN) gene (usually de novo; contiguous-gene syndrome).
Cardiac
Elastin deficiency → arteriopathy → SUPRAVALVULAR AORTIC STENOSIS (classic) + arterial/renal stenoses + hypertension (progressive → lifelong surveillance).
Metabolic
Transient infantile HYPERCALCAEMIA → avoid vitamin D/calcium supplements.
Personality
Overly FRIENDLY/hypersocial “COCKTAIL-PARTY personality”; mild-moderate LD with strong verbal but weak VISUOSPATIAL skills; hyperacusis.
Facies
“Elfin”: broad forehead, periorbital fullness, STELLATE IRIS, long philtrum, full lips, wide mouth.
Safety
Sudden-death risk (coronary ostial stenosis) — cautious anaesthesia.
Diagnosis/Rx
FISH/microarray for 7q11.23 (ELN) deletion; echo + serum calcium. MDT + cardiac surveillance + avoid Ca/vit D + educational support.
What & Why

Cri du Chat (“cry of the cat”) syndrome is caused by loss of the short (p) arm of chromosome 5 (5p−), named for its most distinctive feature: a high-pitched, cat-like cry in infancy. It’s the commonest deletion (contiguous-gene) syndrome — the classic triad is cat-like cry + microcephaly + severe learning disability — illustrating that losing a chunk of a chromosome (a deletion) causes a distinct multisystem syndrome.

The core mechanism: a partial (or complete) deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−) — usually a de novo terminal deletion (~80–90%), most often paternal origin; ~10–15% from an unbalanced parental translocation. The cry maps to 5p15.3 and other features to 5p15.2 — and the size of the deletion determines severity.
Clinical Features
  • High-pitched, monotonous, “cat-like” cry — due to laryngeal (small/floppy larynx) + neurological abnormalities; tends to fade with age (a diagnostic clue mainly in infancy)
  • Microcephaly + a characteristic round “moon” face (in infancy)
  • Craniofacial: hypertelorism (wide-spaced eyes), micrognathia (small jaw), epicanthic folds, down-slanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears
  • Feeding difficulties + poor weight gain / failure to thrive, with hypotonia in infancy (poor suck/swallow)
  • Severe psychomotor + intellectual disability, developmental delay, marked speech/language delay
  • Less frequent: congenital heart defects, renal anomalies, scoliosis, recurrent respiratory infections (a major cause of infant death), behavioural problems; the facial features + cry evolve/coarsen with age
Investigations & Management
  • Karyotype — confirmatory (visualises the 5p deletion); FISH / chromosomal microarray for doubtful/small deletions (defines size/breakpoints); echocardiography, renal ultrasound for malformations
  • No specific therapy — MDT supportive care; early rehabilitative + educational intervention improves outcomes (physiotherapy, SALT, OT, special education)
  • Feeding support (may need NG/gastrostomy), treat recurrent chest infections, manage cardiac/renal anomalies, behavioural support
  • Genetic counselling — usually de novo (low recurrence), but parental karyotyping is needed to exclude a balanced translocation carrier (higher recurrence risk); survival into adulthood common with support
Exam Pearls
What it is
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−); commonest deletion syndrome; usually de novo.
Signature
High-pitched, CAT-LIKE CRY in infancy (laryngeal/neurological; fades with age).
Features
MICROCEPHALY + round “moon” face, HYPERTELORISM, epicanthic folds, MICROGNATHIA, low-set ears; feeding difficulty/failure to thrive; hypotonia; SEVERE intellectual disability + speech delay.
Severity
Deletion SIZE determines severity (5p15.3 = cry; 5p15.2 = other features).
Diagnosis/Rx
KARYOTYPE (± FISH/microarray). Supportive MDT + early intervention; genetic counselling (check parental karyotype for translocation).
What & Why

Pierre Robin sequence is a triad of a small lower jaw (micrognathia), a tongue that falls backwards (glossoptosis), and upper-airway obstruction, usually with a U-shaped cleft palate. It’s a neonatal AIRWAY EMERGENCY — the backward-displaced tongue can obstruct breathing from the first hours of life — and it’s a “sequence” (a cascade of malformations from one initiating defect). It’s also a marker for underlying syndromes (especially Stickler syndrome and 22q11 deletion).

Why it’s a “SEQUENCE”, not a syndrome: a sequence = a chain of malformations from a single initiating event. Here: the primary defect is mandibular hypoplasia (micrognathia) early in gestation → the small jaw forces the tongue up + back (glossoptosis) → the elevated tongue blocks the palatal shelves from fusing → cleft palate + airway obstruction. One cause (small jaw) → everything else follows (why the cleft is typically a wide U-shape).
The Triad (+ Cleft Palate)
FeatureDetail
Micrognathia (small/receding mandible)The initiating defect
Glossoptosis (posterior/downward tongue displacement)Obstructs the airway
Airway obstructionThe core danger — tongue-base obstruction
Cleft palate (~90%; classically U-shaped)Frequent but not part of the diagnostic triad
Isolated vs Syndromic
  • Isolated (non-syndromic) PRS — occurs alone (often the more airway-severe group)
  • Syndromic PRS (~half of cases) — part of a wider syndrome. The commonest association is STICKLER syndrome (collagen disorder → myopia/retinal detachment, hearing loss, joint problems); also 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge), Treacher Collins, fetal alcohol syndrome
  • All PRS infants need assessment for an underlying syndrome (genetics, ophthalmology for Stickler, echo for cardiac defects — ~20% have CHD)
Clinical Features / Complications & Investigations
  • Airway obstruction / respiratory distress from birth (stridor, retractions, desaturation, apnoea, OSA) — can be life-threatening in the first hours
  • Feeding difficulties — poor suck/swallow, worsened by the cleft palate → aspiration and failure to thrive; recurrent otitis media/hearing issues
  • Clinical diagnosis (the triad); may be picked up antenatally (micrognathia on USS/MRI)
  • Airway assessment: nasoendoscopy/bronchoscopy (site of obstruction), polysomnography (sleep study); screen for syndromes (genetics, ophthalmology for Stickler, echo, hearing); feeding/swallow assessment
Management
🫁 Airway (stepwise, conservative first)
  • PRONE (or lateral) positioning — first-line — gravity pulls the tongue forward, opening the airway (many need nothing more)
  • Nasopharyngeal airway if positioning insufficient; CPAP / non-invasive ventilation; rarely intubation (difficult airway)
  • Surgical (if severe): tongue-lip adhesion (glossopexy), mandibular distraction osteogenesis, or tracheostomy (last resort)
🍼 Feeding + longer-term
  • Specialised feeding techniques/positioning, cleft feeding devices; NG tube or gastrostomy if aspiration/failure to thrive
  • Cleft palate repair (later, ~6–12 months); the jaw often grows/“catches up” with age, improving the airway
  • MDT: neonatology, ENT, plastics/maxillofacial, SALT, genetics, ophthalmology
Exam Pearls
What it is
A SEQUENCE (one defect → cascade): micrognathia → glossoptosis → airway obstruction (+ U-shaped cleft palate ~90%).
Mechanism
Small jaw pushes tongue up/back → tongue blocks palatal shelf fusion → cleft palate + airway obstruction.
Danger
Neonatal AIRWAY EMERGENCY + feeding difficulties/aspiration/failure to thrive.
Syndromic
~Half are syndromic — commonest = STICKLER syndrome (screen ophthalmology); also 22q11/DiGeorge. ~20% have CHD.
Airway Rx
PRONE positioning first (tongue falls forward) → nasopharyngeal airway → CPAP → surgery (tongue-lip adhesion, mandibular distraction, tracheostomy).
Longer-term
Feeding support (± NG/gastrostomy); cleft palate repair later; jaw catch-up growth improves airway with age. Diagnosis clinical; nasoendoscopy + sleep study + syndrome screen.
What & Why

Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome disorder in males caused by ≥1 extra X chromosome (usually 47,XXY), producing small testes, hypogonadism, infertility, tall stature, and gynaecomastia. It’s the commonest sex-chromosome disorder AND the commonest genetic cause of male hypogonadism and infertility, is frequently underdiagnosed (often only picked up at puberty for delayed development, or in adulthood at an infertility clinic), and — like Turner’s — produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (low sex hormone, high FSH/LH), making it the natural male counterpart to Turner syndrome.

The core mechanism: an extra X chromosome (47,XXY) from meiotic non-disjunction (either parent). The extra X causes primary testicular failure — small, fibrotic testes (hyalinised seminiferous tubules) → low testosterone + impaired spermatogenesis. Low testosterone → loss of negative feedback → HIGH FSH and LH = hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (analogous to Turner’s, but male).

Clinical Features
👶 Neonate / childhood
  • Usually normal appearance at birth; may have cryptorchidism, micropenis, hypospadias
  • Childhood often normal; may have learning/language difficulties, behavioural problems (a reason to suspect it in a boy with developmental concerns)
🧑 Puberty / adolescence (classic)
  • Small, firm testes (a key sign — testes fail to grow despite puberty)
  • Delayed/incomplete puberty, incomplete virilisation (reduced facial/body hair, poor muscle development)
  • Gynaecomastia (~50%)
  • Tall stature with a eunuchoid habitus (long limbs — from delayed epiphyseal fusion due to low testosterone), reduced muscle bulk
🧔 Adults
  • Infertility (azoospermia/oligospermia — the majority are subfertile; often diagnosed here)
  • Androgen deficiency: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, low energy, osteoporosis; small testes/penis, sparse body hair
  • Increased risk of: breast cancer (from gynaecomastia — much higher than other men), osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome/type 2 diabetes, venous thromboembolism (VTE), autoimmune disease, mediastinal germ cell tumours
Investigations
  • Karyotype — the definitive diagnostic test (47,XXY; if mosaicism suspected, karyotype more cells / buccal mucosa)
  • Hormone profile: low testosterone; HIGH FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism); ↑ SHBG; relatively ↑ oestradiol
  • Semen analysis (azoospermia/oligospermia); bone density (osteoporosis), metabolic screen
Management
  • Testosterone replacement therapy — the mainstay: induces/maintains virilisation + secondary sexual characteristics, improves muscle/bone, libido, energy, mood. Does NOT restore fertility (started around puberty)
  • Fertility: most are infertile, but sperm retrieval (micro-TESE) + ICSI can achieve biological fatherhood in some — ideally discussed before/early in testosterone therapy (exogenous testosterone suppresses any remaining spermatogenesis)
  • Gynaecomastia management (surgery if psychosocial impact); osteoporosis prevention/treatment, metabolic screening, breast awareness
  • Educational/speech/behavioural + psychological support; genetic counselling
Exam Pearls
What it is
47,XXY (extra X); commonest sex-chromosome disorder + commonest cause of male hypogonadism/infertility. Non-disjunction.
Endocrine
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: LOW testosterone, HIGH FSH/LH (small firm testes = primary testicular failure).
Features
TALL stature (eunuchoid, long limbs), small firm testes, GYNAECOMASTIA (~50%), delayed/incomplete puberty, reduced facial/body hair, INFERTILITY (azoospermia).
Presentation
Often diagnosed at puberty (delayed development) or in adulthood (infertility clinic); childhood learning/behavioural difficulties.
Increased risk
Breast cancer, osteoporosis, VTE, metabolic syndrome/type 2 diabetes.
Turner counterpart
Both hypergonadotropic hypogonadism; extra X/tall vs missing X/short.
Diagnosis/Rx
KARYOTYPE (47,XXY); FSH/LH high, testosterone low. TESTOSTERONE replacement (doesn’t restore fertility) + micro-TESE/ICSI for fertility + osteoporosis/metabolic care + genetic counselling.
